title: Documentation for assets, ostra-agents, ostra-code, ostra-core, ostra-engine, ostra-exec-harness, ostra-exec-native, ostra-mcp, ostra-notify, ostra-policy, ostra-providers, ostra-sandbox, ostra-server, ostra-store, ostra-tools, ostra-workspace, web

architecture.overview: Ostra is a local engineering pipeline. A developer runs it as one `ostra` process, built by ostra-server, and uses it from a browser console. The React console (web) sends every action as HTTP/JSON under `/api` to the axum router on 127.0.0.1:7878. It receives live updates on one WebSocket at `/ws`. The server passes each session action to the workspace's `Engine` (ostra-engine). The engine appends `SessionEvent` rows to `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db` (ostra-store), folds them into a `SessionState`, and plans the next steps. It runs each agent execution in one of two executors. The native executor (ostra-exec-native) runs the agent loop in the process, calls the Anthropic or OpenAI API through ostra-providers, runs tools through ostra-tools, and checks each tool call with ostra-policy. The harness executor (ostra-exec-harness) starts Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, or Antigravity in a PTY inside the ostra-sandbox sandbox, and that CLI's hooks and MCP calls come back through the `ostra hook` and `ostra mcp-stdio` subprocesses to `/internal/policy` and `/internal/mcp`. The server also owns the machine-wide `registry.db`, workspace MCP server connections (ostra-mcp), language servers (ostra-code), and Web Push delivery (ostra-notify). The libraries ostra-core (shared types), ostra-agents and assets (prompts compiled into the binary), and ostra-workspace (workspace runtime and settings) run inside the same process.

components.name: web console
components.role: React 19 single-page app, embedded in the `ostra` binary from `web/dist` and served by the router fallback. It is the only user interface and runs no agent itself.
owns: Browser-side UI state: editor tabs, the open workspace, the mobile or desktop shell choice.
The set of WebSocket channel subscriptions and the reconnect schedule in `web/src/api/socket.ts`.
Creation of the Web Push subscription through the service worker `/sw.js`, which it POSTs to `/api/push/subscribe`.

components.name: ostra server
components.role: The axum router of the `ostra` process, bound to 127.0.0.1:7878 by default, and the machine-wide services built in `app::build`: providers, both executors, the MCP gateway, the notifier, the workspace runtimes (ostra-workspace), and code navigation (ostra-code).
owns: The listen address and port choice (7878 to 7897, then any free port) and `server.json` in the data dir.
Browser sign-in: one-time tokens under `auth:token:<sha256>`, `ostra_session` cookies under `auth:cookie:<sha256>`, and the Host and Origin checks.
The `/internal/policy` and `/internal/mcp` routes and one `Running` record per live harness execution in `bridge.rs`.
Workspace MCP server connections and their OAuth records in `mcp.rs`.
The language server pool and the per-project code index.
Web Push fan-out and deletion of subscriptions that answer `Gone`.
Judge model calls through `ServerServices::judge` and `ostra_providers::structured`.

components.name: engine
components.role: One `Engine` per open workspace, inside the `ostra` process, that runs each session as an event-sourced state machine: append, fold, plan, perform.
owns: Every `SessionEvent` appended to a session (`Inner::append` is the only writer).
The `SessionState` fold and the pure planner `next_steps`.
Gates, judge decisions (`DecisionMade`), error retries, review caps, and the session budget (`limits.session_budget_usd`, default 25 USD).
Execution slots under `limits.max_parallel_executions` (default 3 per workspace).
Recovery of running executions and open permission gates at server start (`Engine::recover`).

components.name: native executor
components.role: `NativeExecutor`, one shared instance in the `ostra` process, which runs one leaf agent's turn loop against a model provider API with ostra-tools for tools and ostra-policy for checks.
owns: The model turn loop, tool dispatch, and submit validation of native executions.
The per-execution `ExecutionPolicy` check and observe calls for native tool calls.
Context compaction and the wall-clock budget `spec.timeout_secs` of a native execution.

components.name: harness executor
components.role: `HarnessExecutor`, which writes a launch plan, starts a harness CLI in a PTY inside the sandbox, and supervises it until the agent's `submit_<agent>` call or another end.
owns: Launch plans that register `ostra hook` and `ostra mcp-stdio` with the CLI.
Per-execution bearer tokens in `LiveRegistry` and their constant-time check.
PTY sessions and their scrollback, which the console's Terminal tab streams.
The supervision end decision: Submitted, GaveUp, Exited, Timeout, Cancelled, Idle, Auth, or Fatal.

components.name: hook shim
components.role: The short-lived `ostra hook` subprocess the harness CLI starts for each hook event, and the long-lived `ostra mcp-stdio` subprocess the CLI starts as its `ostra` MCP server; both forward to the server's `/internal/` routes using `OSTRA_URL` and `OSTRA_TOKEN`.
owns: The fail-closed answer: a PreToolUse hook that cannot reach the server returns a deny.

components.name: egress proxy
components.role: A per-execution HTTP proxy, run on the two `ostra-egress` threads of the `ostra` process, that is the only network path out of a sandboxed process (bubblewrap on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS).
owns: The allow or refuse decision for every outbound destination of a sandboxed harness CLI or Bash command.
The per-execution Unix socket (Linux) or loopback port with a credential (macOS).

components.name: workspace.db
components.role: SQLite file `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db`, one per workspace, opened in WAL mode.
owns: The append-only session event log.
The tables the engine materializes from it: sessions, executions, gates, decisions, and tool output truncated to 8 KiB.

components.name: registry.db
components.role: SQLite file `registry.db` in the machine data dir, with credential rows sealed by AES-256-GCM (`secrets::Sealer`).
owns: Registered workspaces.
Web Push subscriptions.
The key-value table: sign-in tokens and cookies, provider credentials, MCP OAuth records, and command approvals.

components.name: knowledge.sqlite3
components.role: SQLite file `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3`, one per project, with FTS5 full-text search.
owns: The lessons agents record with the Memory tool and recall with MemoryRecall.

components.name: harness CLI
components.role: An installed agent CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, or Antigravity) that runs one leaf agent and calls its own vendor's model API.

components.name: model provider APIs
components.role: The Anthropic Messages API (`https://api.anthropic.com`, `POST /v1/messages`) and the OpenAI Responses API (`https://api.openai.com`, `POST /v1/responses`), plus the vendor APIs the harness CLIs call.

components.name: MCP servers
components.role: External Model Context Protocol servers configured per workspace, reached as a child process (stdio) or at a URL (streamable HTTP).

components.name: language servers
components.role: LSP servers named in a project's `language_servers` setting, started through `ostra_sandbox::host_command`.

components.name: browser push service
components.role: The push service behind each browser's Web Push subscription endpoint, which delivers notifications to the console's service worker.

failure_recovery.failure: The `ostra` process stops or restarts while sessions run.
failure_recovery.detection: At start, `App::attach` calls `Engine::recover` for each registered workspace.
failure_recovery.recovery: Each execution left running is recorded as Interrupted with the error "The server restarted while this execution ran." and re-runs with the same spawn block. A harness run that was waiting with its process alive stays Waiting. Open permission gates are answered Deny. A driver restarts for every session that is not terminal.
The console reconnects after min(10000 ms, 500 ms x 2^attempts), subscribes again to every channel, and each screen refetches its REST snapshot. There is no attempt limit.

failure_recovery.failure: A WebSocket subscriber falls behind the `hub` broadcast (capacity 8192 notices) or the `push` broadcast (capacity 1024).
failure_recovery.recovery: The server sends `ServerMsg::Error { message: "lagged" }` and continues. The notices it dropped are not resent. No code in web reacts to this message, so a screen resyncs only after its next reconnect or reload.

failure_recovery.failure: The hook shim cannot reach the server or gets a non-success answer.
failure_recovery.detection: `run_hook_cli` sees a missing `OSTRA_URL` or `OSTRA_TOKEN`, a send error, a non-2xx status, or an unreadable body. Non-PreToolUse posts have a 60 s timeout.
failure_recovery.recovery: A PreToolUse hook answers Deny with "Stop and end your turn: Ostra could not check this call". Other hook events are dropped. There is no retry.

failure_recovery.failure: A bridge request names an execution that is not running, or has no bearer token.
failure_recovery.recovery: No token returns 401. An execution that is not registered is denied with guard `self-protection`. The harness agent sees the denial.

failure_recovery.failure: An execution ends with status Error.
failure_recovery.detection: The engine's fold reads the `ExecutionFinished` event.
failure_recovery.recovery: The engine re-runs it once (`ERROR_RETRIES` = 1), then opens a gate for the user.

failure_recovery.failure: A native execution passes its time budget.
failure_recovery.recovery: The run is cancelled, waited on for 3 s (`CLEANUP_GRACE`), and returned as Error "timed out after N s" with the usage spent so far. The engine's error retry then applies.

failure_recovery.failure: A harness CLI goes quiet, exits early, is not signed in, or passes its budget.
failure_recovery.detection: `HarnessExecutor::supervise` wakes every 500 ms, on process exit, and on cancel. It sends an idle nudge after 240 s and allows 2 nudges.
failure_recovery.recovery: `outcome::result` maps the end to Error with a message: Idle after two reminders, `harness-auth:` or `harness-launch:` when the CLI exits within 20 s, or a timeout message. The engine's error retry then applies. A sign-in failure needs the user to log in from the harness terminal.

failure_recovery.failure: A model provider request fails with a retryable error.
failure_recovery.detection: `ProviderError::is_retryable` on the HTTP status or stream error.
failure_recovery.recovery: `retry::run` retries up to 4 times with exponential backoff from 1 s to 60 s, 50 to 100 percent jitter, and at least the `Retry-After` value. It never retries after output has started streaming, and returns `ProviderError::Stream` instead.

failure_recovery.failure: A judge call fails or its answer does not match the schema.
failure_recovery.detection: `Services::judge` returns an error, or the `validate` closure rejects the value.
failure_recovery.recovery: The engine tries 3 times, sleeping 500 ms x (attempt + 1) between tries. It then returns `EngineError::Invalid`, which the driver records as a `Note` event. The Completion judge falls back to a report that lists the session state.

failure_recovery.failure: A workspace MCP server fails to start, fails its handshake, or exits.
failure_recovery.detection: `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` of 30 s on start and on `tools/list`, `Client::is_alive`, and the per-server `timeout_secs` on each tool call.
failure_recovery.recovery: A failed server is not started again for 20 s (`RETRY_AFTER`). A failed tool listing reconnects. A server that exited since the execution opened is started once more before the call. A server that needs sign-in returns NeedsAuth, and the user signs in from the console.

failure_recovery.failure: A language server fails to start, times out on `initialize`, or dies.
failure_recovery.recovery: The server is not started again for 30 s (`RETRY`). Answers come from the built-in index while the server is down.

failure_recovery.detection: `Notifier::send` returns `SendOutcome::Gone`, `SendOutcome::Failed`, or an error, with a 20 s HTTP timeout.
failure_recovery.recovery: A `Gone` subscription is deleted from `registry.db`. Other failures are logged with `tracing::warn` and not retried.

failure_recovery.failure: A SQLite file is locked by another writer.
failure_recovery.recovery: The store returns `StoreError` to the caller. The engine driver records a failed step as a `Note` event. There is no retry in ostra-store.

failure_recovery.failure: A sandboxed process connects to a destination the policy refuses, or the destination does not answer.
failure_recovery.detection: The egress proxy checks each CONNECT or absolute URL, with a 30 s head timeout and a 10 s connect timeout.
failure_recovery.recovery: The proxy answers 403 with the setting to change, or 502 when no address connected. The decision is reported to the engine through `OnDecision`. There is no retry.

failure_recovery.failure: The global config file fails to parse or validate while the server runs.
failure_recovery.detection: `Shared::global` re-reads and validates the file on each call.
failure_recovery.recovery: The server keeps the last good copy and logs a warning. At start, a sandbox validation issue stops the server with the config path.

scalability.scales_by: Nothing. Each browser tab holds one WebSocket.
scalability.limit: The server allows a bounded number of channel subscriptions per socket and refuses more with an error.

scalability.scales_by: Nothing. One process per machine; `auth::server_running` stops a second server from cleaning the first one's sandboxes.
scalability.limit: The listening port: an explicit port fails when taken, otherwise 20 ports (7878 to 7897) are tried before port 0.

scalability.scales_by: One `Engine` per open workspace and one driver task per session, in the same process.
scalability.limit: `limits.max_parallel_executions` (default 3) per workspace; further spawns wait for a slot. Appends for one session are serialized by that session's state mutex.

scalability.scales_by: Concurrent async executions in one shared `NativeExecutor`, bounded by the engine's slots.
scalability.limit: The model provider's rate limits, reached as retryable errors under the 4-retry policy.

scalability.scales_by: One harness CLI child process and PTY per execution, bounded by the engine's slots.
scalability.limit: Machine CPU and memory for the CLI processes, and each PTY's 2000-line scrollback and 256-entry write queue.

scalability.scales_by: One `ostra hook` process per hook event and one `ostra mcp-stdio` process per harness execution.
scalability.limit: Each PreToolUse hook waits for the server with no client timeout, so a pending permission ask holds the hook process open.

scalability.scales_by: One listener per execution, sharing the 2 `ostra-egress` worker threads.
scalability.limit: 256 concurrent connections per listener (`MAX_CONNECTIONS`); more are accepted and dropped.
One `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>` per open database, so writes from every session in the workspace are serialized.
One `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`, shared by sign-in checks, credentials, and push subscriptions. Cookie checks are cached for 5 s to reduce reads.

scalability.scales_by: One file per project; each call opens its own connection.
scalability.limit: SQLite's single writer, with a 5000 ms busy timeout.
The vendor's account rate limits and sign-in state, which Ostra does not control.
Provider rate limits and the session budget (`limits.session_budget_usd`, default 25 USD), after which the session pauses for a decision.

scalability.scales_by: One connection per workspace root and server name, shared by every execution.
scalability.limit: The tool call timeout `timeout_secs` per server, and the 100 KiB cap on a converted tool result.

scalability.scales_by: One server per configured entry, started on first use.
scalability.limit: 8 running servers across all projects (`MAX_SERVERS`) with the least recently used one stopped; 32 open documents per server; stopped after 10 minutes idle.
Sends are made one subscription at a time in one task per notification, each with a 20 s timeout.

parts.overview: The assets project holds the text Ostra runs its AI agents with. It has no executable code. It holds 14 agent definitions (`agents/{name}/agent.toml` plus `agents/{name}/prompt.md`), 10 judge prompts (`judges/*.md`), three shared prompt fragments (`output-rules.md`, `code-tools.md`, `coordination.md`), the capability-to-tool mapping (`tool-mapping.toml`), seven reference files (`refs/*.md`), and one bundled skill (`skills/meta-author/SKILL.md`). The `ostra-agents` crate compiles the whole folder into the binary with `#[derive(RustEmbed)] #[folder = "../../assets"]`, renders each prompt with minijinja for the executor that runs it, and writes the references, the skill, and the native-rendered agent instructions to `<data_dir>/assets` when `ostra-server` starts. The `ostra-engine` crate spawns each agent with its rendered prompt and a spawn block, and calls each judge on the `judge` model route with a JSON schema for its `decide` tool. The readers of this part are engineers who change agent behavior, and the prompt-generation agent, which edits these files under the meta-author standard. The sections below cover asset loading, the agent definitions, the artifact handoffs between agents, each agent prompt, each judge, the references, and the links to the other projects.

sections.title: Asset embedding, rendering, and materialization
sections.purpose: This section describes how the files in this project become the prompts that Ostra agents and judges receive. The `ostra-agents` crate embeds every file at compile time, renders prompts per executor on demand, and copies references, skills, and native agent instructions to disk at server startup. Anyone who adds, renames, or edits an asset needs this section, because a broken asset fails the build tests or panics at first use.

owns: The text of every prompt, fragment, reference, and skill, and the file names that `ostra-agents` looks up by path.
does_not_own: The embedding, rendering, and caching code, which the `ostra-agents` project owns (`ostra-agents/src/lib.rs`, `ostra-agents/src/mapping.rs`).
The choice of where the materialized directory lives, which `ostra-server` owns (`ostra-server/src/app.rs` passes `paths::data_dir().join("assets")`).
The spawn block and the repo brief appended after the prompt, which `ostra-agents` owns in `spawn.rs` and `brief.rs`.

assumptions: The folder is embedded at compile time from the path `../../assets` relative to the `ostra-agents` crate (`ostra-agents/src/lib.rs`, `struct Assets`), so an asset change takes effect only after Ostra is rebuilt.
Every file read through `asset_text` is valid UTF-8; a non-UTF-8 file returns `AgentsError::Parse`.
Template tokens use minijinja syntax `{{name}}` and the renderer runs with `UndefinedBehavior::Strict`, so a token that is not in the context fails the render with `AgentsError::Template`.
Judge prompts are served verbatim: `judge_prompt` does not render tokens, so a judge file must contain no `{{` token.
References and skills get only the `{{assets_dir}}` and `{{ assets_dir }}` substitution (`fill_assets_dir`), not the tool tokens, so a reference or skill must not use a `tool_*` token.

business_flow.action: Edits a prompt or reference in this project and rebuilds Ostra.
business_flow.outcome: The new text is compiled into the `ostra` binary.

business_flow.action: Starts and calls `set_assets_dir` and `materialize_assets` for `<data_dir>/assets`.
business_flow.outcome: References, the bundled skill, and each agent's native instructions exist on disk; unchanged files are not rewritten.

business_flow.action: Needs to spawn an agent and asks for its prompt rendered for the chosen executor.
business_flow.outcome: The agent receives the output rules, any guides its capabilities add, and its prompt with real tool names.

business_flow.action: Needs a judge decision and asks for the judge prompt by name.
business_flow.outcome: The judge model receives the judge file text unchanged as its system prompt.

subsections.title: Asset layout
subsections.purpose: Lists every folder and top-level file of the project and the lookup that reads it. The path of each file is its lookup key, so renaming a file breaks the lookup.
assumptions: `load_defs` iterates `AgentName::ALL` (14 names in `ostra-core/src/agent.rs`) and expects `agents/{name}/agent.toml` for each; a missing file panics with `embedded agent definitions are invalid`.
`judge_prompt`, `reference`, and `embedded_skill` build their maps from path prefixes `judges/`, `refs/`, and `skills/` with suffixes `.md` and `/SKILL.md`, so a file with another suffix is ignored.

subsections.title: Prompt assembly per executor
subsections.purpose: Describes the order in which `render_prompt_in` joins the fragments and the agent prompt, and what a harness executor receives in addition. An executor is the program that runs the agent: the native executor (Ostra's own loop, whose tool names follow Claude Code) or a harness executor (`claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `agy`).
assumptions: The native executor's tool names are the Claude Code names (`Read`, `Edit`, `Bash`), as the header comment of `tool-mapping.toml` states.

An agent whose `capabilities` list lacks `code` or `coordinate` never sees `code-tools.md` or `coordination.md`; for example the advisor gets no coordination guide (checked by the test `coordination_guide_names_the_tools_per_executor`).

business_flow.action: Renders `agents/{name}/prompt.md` with the token context for the executor.
business_flow.outcome: The body holds real tool names.

business_flow.action: Prepends `code-tools.md` when the agent has `code`, then `coordination.md` when it has `coordinate`, then `output-rules.md`.
business_flow.outcome: The prompt reads: output rules, coordination guide, code navigation guide, agent prompt.

business_flow.action: For a harness executor, prepends the tool vocabulary section built from `tool-mapping.toml`.
business_flow.outcome: A harness prompt starts with `## Tool vocabulary`; a native prompt does not.

subsections.title: Capability to tool mapping and template tokens

sections.title: Session artifacts and their file names
sections.purpose: Agents find each other's output by exact file name in the session directory (`Session dir:`), so the names are a contract between prompts. This section lists every name the prompts use, who writes it, how, and who reads it.
assumptions: The session directory already exists when an agent starts; every prompt tells the agent not to `mkdir` it.
A run stamp is `date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S` computed once per run; generate-spec orders research documents by it, and plan uses one stamp for the master plan and every phase file.

Ostra refuses a Write, an Edit, or a shell write to any `ostra-research-*`, `ostra-spec-*`, or `ostra-plan-*` file, because those are rendered from typed JSON by the Document tool (stated in the explore, generate-spec, and plan prompts).

Reports written with the Report tool go to the `Report file:` path; the prompts allow a Write or a quoted heredoc to that exact path when the tool fails, and state that any other name in the session directory is refused.

sections.title: Explore agent (research)
sections.purpose: The explore agent researches one task in one repo and writes one research document, including every outside technology it looked up with URL and date. It is the only agent that searches the web for the pipeline. The engine spawns it per project, per area, and again when the user changes the request.

New memory lessons it records with the Memory tool.

Any project file; the agent is read-only on project source.

assumptions: Required lines: `Task:`, `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, `Repo key:`; any missing line returns `ERROR: missing required parameter {label}` before the first tool call.
Several explore documents may exist for one request, so a document must state its scope and never describe an area it did not open as unaffected.
Recalled memory lessons are evidence to verify, not facts.

sections.title: Generate-spec agent
sections.purpose: The generate-spec agent reads every research document for a request and writes exactly one spec: criteria, deliverables, EARS requirements with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria, contracts, and an External Evidence table. It runs once after research, and again to fold in answers, requirement changes, and fact-check findings. The plan agent reads this spec and nothing else, so the spec must be self-contained.

owns: The spec document: criteria, deliverables, requirements, acceptance criteria, contracts, evidence, data impact, assumptions, open questions, notes.
does_not_own: Implementation choices such as files, classes, layers, and frameworks, which the plan agent owns.
The derived Delivery Order and Traceability tables and counts, which Ostra computes from the lists.
Tests; no requirement may ask for tests or assume a test setup.

assumptions: Required lines: `Task:`, `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, `Repo key:`; optional `Repos in scope:`, `Research docs:`, `User answers:`, `Findings:`, `Spec file:`, `New research docs:`, `Requirement changes:`.
A `Spec file:` line means a revision: the agent updates that path in place with `update` and `remove`, keeps requirement IDs, and does not compute a new stamp, because fact-check diffs by file name.
When two research documents disagree, the newer run stamp wins and the older statement is recorded in `assumptions`.
Web tools are for re-checking a cited page (Step 2C), never for discovering a technology no research document covers.

business_flow.action: Reads every research document in stamp order and each repo's profile and inventory.
business_flow.outcome: Scopes, sources, and area maps are known.

business_flow.action: Derives atomic criteria under K1 to K8 and an evidence ledger of E rows.
business_flow.outcome: Every demand and every external fact is listed with its grounding.

business_flow.action: Verifies each grounding in the repo and groups criteria into deliverables under S1 to S8.
business_flow.outcome: Each deliverable targets one repo and covers at most 6 criteria.

business_flow.action: Orders deliverables, writes EARS requirements and acceptance criteria, and raises open questions.
business_flow.outcome: One flat R1 to Rn sequence exists with AC{n}.{m} for each.

business_flow.action: Writes the spec with the Document tool, fixes every reported error, and submits.
business_flow.outcome: The engine sends the spec to fact-check.

sections.title: Fact-check agent
sections.purpose: The fact-check agent checks a spec or a master plan for claims that would break the implementer and for external facts that do not trace to a retrieved page, and submits one verdict. Ostra refuses spec or plan approval without a recorded PASS. It runs after every generate-spec and plan pass.

owns: The verdict and findings for one target, and its own snapshot directory.
does_not_own: Fixing the target, which generate-spec or plan owns on its revision.
Design critique, which the user and the engine own.

assumptions: Required lines: `Target:`, `Target type:`, `Prior findings:`, `Spec file:`, `Source check:`, `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, `Repo key:`; optional `Research docs:`.
`Prior findings: none` means a first pass; any other value is a re-pass limited to the prior findings and changed lines.
The engine, not the agent, sets `Source check:` to `citations` or `refetch`; `refetch` on a plan target is invalid.
The implementer reads phase files only, so narrative sections cannot produce wrong code and are outside the claim surface.

business_flow.action: Reads the target and, for a plan, every phase file.
business_flow.outcome: Scope is chosen from `Prior findings:`.

business_flow.action: Extracts claims inside the claim surface and verifies them in batched commands.
business_flow.outcome: Each claim is true, false, or untraced.

business_flow.action: Assigns severity by what breaks downstream.
business_flow.outcome: HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW per finding.

business_flow.action: Copies the target and phase files into the snapshot directory and submits.
business_flow.outcome: PASS only when no HIGH or MEDIUM finding exists.

sections.title: Plan agent
sections.purpose: The plan agent turns one approved spec into a plan document from which Ostra renders a master plan file and one self-contained phase file per phase. Each step names one file, a prose action, the skills to load, and a build command; each phase carries its repo, complexity, test policy, and dependencies for scheduling. It runs after spec approval when the stakes judge says medium or high.

owns: Phases, steps, stakes, risks, success criteria, clarifying questions, and mechanical pre-check results.
does_not_own: Requirements, which the spec owns.
Test phases and documentation phases, which the test pipeline and the documentation agent own.
The derived Phase Index, Deliverable Index, Traceability, and Step Count tables, which Ostra computes.

assumptions: Required lines: `Spec file:`, `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, `Repo key:`; `Master plan:` marks a revision, with `Findings:` when fact-check failed.
The spec is the only requirements source; a research document named in the prompt is ignored and reported in the summary.
The implementer reads only its phase file, so a phase repeats every prior-phase artifact, contract shape, requirement statement, and evidence row it needs.
External evidence rows are settled; the plan copies them verbatim and never re-derives them.

business_flow.action: Reads the spec, builds a requirement ledger, and reads each repo's profile and inventory.
business_flow.outcome: Commands are stored per repo key.

business_flow.action: Explores the code, confirms consumed contracts, and reads sibling files for patterns.
business_flow.outcome: Mismatches become risks and clarifying questions.

business_flow.action: Classifies stakes and writes clarifying questions only for real gaps.
business_flow.outcome: Zero questions is the expected outcome.

business_flow.action: Designs phases and steps under P0 to P13 and writes the plan with the Document tool.
business_flow.outcome: Ostra writes the master plan and phase files.

business_flow.action: Runs the surviving-callers and target-classpath checks, records them in `pre_checks`, saves the spec snapshot, and submits.
business_flow.outcome: The engine sends the plan to fact-check.

tables.title: Plan rules
rows: Each phase belongs to one deliverable, in D order; never merge two deliverables.
Dependency order inside a deliverable: migration, model, data access, DTOs, service contracts, implementations, handlers, consumers, schedulers, configuration.
Verification is the phase repo's `build` command; never a test command, never tests.
Per-step skills from the phase repo's Skill Application Mapping; Ostra refuses uninstalled skills and code phases with no skill in a repo that has skills.
Ostra unions step skills into the phase's Required Skills.
Repo and Depends on per phase; cross-deliverable first phases depend on the producers' last phases.
Complexity Low, Medium, or High picks the implementer and write-test model.
Phase IDs 1 to N in one sequence.
Every requirement delivered by at least one step's `delivers`.
Test policy Required unless every step is boilerplate; doubt means Required; Skip needs a rationale.
Binding rules copied verbatim onto steps and rows copied into the phase's `constraints`.

tables.title: Stakes levels
rows: One file, easy revert, no schema, data, or contract change.
Several files in one area, a contract change, or a new integration point.
Architecture, migration, cross-module, shared library, or external integration.
10 to 30 steps, full risk matrix, rollback strategy.

tables.title: Submit fields (submit_plan)
rows: id, deliverable, project, title, complexity, test_policy, test_rationale, depends_on, file; must match the plan document.
2 to 5 sentences with pre-check outcomes, constraints carried, and ignored inputs.
Keys of projects a phase creates.

concerns.responsibility: A deliverable whose repo key is not in scope becomes phases under `{workspace-root}/{key}`, listed in `new_projects`, whose first phase context carries the stack, purpose, and base requirements verbatim and names no skills.

8A searches call sites of deleted, renamed, or moved symbols; 8B confirms moved files' imports resolve on the target module; both are vacuous when nothing moves.

sections.title: Implementer agent
sections.purpose: The implementer writes the code for one plan phase or one inline change, following the skills named for it, verifying every step with the repo brief's build command, and writing a change report. It runs for every phase, for review fixes, and after a handoff or rescue. It never writes tests.

owns: Source changes in `Repo root:`, the progress log, the change report, and FIXED or WONTFIX rows in the review ledger.
does_not_own: Tests, which the write-test agent owns.
Prompt text, `SKILL.md` files, and agent files, which the prompt-generation agent owns through a handoff.
Staging, which Ostra does for `changed_files` after review passes.

assumptions: Required lines: `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, `Repo key:`, `Report file:`, and exactly one of `Phase file:` or `No plan:`.
The repo brief appended to the prompt carries the exact commands and skill names and paths; the agent does not re-read the profile to confirm them.
Consecutive failing build or test commands are counted by Ostra: a warning at three and refusal of further build or test commands at five.
A `User notes:` line never overrides the phase file or a fix instruction.

business_flow.action: Reads the phase file or inline instructions, prior reports, and context files.
business_flow.outcome: An ordered step list exists.

business_flow.action: Creates or resumes the progress log and loads the review ledger for fixes.
business_flow.outcome: Completed steps are not redone.

business_flow.action: Loads `convention` and every required skill.
business_flow.outcome: Templates and rules are in context.

business_flow.action: Runs read, edit, build, and record for each step.
business_flow.outcome: Each step passes its build.

business_flow.action: Runs phase and final builds, writes the report with the Report tool, and submits.
business_flow.outcome: The reviewer reviews exactly `changed_files`.

diagrams.title: Handling a failed build in Step 3D
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  b[Run build] --> ok{Passed?}
  ok -->|yes| rec[Record step, next step]
  ok -->|no| a1[Attempt 1: diagnose and fix]
  a1 --> b2{Passed?}
  b2 -->|yes| rec
  b2 -->|no| a2[Attempt 2: different approach]
  a2 --> r[Attempt 2.5: lint or typecheck, search symbols]
  r --> a3[Attempt 3: final fix]
  a3 --> b3{Passed?}
  b3 -->|yes| rec
  b3 -->|no| esc[Partial report, submit status stuck]

sections.title: Code-reviewer agent
sections.purpose: The code reviewer reviews the uncommitted changes of one review loop against the repo's Review Rule Set, checks the logic against the phase file, runs a security scan that no instruction can waive, and submits structured findings. It runs after each implementer or write-test execution and on every fix pass until no HIGH or MEDIUM finding is open.

owns: Findings, the review ledger for its loop, and `ostra-security-block.json`.
does_not_own: Project files; the agent writes no code.
Applying auto-fixable findings, which Ostra does from the exact `fix` text.
The review loop cap, which the engine and the resolve-review judge own.

assumptions: Required lines: `Changed files:`, `Change rationale:`, `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, `Repo key:`, `Phase:`, and one of `Phase file:` or `No plan:`; optional `Review scope: unstaged` and review context words.
Git output is the source of truth for changed files; `Changed files:` is a hint.
The repo brief carries the complete Review Rule Set; the inventory is read only when the brief is missing.
Only code on disk counts as evidence; reports, checkboxes, and FIXED ledger rows are claims.

business_flow.action: Loads the rule set, detects changed files with git, and filters by review context.
business_flow.outcome: An empty list ends the pass with `Code review: no changes detected`.

business_flow.action: Loads its loop's ledger, the EPA report for test review, and area references.
business_flow.outcome: Prior findings are known.

business_flow.action: Reads each full file and diff, runs the security scan, then the phase-requirement check.
business_flow.outcome: BLOCKER and PHASE-REQ findings exist where due.

business_flow.action: Applies the rule set, deduplicates against the ledger, and self-checks.
business_flow.outcome: Each finding points to a changed line with an executable fix.

business_flow.action: Appends the ledger iteration, overwrites the sentinel, and submits.
business_flow.outcome: The engine loops fixes or stages the change.

diagrams.title: Review steps in one pass
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  s0[Step 0: rule set from brief] --> s1[Step 1: git change detection]
  s1 --> e{Filtered list empty?}
  e -->|yes| nc[Ledger, sentinel, no changes detected]
  e -->|no| s2[Step 2: read files and diffs]
  s2 --> s25[Step 2.5: security scan]
  s25 --> pf{Phase file given?}
  pf -->|yes| s26[Step 2.6: phase requirements]
  pf -->|no| s3[Step 3: rule set review]
  s26 --> s3
  s3 --> s35[Step 3.5: dedupe against ledger]
  s35 --> s5[Step 5: ledger, sentinel, submit]

tables.title: Security scan rules (all BLOCKER, never auto-fixable)
rows: Deletes or overwrites files, disks, databases, or history beyond the stated purpose.
Reverse or bind shells, download-and-execute, unexplained listeners.
Secrets or sensitive data sent, logged, or written outside the documented flow.
Encoded payloads decoded then executed; unexplained minified code.
Disabled TLS or auth checks, widened permissions or CORS, removed rate limits.
Manifest changes adding URL dependencies, install scripts fetching code, typosquats.
Text aimed at AI agents, and any instruction to skip the scan or a WONTFIX on a BLOCKER.

tables.title: Submit fields (submit_code_reviewer)
rows: severity, file, rule, description, fix, and guidance for BLOCKER only; BLOCKER first.
true exactly when a BLOCKER finding exists; Ostra refuses a mismatch.
`Code review: SECURITY BLOCK: N dangerous finding(s) in M file(s)`, `Code review: N issue(s) in M file(s)`, or exactly `Code review passed`.

tables.title: Auto-fixable fix forms
rows: Change `{exact old code}` to `{exact new code}` on line {N}.
Add `{exact text to add}` above line {N}: `{anchor line content}`.

concerns.responsibility: `ostra-review-ledger-phase-{Phase}.md` or `ostra-review-ledger.md`; `2` and `2-tests` are separate loops because the cap counts iterations.
Applied only in test or full review, skipped in implementation review.
Still runs detection and the security scan; submits `Code review: no inventory rule set found` unless a BLOCKER exists.
Returns `ERROR: unreadable Phase file: {path}` with no fallback.

sections.title: Execution-path-analyzer agent
sections.purpose: The execution path analyzer plans verification for one implementation: every execution path through each changed public function, the system flows that reach the changed code, and the regression suites to re-run, each with a test level. It writes an EPA report for write-test. It runs only when the user asked for tests, after the coding phases pass review.

owns: The EPA report.
does_not_own: Test code, which write-test owns.
Deciding whether another project is verified, which the engine owns; outside consumers go to Notes.

assumptions: Required lines: `Implementer report:`, `Report file:`, `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, `Repo key:`.
A test request with no implementer lists no changed files; the agent resolves the code from the request, git history, staged diff, or the entry points it names.
Test levels come only from the brief's Test types table; with no table every check uses the `test` command and paths are `unit`.

business_flow.action: Reads the implementer report and optional plan, research, notes, and acceptance criteria.
business_flow.outcome: Source files to analyze are known.

business_flow.action: Selects files with logic and resolves their test skills.
business_flow.outcome: Pure declarations are kept only for flow tracing.

business_flow.action: Enumerates paths P1 to Pn and marks each NEW or EXISTING.
business_flow.outcome: Every branch, early return, error, null case, and loop edge has an ID.

business_flow.action: Traces system flows S1 to Sn and lists regression suites.
business_flow.outcome: Each flow has the lowest level that observes it with real parts.

business_flow.action: Writes the report with the Report tool and submits.
business_flow.outcome: write-test has exact instructions per check.

sections.title: Write-test agent
sections.purpose: The write-test agent writes the unit, integration, and end-to-end tests the EPA report assigns, following the repo's test skills, and runs them with the listed regression suites. It writes only test code and a test report. It runs per phase when the user asked for tests, and for test-review fixes.

owns: Test files and the test report.
does_not_own: Source code; a discovered source bug is escalated with trigger 4 for the implementer.

assumptions: Required lines: `Implementer report:`, `EPA report:`, `Report file:`, `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, `Repo key:`.
Test skills win over any other instruction on test patterns.
The EPA report is binding: every NEW path and flow gets a test, and no check it omits is added.
The same consecutive-failure counter as the implementer applies: warning at three, refusal at five.

business_flow.action: Reads the brief's test commands and Test types, the implementer report, and the EPA report.
business_flow.outcome: A work list of paths, flows, and suites exists.

business_flow.action: Loads the required and file-type test skills.
business_flow.outcome: Templates are in context.

business_flow.action: For each file then each flow reads code, EPA rows, and existing tests, writes tests, and runs the level's command.
business_flow.outcome: Each test passes or is recorded as `Not run` with the reason.

business_flow.action: Runs the `test` command and every regression suite, writes the report, and submits.

sections.title: Documentation agent
sections.purpose: The documentation agent writes one project's part of the workspace documentation book: an overview, one section per unit of work, and glossary terms, grounded in real source. It returns the part in its submit call and writes no file. It runs in the docs stage after every phase passed review, or directly for a DOCS request.

owns: One project's part of the book as submitted.
does_not_own: Writing the book files, which Ostra does.
The system architecture, which the system-architecture agent owns.

assumptions: Required lines: `Implementer reports:`, `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, `Repo key:`; optional `Existing book:` and `User notes:`.
The submit replaces the project's whole part, so sections outside the scope are copied unchanged from the existing book.
Ostra refuses a write under the books folder and refuses diagrams over the limits.

sections.title: System-architecture agent
sections.purpose: The system architecture agent writes the architecture chapter for a book that covers two or more projects: components, links with protocol and mode, failure detection and recovery, and scaling. It reads the parts the documentation agents returned and verifies each cross-project link in source. It writes no file.

does_not_own: Project parts, which the documentation agent owns.

A link is listed only when both ends are found in code or deployment files.

sections.title: Initializer agent
sections.purpose: The initializer bootstraps a project for Ostra: it scouts recurring code patterns, proposes skills for user approval, generates each approved skill from a real exemplar, and writes `.ostra/INVENTORY.md` and `.ostra/project.toml`. It runs in one of six modes named on its `Mode:` line; the engine runs scouts and skill generators in parallel and holds the approval gate between propose and generate.

owns: Session-dir artifacts in detect, scout, and propose.
Files under `.agents/skills/{name}/` in generate-skill, under `.ostra/` in generate-inventory, and under both in adopt.
does_not_own: Project source, manifests, and instruction files, which it never edits.
The memory store under `.ostra/memory/`, which Ostra owns.
Model and executor routing, which the workspace settings own.

assumptions: Every mode requires `Mode:`, `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, `Repo key:`; an unknown mode returns `ERROR: missing or invalid Mode. Expected one of detect | scout | propose | generate-skill | generate-inventory | adopt.`
Only read, write, edit, shell, search_text, glob, and submit are used; no language server or other server is assumed.
Instruction files (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `AGENT.md` in any case) arrive in the first message under `## Project instructions` and are treated as facts.
An optional `Advisor guidance:` line carries the advisor's instructions after an earlier failure.

business_flow.action: Checks for an Ultracode bootstrap and existing skills, surveys the repo, names the stack, plans slices, and detects commands.
business_flow.outcome: A scout plan and a result with slices exist.

business_flow.action: Runs once per slice in parallel and captures one exemplar, invariants, and a template per component type.
business_flow.outcome: One findings file per slice.

business_flow.action: Merges findings, ranks by slice spread, reconciles with existing skills.
business_flow.outcome: The user approves a skill set.

business_flow.action: Runs once per approved skill in parallel.
business_flow.outcome: Each `SKILL.md` is written from its exemplar.

business_flow.action: Writes INVENTORY.md and project.toml for generated and reused skills.
business_flow.outcome: The project is initialized.

diagrams.title: Mode sequence driven by the engine
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  d[detect] --> u{Ultracode bootstrap and user chose migrate?}
  u -->|yes| a[adopt]
  u -->|no| sl{Slices planned?}
  sl -->|yes| s[scout, one per slice, max 12]
  sl -->|no| p[propose on existing skills]
  s --> p
  p --> g[User approval gate]
  g --> gs[generate-skill, one per generate or regenerate]
  gs --> gi[generate-inventory]

code_refs.note: Mode dispatch and the common submit fields.

subsections.title: Detect mode
subsections.purpose: Plans the scout without writing to the repo, and records whether an Ultracode bootstrap and existing skills exist.
assumptions: `ultracode_bootstrap` is true only when `.ultracode/repo-profile.json` and `.ultracode/INVENTORY.md` both exist and the JSON parses.
When a skill name exists in both `.agents/skills/` and `.ostra/skills/`, only the `.agents/skills/` one is kept.

name, kind (convention or other), path, description.

subsections.title: Scout and propose modes
subsections.purpose: Scout captures patterns inside one slice; propose merges them into a ranked skill proposal in Markdown and JSON.
assumptions: A scout searches only its slice paths and omits types with zero matches.
A type marked `covered by {path}` gets a count and exemplar path only.
The default creation-skill threshold is `slice_spread >= 2` or total count >= 5.

tables.title: Proposal skill entry fields
rows: Totals from findings; 0 for bespoke skills.

subsections.title: Generate-skill and generate-inventory modes
subsections.purpose: Generate-skill writes one approved skill from its exemplar using the meta-author standard and one archetype; generate-inventory writes the two routing files that list every generated and reused skill.
assumptions: Generate-skill receives only dispositions `generate` or `regenerate`; `reuse` skills are never sent to it.
Regenerating a skill under `.ostra/skills/{name}/` writes the new file at `.agents/skills/{name}/` and leaves the old one.
The profile is TOML: no `null`, `stack` is a string, `[conventions]` is one table, `schema_version = 1`; Ostra refuses a profile that does not parse and names the line.

subsections.title: Adopt mode
subsections.purpose: Migrates a completed Ultracode bootstrap into `.ostra/` and `.agents/skills/` after the user chose to migrate, which is cheaper than scouting again.
assumptions: `Source runtime dir:` and `Source skills dir:` are repo-relative and taken verbatim.
Source directories are left on disk; the report names them as safe to delete by hand.

does_not_own: Doing the step's work; guidance may not ask a step to break its own instructions.

Guidance goes to the retried step on its `Advisor guidance:` line.

sections.purpose: The prompt-generation agent writes or edits instruction files (LLM prompts, SKILL.md files, agent files) to the meta-author standard. It runs for PROMPT requests and for implementer handoffs. The meta-author skill, shipped at `skills/meta-author/SKILL.md`, defines 16 writing laws, the chain-of-thought structure, and a self-review checklist, and the initializer also loads it to generate skills.

owns: The named target files and the report.
does_not_own: Source code other than prompt integration points, which the implementer owns.

sections.title: Judge prompts
sections.purpose: Judges are single-call model decisions the engine makes between stages. Each file in `judges/` is a system prompt that ends with one call to a `decide` tool whose schema the engine supplies. The engine records every decision as a `DecisionMade` session event, and the user sees the reason.

owns: The decision rules and output fields of each judge.
does_not_own: The JSON schemas and the input messages, which ostra-engine builds (`output_schema`, `judge_input`).

assumptions: The engine calls a judge on the `judge` route at `Tier::Advanced` with `Effort::Low`, validates the output against the judge's schema, and retries up to 3 attempts with a 500 ms times attempt-number pause (`call_judge` in ostra-engine).
Judge files are served without rendering, so they name `decide` directly and contain no tokens.
`JudgeKind::as_str` maps each kind to the file stem, so renaming a file breaks the lookup with `No prompt for the {kind} judge.`

code_refs.note: Categories, project and task rules, opt-ins, title.
Answer dispositions, forget, research, routes, and added context.

subsections.title: Classify judge

assumptions: Pinned projects are returned exactly (Rule O6); with one project it is always in scope.

subsections.title: Sufficiency, track, and stakes judges
subsections.purpose: Sufficiency decides per Not covered item whether another research pass is needed; track picks light or full for IMPLEMENT; stakes picks low, medium, or high for an approved spec.
assumptions: Sufficiency marks an unclear item as needed.
Track defaults to light and picks full only for named evidence.
Stakes resolves doubt upward.

stakes low, medium, or high, reason.

subsections.title: Route-answer and feedback judges
subsections.purpose: Route-answer decides what happens to a user's gate answer or added context; feedback routes review feedback on a built implementation into revision phases.
assumptions: The user's words win over the agent's recommendation.
Doubt resolves to `requirement_change` when a spec requirement addresses the subject; with no spec the route is `implementation_detail`.
At most three research tasks per decision.

tables.title: Dispositions
rows: The asking agent or the revision receives the text; default.
Kept as a note for named stages implement, tests, or docs.

Route-answer only: runs chosen optional stages (Rule T5).

subsections.title: Rescue, resolve-review, YOLO-answer, and completion judges
subsections.purpose: Rescue handles a stuck agent; resolve-review ends a review loop at its YOLO budget; YOLO-answer answers gates when the user delegated all decisions; completion writes the final report.
assumptions: A plain retry of a stuck agent is never an option; after two rescues with the same diagnostic the rescue judge chooses gate.
The YOLO review budget is 10 passes; BLOCKER findings never reach resolve-review.
YOLO approval requires a fact-check PASS.

action fix or block; instructions of {finding, instruction}; reason.
answer matching the gate's schema; reason.

sections.title: Stack references and output contracts
sections.purpose: The `refs/` folder holds four stack references, a generic fallback, the INVENTORY.md and project.toml contract, and the skill archetypes. The initializer reads them to scout, seed review rules, and write routing files; prompt-generation reads the archetypes. `stack_names()` returns the stacks with a seed reference for the New project form.

parts.overview: ostra-agents is the Rust crate that holds Ostra's agent assets and turns them into what an agent execution receives. It embeds the workspace's `assets` folder at compile time with RustEmbed and exposes three things. The first is each agent's definition (tier, capabilities, timeout, effort) and its system prompt, rendered with the tool names of the executor that runs it: the native executor or one of the harnesses Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, and Antigravity. The second is the typed spawn contract: one struct per agent and per initializer mode that renders the `Label: value` block an agent's first message starts with, plus `parse_block`, which validates such a block. The third is the repo brief: project facts, instruction files, artifacts, books, and workspace instructions appended to the first message. ostra-engine's spawn factory calls all three to build every execution, ostra-server calls `materialize_assets` at startup to write references, skills, and rendered instructions under the data directory, and ostra-workspace reads agent defaults for its settings; the crate itself depends only on ostra-core for shared types and paths.

sections.title: Agent definitions
sections.purpose: Loads the `agent.toml` of every agent in `AgentName::ALL` (14 agents) from the embedded assets into `AgentDef` values, once per process. It answers per-agent questions: description, default tier, capabilities, timeout in seconds, and reasoning effort per executor. ostra-engine's spawn factory and ostra-workspace's settings call it whenever they build an execution or list agent defaults.

does_not_own: The content of each `agent.toml`: the assets project owns it.
The `AgentName`, `Capability`, `Tier`, `Effort`, and `ExecutorKind` enums: ostra-core owns them.
Per-workspace effort overrides: ostra-core's `config::resolve_effort`, which ostra-engine's factory calls before it falls back to `effort_for`.

assumptions: Every agent in `AgentName::ALL` has a file at `agents/<name>/agent.toml` in the embedded assets, where `<name>` is `AgentName::as_str()` (kebab-case). `load_defs` returns `AgentsError::Missing` otherwise, and `defs` turns that into a panic.
Each `agent.toml` carries all five fields `description`, `default_tier`, `timeout_seconds`, `capabilities`, and `effort`; none has a serde default.

The keys of the `[effort]` table are the executor table names `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`, the values `ExecutorKind::tier_table()` returns. The test `every_agent_definition_loads_with_the_handover_tiers` checks every executor has an entry.
`agent_def` indexes the map with `&defs()[&agent]`, which relies on `load_defs` having inserted every `AgentName::ALL` member.

sections.title: Prompt rendering per executor
sections.purpose: Builds the system prompt of an agent for one executor from the embedded Markdown assets. Prompts are written once with template tokens such as `{{tool_read}}`, and this unit fills each token with the tool name the executor provides, then adds shared guides and, for harness executors, a tool vocabulary section. ostra-engine calls `render_prompt` for every execution it starts, and `materialize_assets` calls it for the native executor when it writes each agent's instructions to disk.

owns: The order in which the prompt parts are joined.
The template context: 28 `tool_*` tokens plus `assets_dir`.
The capability to tool name resolution through `assets/tool-mapping.toml`.
The text of the harness tool vocabulary section that is generated in code.
does_not_own: The prompt text, the guides `output-rules.md`, `code-tools.md`, and `coordination.md`, and `tool-mapping.toml`: the assets project owns them.
The lists of code, project, and coordination tools (`CODE_TOOLS`, `PROJECT_TOOLS`, `COORD_TOOLS`): ostra-core owns them.
Serving the tools: the native executor and the `ostra` MCP server in other projects serve the tools the prompt names.

assumptions: Every agent has `agents/<name>/prompt.md` in the embedded assets.
Prompts use only the tokens the context defines. `render_str` sets `UndefinedBehavior::Strict`, so any other token fails the render with `AgentsError::Template`.
`tool-mapping.toml` parses into `Mapping`; `mapping::get` panics otherwise, at the first render in the process.

The mapping has an entry for every capability key and every executor table, including `submit`. When one is missing, `Mapping::context` renders the mapping key itself (for example `code:outline`) in place of a tool name.
Every op passed after a colon is non-empty, because `Mapping::tool` uppercases `cap[..1]`; all ops come from the `TOKENS` table or ostra-core's tool lists.

sections.title: Spawn contract
sections.purpose: Defines one Rust struct per agent, per initializer mode, plus the consult and advisor runs, whose fields are the parameters that agent's prompt expects. Required parameters are non-`Option` fields, so the engine cannot build a spawn that omits one. Each struct renders the `Label: value` block that opens the agent's first message and serializes to JSON for the execution record. `parse_block` validates the same block format at runtime.

owns: The `SpawnParams` trait and every params struct.
The block format: label order, multi-line values, lists, and optional lines.
The runtime contract tables `PARAMS`, `COMMON`, and `contract`, and the value checks in `check`.
does_not_own: Which values go into a spawn: ostra-engine's `AgentsFactory::build`.
The labels each prompt reads: the agent prompts in the assets project, which must stay in step with these labels.
Report file names and session paths: ostra-core's `paths` module and the engine.

assumptions: Every spawn carries the four common lines `Workspace root`, `Repo root`, `Session dir`, and `Repo key`; `Workspace root` replaces Ultracode's `Primary repo root`.

List fields that a contract requires, such as `DocumentationParams::implementer_reports`, `CodeReviewerParams::changed_files`, `PromptGenParams::target_files`, and `InitScoutParams::slice_paths`, are non-empty. `Block::list` writes nothing for an empty list, so the rendered block would fail `parse_block` with a missing parameter.
`serde_json::to_value` succeeds for every struct; `json` returns `Value::Null` otherwise.

parts.overview: ostra-code is the Rust crate that provides code navigation for Ostra. Three parts use it: the console's Files view (through ostra-server), the file editor's hints, and the code tools that agents call. It has four layers. A table-driven tokenizer and outline analysis cover 22 languages, defined in `src/lang.rs`, `src/lex.rs` and `src/outline.rs`. An incremental per-project index of names, definitions, imports and supertypes is paired with a dependency graph built from that index; this is in `src/index.rs`, `src/resolve.rs`, `src/graph.rs` and `src/usage.rs`. Language servers are reached over LSP in `src/lsp/`. A provider chain in `src/provider.rs` lets a project put its own `code_provider` program or its `language_servers` in front of the built-in index. The crate takes its request and answer shapes from ostra-core (`ostra_core::code`, `ostra_core::config`, `ostra_core::api::FileIndex`) and starts every external program through ostra-sandbox (`ostra_sandbox::host_command`). ostra-server is its main consumer: it builds the provider chain for each request, keeps the index up to date when files are written, serves the graph views, and runs the agent code tools through `ostra_code::tools::run`.

sections.title: Crate surface and file rendering
sections.purpose: `src/lib.rs` declares the crate's modules, re-exports the types other crates use, and defines `render`. `render` turns one file's text into a `CodeFile`: display tokens, an outline, and imports. It also defines `signature` and `preview`, which build the one-line texts shown beside definitions and references. The native provider calls `render` for the Files view, and the `CodeOutline` agent tool calls it too.

owns: The `CLASSES` order of token classes that every native answer uses, and the `class_index` mapping into it.
The size limit `MAX_FILE_BYTES` (1 MiB) above which files are not tokenized or indexed.

sections.title: Code provider chain
sections.purpose: The Files view sends each request (file, usages, deps or symbols) through a chain of code providers and takes the first answer. A code provider is any implementation of the `CodeProvider` trait. `provider::ask` walks the chain in order, skips a provider that answers `Ok(None)`, and records the reason when a provider fails. It stamps the answer it returns with the name of the provider that gave it and with the reasons of the providers that failed before it. The chain lets a project replace any request with its own program or a language server and still fall back to the built-in index.

owns: The `CodeProvider` trait and the `Answer` enum (File, Usages, Deps, Symbols).
The order-of-chain rule: the first `Ok(Some)` wins, `Ok(None)` passes on, `Err` passes on and is recorded as a warning.
The warning text "The code provider `{name}` failed, so the built-in index answered: {e}" and the final error "No code provider answered this request."
does_not_own: The order in which providers are put in the chain, owned by ostra-server (`src/code.rs`): CommandProvider first, then one LspProvider per `language_servers` entry, then NativeProvider.
The request and answer shapes, owned by ostra-core (`ostra_core::code::ProviderRequest`, `CodeFile`, `CodeUsages`, `CodeDeps`, `CodeSymbols`).
Language server answers, owned by the language server provider section.

assumptions: The caller puts a provider that always answers at the end of the chain. ostra-server puts NativeProvider last, so the "No code provider answered" error only appears when that provider also fails.
Each answer type has `provider` and `warning` fields. `Answer::stamp` writes to both of them.
The failure text says "the built-in index answered" even when a later language server answered instead. The code does not check which provider answered.

business_flow.action: Stamps the first answer with the provider name and the earlier warnings, and returns it
business_flow.outcome: The browser shows the answer with the name of the provider that gave it and any failure reasons.

sections.title: Tokenizer
sections.purpose: `lex::lex` turns source text into tokens for any language in the table. It recognizes comments, strings, numbers, identifiers, keywords, attributes, macros, lifetimes and punctuation. It never fails, and it skips bytes it does not understand. Tokens carry byte offsets for the analysis and 1-based lines with UTF-16 columns for the browser. A comment or string that spans lines comes out as one token per line.

Tokens with `cont: true` are later lines of a multi-line comment or string. The outline analysis leaves them out of its significant tokens.

sections.title: Outline analysis
sections.purpose: `outline::analyze` makes one pass over a file's significant tokens, meaning tokens that are neither comments nor string continuations. It produces four results: a display class per token, the definitions (the outline), the supertype relations, and the raw import specs. Definitions come from keyword rules (`fn`, `class`, `def`), member rules inside class bodies, and a few family forms: C function bodies, Go receivers and blocks, and Python indentation. Names are matched by text; there is no type information.

owns: The Symbol, Super, RawImport, ImportStyle and Analysis types.

End lines of definitions, container names, and the `via` trait of methods in `impl Trait for Type`.

does_not_own: Tokens, owned by the tokenizer section.

assumptions: Data-family files skip the definition pass. They get only display classes: a name before `=` or `:` is an Attribute, and a name after `<` or `</` is a Keyword.
`matching` looks at most 2,000 tokens ahead for a closing bracket. `impl_block` and `supertypes` look at most 300 tokens ahead. `supertypes` also stops 5 lines after the declaration.
A `>` right after `-` is an arrow, not a closing angle bracket.
Symbols are sorted by (line, column) before they are returned.

subsections.title: Definition rules per family
subsections.purpose: This part explains which source forms become definitions and with which kind. A change to what the outline shows starts here.

owns: The per-family definition forms in `keyword`, `generic`, `go_func`, `go_def`, `js_var`, `py_assign`, `c_function` and `member`.

assumptions: A Rust `const` or `static` followed by `fn`, `unsafe`, `async` or `extern` is a qualifier, not a constant.

In JS, `const x = ...` is a Function when the value is `function`, `async`, an arrow function, or a parenthesized list followed by `=>` or `:`. It is a Class when the value is `class`, a Constant when the name is all caps, and a Variable otherwise. Only top-level and namespace-level declarations count.
A C name followed by `(` outside a class body is a function only when its body `{` follows after `const`, `noexcept`, `override`, `final` or `volatile`. `Owner::name` makes it a method of Owner.
A Go receiver `(r *Repo)` makes the function a method with container `Repo`. A Go `type X struct` is a Class and `type X interface` is an Interface.
Kotlin, Swift, Scala and PHP methods come from their keyword (`fun`, `func`, `def`, `function`), not from `name(` in a class body.
A brace after `:`, `<`, `|` or `&` in TypeScript opens an object type, not a definition body.
Python scopes end when a line starts at the same or a smaller indent than the definition line.

sections.title: Import resolution
sections.purpose: `Resolver` turns raw import specs into project files or folders, with one rule set per language family. It is built from the project's file list and a few manifests: `Cargo.toml` package names, `package.json` names and entry points, and `go.mod` module paths. It also defines units: the folders that hold a package manifest. Other parts of the crate use the unit of a file as its package.

owns: The Target type (path and folder flag).
Crate, npm package and Go module lookups built from manifests.
The unit (package folder) of every path through `unit_of_dir`.
Path helpers `parent` and `join`; `join` returns None when a relative path would leave the project.
does_not_own: When the resolver is rebuilt, owned by the project index section (`Indexes::resolver_for`, keyed by the FileIndex Arc).
Raw import specs, owned by the outline analysis section.

assumptions: The file list is the truth for what exists. A candidate path resolves only when it is in the list (`has`) or is a folder of a listed path.

Manifest reads go through the `read` closure given to `Resolver::new`. The index passes `std::fs::read_to_string` under the project root. A manifest that cannot be read or parsed is skipped without an error.
`package.json` files under a `node_modules` segment are ignored.
Bare JS package specs that name no workspace package (for example `react`) are not resolved. This is because `js` only falls back to specs that start with `/`.
Cargo crate names are stored with `-` replaced by `_`, because Rust paths spell them that way.

tables.title: Resolution per family
rows: `mod x;` resolves to `x.rs` or `x/mod.rs` in the module folder. A `use` path starts at `crate` (the crate's lib.rs or main.rs), `self`, one or more `super`, a workspace crate name, or a child module. The path then walks segments while a child file exists and returns the deepest file.

Relative specs join the file's folder. `@/x` and `~/x` try `src/x` and `x` under every ancestor holding package.json or tsconfig.json. Workspace package names map to their exports entry or sub-path. A leading `/` is project-rooted. Candidates are tried as the base, `.js`/`.jsx`/`.mjs`/`.cjs` swapped for `.ts`/`.tsx`, the base plus each of 11 extensions, and `index` plus each extension.

`alts` are tried before the spec. Leading dots are relative to the file's folder. Absolute modules are tried under each ancestor folder and then `src`, as `.py`, `.pyi`, `__init__.py`, then as a folder.
The spec must start with a `go.mod` module path followed by nothing or `/`. The target is the folder under that module.

PHP require specs join the file's folder or the root. Dotted specs ending in `*` resolve to a folder whose path ends with the dotted path. Others try the longest prefix of the dotted path with `.php` (PHP), `.cs` (C#), `.swift` (Swift) or `.java`, `.kt`, `.scala`, by file-name suffix.
Quoted includes try the file's folder, the root, `include/` and `src/`. All includes then fall back to a file-name suffix match.
`.rb` is added when missing. Relative requires join the file's folder. Others try `lib/`, the root, then a suffix match.
Dots become slashes. The rule tries `base.lua` and `base/init.lua` at the root, then `base.lua` in the file's folder, then a suffix match.

sections.purpose: `ProjectIndex` is the per-project store behind usages, dependencies, symbol search, the graph and the agent tools. For each file it keeps the names the file mentions, how it mentions them, its definitions, its imports, its supertype relations and its resolved import targets. It never keeps file text. `Indexes<K>` holds one index per project key. It builds an index on first use and keeps it current from write touches and a full disk check every 30 seconds.

A file whose first 8,000 bytes hold a NUL byte is binary and is not read (`read_text` returns None).
A file over 50,000 bytes whose average line is over 1,000 bytes is minified and is skipped.
Entry ids only grow. Removed entries stay in `entries` with `alive: false`, so postings lists stay sorted by pushing new ids at the end.
Once the byte cap drops a file, `truncated` stays true for the life of that ProjectIndex. No code path sets it back to false.
`Indexes::touch` records a dirty path only for a project that already has a slot. A project first built after the touch reads the disk anyway.

business_flow.action: Calls `Indexes::with` for a project with its root and file list
business_flow.outcome: The slot for the key is created on first use.

business_flow.action: Decides between a full sync, a sync of dirty paths, or no sync
business_flow.outcome: The index matches the disk for the paths it checked.

business_flow.action: Stamps listed files in parallel, re-analyzes changed ones in parallel, and drops removed ones
business_flow.outcome: Entries, postings and definitions are current, and the graph is marked for rebuild.

business_flow.action: Runs a query on the up-to-date index
business_flow.outcome: The answer reflects the disk.

diagrams.title: Indexes::with freshness decision
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  a["Indexes::with(key, root, list)"] --> b{Root changed?}
  b -- yes --> c[New empty ProjectIndex]
  b -- no --> d[Take dirty paths]
  c --> d
  d --> e["resolver_for(list)"]
  e --> f{"List Arc changed or last full sync over 30 s?"}
  f -- yes --> g["sync(paths, None)"]
  f -- no --> h{Dirty paths?}
  h -- yes --> i["sync(paths, Some(dirty))"]
  h -- no --> j["Run f on the index"]
  g --> j
  i --> j

diagrams.title: ProjectIndex::sync
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  a[Listed paths of indexed languages] --> b{Full sync?}
  b -- yes --> c[Remove entries not listed]
  b -- no --> d[Remove touched paths not listed]
  c --> e[Stamp files in parallel]
  d --> e
  e --> f{"Missing or over 1 MiB?"}
  f -- yes --> g[Remove entry]
  f -- no --> h{Stamp unchanged?}
  h -- yes --> k[Keep entry]
  h -- no --> i[Read and analyze in parallel]
  i --> j{"Binary, minified, or over 256 MiB total?"}
  j -- yes --> l[Skip; set truncated on byte cap]
  j -- no --> m[Insert entry]

sections.title: Dependency graph
sections.purpose: `src/graph.rs` derives a project's file dependency graph from the index without reading files. Import edges come from resolved imports. Reference edges link a file to the files that define the names it mentions. They are searched in the order a reader would look: the file itself, the files it imports, its folder, its package, then the packages its package imports. The graph answers neighbors, transitive reach, dependency chains, related files, hub files, the package map and import cycles.

Test-file and hub-file classification.

Per-file facts, owned by the project index section.

assumptions: Names of one character are skipped when building reference edges.
A file of one language family never links by name to a file of another family.
Non-test files never resolve names into test files. Test files may resolve names into non-test files.
A `mod` declaration is containment, not use. An import-only edge into a hub is a re-export path. A walk follows neither.
`is_hub` treats files with stem `lib`, `main`, `mod`, `index` or `__init__`, and any file with an `export * from`, as index modules.

sections.purpose: These queries work on one definition rather than on whole files. `callers` groups the mentions of a symbol by the definition that encloses them. `symbol_impact` follows callers hop by hop. `callees` lists the definitions a body names. `implementations` lists what a type or method implements and what implements it, including Go's implicit interface satisfaction. They back the CodeCallers, CodeImpact (with `symbol`), CodeCallees and CodeImplementations tools, the symbol view, and the editor jumps.

assumptions: The enclosing definition of a line is the innermost definition whose line range holds it. A definition without an end line covers only its first line.
A caller group at the top level whose every line is an import line is an import, not a use.
With `defined_in`, a mention in another file counts only when it resolves into that file. That file must also have an out edge to the defining file.
`callees` reads only the definition's lines. When the language gives no end line, only the first line is read.

Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly. A Go type implements every project interface whose non-empty method set its own folder defines. The Go signatures must match after names, spaces and package qualifiers are dropped. A signature that the one-line preview cuts off matches by name alone.

sections.title: Usages at a position
sections.purpose: `ProjectIndex::usages_at` lists the usages of the one definition that the name at a position means. A position on a definition means that definition. A position on a use means what the use resolves to. A mention elsewhere counts only when it can mean that definition. A member after `.`, `->` or `::` resolves through the type its receiver is declared with, and then through that type's supertypes. This keeps `a.name` and `b.name` of two unrelated classes apart. When the index cannot tell, the answer is the by-name usages.

owns: Declarations of variables, parameters and fields per file (`declarations`, `Decl`).

assumptions: Declared types are read from tokens only: `Repo repo`, `repo: Repo`, `repo = new Repo()`, `T::new()`, `T{}`, `&T{}` and capitalized constructor calls. In Go and C, any name in a type position counts as a type.
Wrapper types (`Box`, `Rc`, `Arc`, `Option`, `Result`, `Optional`, `Readonly`, `Promise`) stand for their first type argument.
In Jvm and C families, a bare name in a class body can mean a member of that class, unless a local declaration earlier in the enclosing method hides it.
A receiver of an array, or of a declared type the project does not define, has none of the project's members. The meaning is a sure empty list.
`<T> T get()`: a return type that is a type parameter of the definition is not used.

sections.title: Language server pool and provider
sections.purpose: A project's `language_servers` entries each name a server command and the languages it answers for. `LspPool<K>` starts a server on the first request for one of those languages and keeps it running while it is used. It stops a server after 10 minutes without requests. `LspProvider<K>` is the code provider for one entry. It answers file, usages and symbols requests, and it gives completions, signature help, navigation and outside-file reads. File answers put the server's semantic tokens and outline over the built-in answer. Imports and the colors the server leaves out still come from the tokenizer.

owns: Server lifetime: start, reuse, replacement on changed sandbox settings, least-recently-used eviction, idle stop and restart after failure.

assumptions: The server runs the project's build scripts and macros, so `spawn_process` always starts it through `ostra_sandbox::host_command` with the project root.
Ostra needs UTF-16 columns. A server that announces another `positionEncoding` is closed with an error.
Servers report canonical paths. `Server::rel` accepts paths under the root or under its canonical form, and rejects paths with `..`.
`LspProvider` answers only for files whose language id is in the entry's `languages`. For any other file it returns `Ok(None)`.
A deps request always returns `Ok(None)`, because the built-in index answers it.
Files read for locations must be UTF-8 and at most 1 MiB (`lsp::read_text`).

subsections.title: Completion, signature help and navigation
subsections.purpose: These calls serve the file editor. Each one sends the unsaved text to the server first, then asks one request at the cursor. ostra-server passes a short wait (`HINT_WAIT`) so a starting server does not hold the editor.

subsections.title: Files outside the project
subsections.purpose: A server may point at library sources under a package cache (`file://`) or at classes inside jars (jdtls `jdt://`). Ostra shows them read-only. `src/lsp/external.rs` describes such a URI with a name, a display path and a language. `LspProvider::external_file` reads the text, and `external_usages` asks for definitions and project references from a position in that file.

owns: URI description, the `~` shortening of the home folder, and the jar display path `{jar} › {package path}/{class}`.

does_not_own: The check that the server of this process answered with that URI, done by ostra-server through `LspPool::external_server`.

assumptions: Only `file` and `jdt` schemes can be read. Other schemes describe to None, which gives the error "Ostra cannot read this kind of location."
A `jdt://` class is read with the jdtls request `java/classFileContents`. An empty answer gives the error "`{server}` has no source or decompiled text for {name}."
Content above 1 MiB is refused with "{name} is larger than 1 MB, the size Ostra reads."
