sections.title: JSON-RPC client
sections.purpose: `src/lsp/rpc.rs` speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over the Language Server Protocol's `Content-Length` framing. One `Client` owns one server connection and runs three tasks. The writer task frames outgoing messages. The reader task routes responses to their callers and answers the requests a server sends its client. The stderr task keeps the server's last output lines for error messages. The client also tracks the server's progress state for the "still loading" warning.

owns: Request ids, pending replies, timeouts and cancellation (`$/cancelRequest` when a caller stops waiting).
Connection death reasons, which include the server's last stderr line.
Replies to server-to-client requests.
Busy state from `$/progress` and rust-analyzer's `experimental/serverStatus`.
Shutdown: `shutdown` (3 seconds), `exit`, then a kill when the process has not exited after 2 seconds; then the sandbox members are dropped.
does_not_own: The process and sandbox members, which `spawn_process` in the language server section creates and hands over in `Transport`.

assumptions: Headers other than `Content-Length` are ignored, and the header name is matched case-insensitively.
A message above 256 MiB ends the connection.
Once dead, a client stays dead. Every pending request gets the death reason, and new requests fail at once.
Stderr keeps the last 20 non-empty lines, each cut to 300 characters.

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Caller
  participant Cl as Client
  participant W as writer task
  participant S as Language server
  participant R as reader task
  C->>Cl: request(method, params, timeout)
  Cl->>Cl: "check dead, insert pending id"
  Cl->>W: JSON body
  W->>S: "Content-Length header and body"
  S-->>R: response with id
  R-->>Cl: "oneshot reply (result or rpc_error)"
  Cl-->>C: Reply
  Note over Cl,S: "On timeout or drop: $/cancelRequest"

parts.overview: ostra-core is the shared domain crate of the Ostra Rust workspace. It holds the types, constants, and pure functions that every other crate agrees on, and it has no server, database, or network code of its own. It defines these: the IDs, the 14 agents and their capabilities, the executors and model tiers, the three settings files and how a model route resolves from them, the pipeline stages and lanes, the append-only session event log, the contract between the engine and an executor, tool calls and policy decisions, the submit payload of each agent, the typed research, spec, and plan documents, the documentation books, and the REST and WebSocket shapes the browser uses. Fourteen sibling crates depend on it: ostra-server, ostra-engine, ostra-exec-native, ostra-exec-harness, ostra-tools, ostra-policy, ostra-workspace, ostra-sandbox, ostra-store, ostra-agents, ostra-code, ostra-mcp, ostra-notify, and ostra-providers. The React console in web reads the same types from TypeScript bindings that ts-rs generates into web/src/api/gen/. The crate's other modules handle filesystem safety: path derivation, secret paths, git command hardening, process-tree control, and shell discovery.

sections.title: Execution contract
sections.purpose: src/exec.rs is the contract between the engine and whatever runs an execution, either the native loop or a harness in a PTY. The engine builds an ExecutionSpec and an ExecutionHost and calls Executor::run. The executor streams ExecutionDelta values back through the host and returns an ExecutionResult.

owns: ExecutionSpec, ExecContext, ResumeInfo, ExecutionResult, ExecutionStatus, Usage, ExecutionDelta, Wake, and the ExecutionHost and Executor traits.

Implementing ExecutionHost, which ostra-engine does.

assumptions: Executors are Send + Sync and cancel through the tokio_util CancellationToken passed to run.

ExecutionHost methods with default bodies (record_message, transcript, yolo, wait_for_wake) may be left unimplemented by hosts that do not support them; wait_for_wake returning None means no message will come.

sections.title: Documentation books
sections.purpose: src/book.rs defines the documentation books the docs stage writes into a workspace. A book covers a set of projects. The engine writes every book file from the agents' submit payloads, and no agent writes one (Rule B5).

does_not_own: Deciding when a book is written, which the ostra-engine runner decides after the docs stage.

sections.title: Process trees
sections.purpose: src/proctree.rs stops a child process and everything it started as one unit. On Unix the child leads its own process group and Ostra signals the group. On Windows the child runs in a Job Object created with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE and no breakaway, so closing the job's handle, or Ostra exiting, ends the whole tree. The Bash tool, the Windows shell tool, and the MCP stdio client use it.

does_not_own: Spawning commands and choosing when to stop them, which ostra-tools and ostra-mcp do.

assumptions: The caller passes the command to prepare_tokio or prepare_std before spawning, because a Windows child must be in its job before it starts anything, or its first children escape the job.
On Windows the child is created suspended and without a console window; Tree::of_tokio or of_std assigns it to a new job and resumes it through NtResumeProcess, and kills it if either step fails.
adopt_running takes over a child started elsewhere, such as a PTY child; on Windows what it started before the call is not in the job.

parts.overview: ostra-engine is the orchestration crate of Ostra. It runs every session as an event-sourced state machine: it stores each `SessionEvent` in the workspace database, folds the log into a `SessionState`, and hands that state to a pure planner (`next_steps`), which returns the next `Step` values. The runner (`Engine` and its private `Inner`) performs each step. A step spawns an agent execution, calls a judge model, opens a gate for the user, runs a format or `git add` command, applies auto-fixes, or writes the documentation book. After each step the runner appends the resulting events and the planner runs again. The ostra-server crate calls the public `Engine` methods for every HTTP action, and it implements the `Services` trait that gives the engine configuration, executors, judge calls, and push notifications. ostra-agents renders the prompts and spawn blocks through `AgentsFactory`. ostra-store persists events, executions, gates, and decisions. ostra-sandbox runs the project's format command and cleans session caches. ostra-core supplies the shared types: events, gate payloads, submits, paths, and limits. The main sections below follow a session from its creation through the planner, each pipeline stage, the gates and judges that decide between stages, and the views the console reads.

sections.title: Engine public API
sections.purpose: `Engine` is the only type other crates use to act on sessions. ostra-server calls one `Engine` method for each console action: create a task, answer a gate, add context, pause, stop, ask a side-panel question, or read a session. Each method checks its input, appends events through `Inner::append`, and returns a `SessionSummary`, a `GateView`, an `ExecutionId`, or an `EngineError`.

owns: The set of public operations on sessions and the input checks each one makes before any event is written.
The `EngineError` variants and their user-facing messages.
The `EngineNotice` broadcast channel (capacity 4096) that `subscribe` returns.
does_not_own: HTTP routing and authentication, which ostra-server owns.
Persistence of rows, which ostra-store's `WorkspaceDb` owns.
What happens after an event is appended, which the Driver and event log section owns.

assumptions: One `Engine` exists per workspace, built with `Engine::new(workspace_root, workspace_id, db, services)`; every method assumes the `WorkspaceDb` belongs to that workspace.
Methods that spawn background work (`ask`, `inspect_execution`, `ensure_driver`) call `tokio::spawn`, so the caller must be inside a Tokio runtime.
`Engine::state` returns a clone of the folded state; callers assume the clone is a snapshot and never write back to it.
`EngineError::Store` wraps `ostra_store::StoreError`; callers map `NotFound` and `Invalid` to user-facing messages because their text is written for the user.

`resume_execution` needs an open ExecutionFailed or HarnessFailure gate for the execution; any other state is refused.

sections.title: Driver loop and event log
sections.purpose: Every session has one driver task that repeats one cycle: fold, plan, perform. `Inner::append` is the only way an event enters a session: it stores, folds, updates the session row, broadcasts, pushes a notification, and wakes the driver. The driver runs `next_steps` on the current state and starts each step it is not already performing.

owns: The per-session `Live` record: state mutex, wake `Notify`, in-flight step keys, and the `driving` flag.
The order of side effects on append: database event, materialized rows, fold, session row, notices, push, wake.
Which step kinds exist at run time and how each is performed (`Inner::perform`).
does_not_own: Which steps come next, which the Planner section owns.
How the fold interprets each event, which the Session state fold section owns.
Spawning details, which the Spawning an execution section owns.

assumptions: Appends for one session are serialized by the session's state mutex, so the stored `seq` order equals the fold order.
`Step::key` identifies a step uniquely enough that two steps with the same key must never run at once.
The planner is a pure function of `SessionState` and `PlanCtx`; the driver can call it any number of times.
A step failure other than `EngineError::Ended` is recorded as a `Note` event and does not stop the driver.

subsections.title: Appending an event
subsections.purpose: `Inner::append` writes one `SessionEvent` and keeps every derived store in step with it. It runs for every event, from `SessionCreated` to `SessionCompleted`.
assumptions: The state mutex is held across the database write and the fold, so no other append can interleave.
After a session is terminal, an `ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionResumed`, or `CommandStarted` event is refused with `EngineError::Ended`; the check runs under the state lock so it cannot race a stop.
The session's cost is the sum of every execution row's `usage.cost_usd` plus the session's judge cost in `Inner::judge_cost`.

subsections.title: The drive loop
subsections.purpose: `ensure_driver` starts at most one `drive` task per session, guarded by the `driving` flag. `drive` locks the state, computes steps, starts each new step in its own task, and waits for the next wake.
assumptions: Every event append and every finished step calls `wake.notify_one`, so the loop never sleeps while work is ready.

`PlanCtx` is rebuilt each cycle by `plan_ctx`: the session budget from `limits.session_budget_usd` (0 or less means no limit) and each project's non-blank `commands.format` from `.ostra/project.toml`.

diagrams.title: Drive loop decisions
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
    lock[Lock session state] --> term{"Terminal?"}
    term -- yes --> stop[Clear driving flag and exit]
    term -- no --> plan["next_steps(state, plan_ctx)"]
    plan --> each{"Step key already in flight?"}
    each -- yes --> skip[Skip the step]
    each -- no --> run[Spawn task: perform step]
    run --> done["Remove key, notify wake"]
    skip --> wait[Await wake]
    done --> wait
    wait --> lock

sections.purpose: `perform_spawn` turns a planner `SpawnRequest` into a running agent execution. It waits for a slot, resolves the model route, picks the repo root, writes the files some agents read, builds the prompt through the spawn factory, records the execution, runs the executor with an `EngineHost`, and appends the result.

owns: Route resolution per spawn, including the GenerateSkill tier override to Advanced and forced executors.
The `ExecContext` given to executors: permissions, sandbox settings, protected paths, memory database, and project-creation flag.
Synthetic report files for TEST and DOCS sessions and the docs-parts JSON for the architecture agent.
The `SecurityBlock` event after a review with `security_block`.
does_not_own: Prompt and spawn-block rendering, which the Spawn factory section and ostra-agents own.
Running the model and tools, which the executor crates own.
What the result means for the session, which the Session state fold section owns.

assumptions: `Services::executor(kind)` returns `None` for an executor the server does not have; the spawn is then recorded as Denied.
A resumed run keeps its executor and model, and a continued conversation runs on the executor and model it started on, so the prompt cache holds.
An execution cancelled while the fold lists it in `interrupting` is an interruption, not a user stop; its status is rewritten to Interrupted with the interrupt's message.
The review execution's params carry the project's auto-fixable rule IDs under `auto_fixable_ids` so the fold can split findings without reading files.

code_refs.note: A spawn that cannot start becomes an execution with status Denied.

subsections.title: Spawn setup
subsections.purpose: The first half of `perform_spawn` decides whether the spawn resumes a paused or waiting run, continues another run's conversation, or starts fresh, and prepares everything the executor needs.
assumptions: `req.resumes` names a paused run only when its agent matches and its result status is Interrupted or Waiting.
A Waiting run wakes only when `next_delivery` has a message for it; otherwise the spawn returns without doing anything.
A phase whose project does not exist yet (`project_to_create`) runs with the project's session dir as repo root, so its sandbox can write nowhere else until it creates the project (Rule O2).

business_flow.action: Acquires a slot, then returns early when the session is terminal or paused.
business_flow.outcome: No run starts in a stopped or paused session.

business_flow.action: Writes the session context file when the spawn lists it in `context_files`.
business_flow.outcome: A revision reads a current context (Rule F2).

business_flow.action: Resolves the route with `resolve_route` and applies the paused or continued run's executor and model.
business_flow.outcome: A route error or a missing executor is recorded as Denied.

business_flow.action: Loads the profile, inventory, and project docs from the repo root; writes `ostra-test-request.md` or `ostra-docs-request.md` stubs when missing; writes the parts JSON for SystemArchitecture.
business_flow.outcome: The agent's inputs exist on disk.

business_flow.action: Builds the spawn with `SpawnFactory::build`; a build error is recorded as Denied with `spawn: <error>`.
business_flow.outcome: System prompt, first message, spawn block, params, report file, and effort are known.

business_flow.action: For a resume appends MessageDelivered (when waking) and ExecutionResumed and reopens the row; otherwise appends ExecutionStarted and inserts the row.
business_flow.outcome: The execution is recorded before it runs.

subsections.title: Execution slots
subsections.purpose: The engine limits how many executions run at once in a workspace to `limits.max_parallel_executions`. A `Slot` value holds one place; dropping it frees the place and wakes waiting spawns.
assumptions: The limit is re-read from `Services::workspace()` on every attempt, so a settings change applies to spawns already waiting.
A limit below 1 is treated as 1.
A run that waits for a subagent message gives its slot back (Rule H2), so the run it waits for can start.

subsections.title: EngineHost callbacks
subsections.purpose: `EngineHost` implements `ExecutionHost` for one running execution. Executors call it to report activity, usage, native session IDs, transcripts, and permission asks, and harness runs call `wait_for_wake` to wait for a subagent message.
assumptions: Executors report usage counted from zero for each run; `emit` adds `usage_base` so a resumed run's usage includes what it spent before (Rule P2).
The submit tool call ends every run, so a tool call whose name contains `submit_` does not replace the execution's summary line.
`ostra_core::containment::classify` decides which deltas are containment signals.

subsections.title: Permission asks
subsections.purpose: When a tool call needs the user's approval, the executor calls `ask_permission`. The engine opens a Permission gate and blocks the call on a oneshot channel until `answer_gate`, `set_yolo`, `stop_session`, or an interrupt answers it.
assumptions: A dropped channel answers Deny.
If appending the GateOpened event fails, the ask is denied at once.
A Permission gate belongs to its live execution, so the planner never schedules a YOLO answer for it; YOLO is applied inside `ask_permission` instead.

sections.title: Session state fold
sections.purpose: `SessionState` is the whole session as a pure function of its event log. `SessionState::fold` applies every stored event in order with `apply`. The planner, the views, and the judges read only this state, so replaying the log rebuilds exactly what the engine knew.

owns: Every derived field of `SessionState`: tracks, loops, gates, decisions, notes, asks, and interrupts.
The meaning of each `SessionEvent`.
Helpers other sections use: `full_request`, `primary`, `research_docs`, `ledger_path`, `purpose_key`, `stage_of`.
does_not_own: Writing events, which the Driver and event log section owns.
The event types themselves, which ostra-core defines in `ostra_core::event`.

assumptions: Events arrive in `seq` order; `apply` sets `last_seq` and `updated_at` from each one.
Facts from outside the log that change behavior are recorded in events at spawn time, such as `auto_fixable_ids` in review params, so the fold never reads files.
An event that names an unknown execution, gate, or decision is ignored.

subsections.title: The request agents read
subsections.purpose: `full_request` builds the request text every agent receives: the original request, the attached files as absolute paths with their tags, the uploads, and every delivered amendment. `added_context` builds only the delivered amendments for a spawn whose task was written before them.
assumptions: An attached file of project `artifacts::TAG_ROOT` resolves under the workspace artifacts folder; any other resolves under its project path.
Paths are written with forward slashes on every OS.
Only amendments with `delivered` true join the request; pending, remembered, and discarded ones do not.

subsections.title: Purpose keys, loop keys, and stage kinds
subsections.purpose: Several maps index executions by what they do rather than by ID. `purpose_key` names one work loop, review loop, or stage; `purpose_loop` maps an execution to its phase loop `(phase, tests)`; `stage_of` maps a purpose to a `StageKind` for the console lanes.
assumptions: All work passes of one phase loop share a key (`work:<phase>:<tests>`), so a pause resume or a waiting wake reaches the loop's next spawn whatever its WorkKind.
Explore, Docs, Init, and other purposes use their JSON form as key, so each task or project is distinct.

sections.title: Planner
sections.purpose: `next_steps` is a pure function from `SessionState` and `PlanCtx` to the steps the runner should perform now. It holds every gate and ordering rule of the pipeline in code, so the conformance fixtures can test the pipeline from an event history alone. The runner calls it after every event.

owns: The order of stages per category and the conditions for moving between them.
The guards every step passes in `Planner::push`.
The inputs each spawn receives (`SpawnInputs`).
does_not_own: Performing steps, which the Driver and event log section owns.
Interpreting results, which the Session state fold section owns.

assumptions: The planner reads no files and calls no services; everything it needs is in the state or `PlanCtx`.
Returning a step that is already in flight is harmless because the runner skips keys in its in-flight set.
A paused, terminal, or not yet created session plans nothing (Rule P1).

subsections.title: Step kinds and step keys
subsections.purpose: `Step` lists every action the planner can ask for. `Step::key` is the identity the runner uses to avoid starting a step twice; `Step::summary` is the compact form the conformance fixtures compare.
assumptions: Init spawns include the project in their key, because each created project runs its own init in one session.
A gate's key is its payload kind plus an owner from `gate_owner`, so one gate per kind and owner is planned at a time.

subsections.title: Guards on every planned step
subsections.purpose: `Planner::push` applies session-wide rules to each step before it is added. A step can be dropped, changed into a resume or a continuation, or replaced by a budget gate.
assumptions: The budget counts only finished executions (`spent_usd`); running executions count when they finish.
`budget_raised` holds every raise the user made; the limit is the workspace budget plus that sum.

    s[Step planned] --> held{"Spawn, command, or autofix in a project awaiting init?"}

sections.title: Spec and plan stages
sections.purpose: The spec and the plan each have an `ArtifactTrack`: generation runs, the current submit, a version number, fact-check passes, open questions, approval, and failure state. The planner drives both through the same cycle: generate, ask open questions, fact-check, and ask for approval.

Rules D3, D3a, D3b, D4, D5, and D10 as the planner and fold apply them.
does_not_own: Answer routing for these gates, which the Answer routing section owns.
Phase creation from the approved plan, which the Phase scheduling section owns.

assumptions: A new version is counted only when a generation run ends Ok with a submit that parses; every new version revokes approval.
An approval counts only for the version it was asked on and only after a fact-check PASS on that version.
The spec and the plan are written in the session root, and cross-project stages carry the primary project's key.

subsections.title: Spec cycle
subsections.purpose: `spec_flow` returns true once the spec is done for the category: a fact-check PASS, plus approval when the category needs it. SPEC sessions skip approval; PLAN and full-track IMPLEMENT sessions need it.
assumptions: A revision receives only input its spec does not reflect yet: new answers, new changes, and research documents not in `applied.docs`, plus the existing spec path so it edits in place.
Open questions are asked before any fact-check of the version that has them (Rule D3).

subsections.title: Plan cycle
subsections.purpose: `plan_flow` runs only after the spec exists. The plan agent reads the spec, its own earlier plan, and findings on a FAIL re-run, and nothing else (Rule D4). Clarifying questions from the plan change requirements, so their answers go into the spec first (Rule D10).
assumptions: When the plan is invalidated by a spec change, the next plan run gets no findings and revises the earlier plan in place; its start clears `invalidated`, pending findings, and the FAIL count.
A plan fact-check always uses the `citations` source check and receives the spec file (Rules D3b, D5).

subsections.title: Fact-check passes
subsections.purpose: Each fact-check pass is recorded against the artifact version it checked. A PASS resets the FAIL count; a FAIL stores the findings and asks for another generation run.
assumptions: A pass whose verdict is Error, or whose run did not end Ok with a valid submit, is not a result: the pass is removed and one Error is retried automatically.
The first spec pass uses `refetch` when the spec has External Evidence rows; every later pass and every plan pass uses `citations` (Rule D3b).
Prior findings are `none` on a first pass, `no findings on the previous pass` after a clean pass, and the previous findings text otherwise (Rule D3a).

subsections.title: Requirement changes after the spec exists
subsections.purpose: `requirement_change` implements Rule D10: a change to requirements after the spec exists restarts at the spec. It adds the change, marks the spec for a run, revokes spec approval, and when a plan exists or ran, revokes plan approval and invalidates the plan.
assumptions: Plan approval feedback, plan question answers, plan recurring-gate text, amendments routed as requirement changes, and phase-gate answers routed as requirement changes all go through this function.
After the spec is approved again, `approve_spec` marks the invalidated plan for a run and builds any feedback round that waited for the spec.

sections.purpose: An IMPLEMENT session builds phases. The Track judge chooses light or full; the Stakes judge decides whether a full-track session writes a plan. Phases come from the approved plan or are created inline, one per project. The planner starts a phase when its dependencies passed review and no other implement pipeline runs in its project.

Dependency readiness (`deps_passed`) and removal of dependents of blocked phases (`removed_phases`).
does_not_own: What happens inside a phase, which the Work loops section owns.

Inline phases depend on the previous inline phase, so they run in scope order (Rule M5).
A plan phase whose dependency list names a missing phase or itself depends on every earlier phase (Rule M5).
A plan phase in a project that is neither in the workspace nor a planned new project is blocked at once.

sections.title: Work loops
sections.purpose: Each phase has two `WorkLoop` values: `impl_loop` for the implementation and `test_loop` for tests. A loop alternates work passes and code reviews until the review leaves no HIGH or MEDIUM finding, then stages the changed files. `LoopNext` says what the loop does next; the fold changes it when an execution ends or a gate is answered, and the planner turns it into a step.

owns: `WorkLoop` and `LoopNext` for every phase.
Fix, blocker, rescue, and handoff instructions sent to agents.
Review caps, YOLO resolution rounds, and loop-level retries.
does_not_own: The review itself, which the code-reviewer agent in ostra-agents owns.
Applying auto-fixes, which the Auto-fixes section owns.
Staging command execution, which the runner's `perform_command` owns.

assumptions: Only one execution runs per loop; `loop_finished` ignores a result from an execution that is not the loop's `running` one.
`in_flight` holds the step the running execution performs, so an interruption can restore it.
The work agent runs the first pass and a rerun or resume while `work_count` is at most 1; later passes use the fix agent.

subsections.title: Work pass outcomes
subsections.purpose: A work pass is an implementer, write-test, prompt-generation, or verify run. Its submit is read as an `ImplementerSubmit` or a `ReportSubmit`; its status decides whether the loop reviews, rescues, hands off, stages, or ends.
assumptions: A submit that parses as neither type fails the loop with the missing-submit message.
Changed files accumulate in `changed` across passes; the implement loop's report path becomes the phase's `implementer_report`.
Files ending in `.md`, `.mdx`, `.txt`, or a `.toml` whose path contains `agent` are instruction files for ReviewMode IfCodeChanged.

subsections.title: Review outcomes
subsections.purpose: A review pass increments `iterations` and splits the findings. BLOCKER findings go alone to the fix agent without any cap (Hard rule 21). Auto-fixable findings are applied by the engine. HIGH and MEDIUM findings go to the fix agent until the cap. LOW findings are recorded as leftovers and do not keep the loop open.
assumptions: A finding is auto-fixable when its rule ID is in the project's auto-fixable IDs recorded at spawn, it is not BLOCKER, and its rule does not start with `SEC-BLOCK` or `PHASE-REQ`.
A review with `security_block` true is treated as a BLOCKER even when no finding has that severity.

subsections.title: Review cap and YOLO resolution
subsections.purpose: The cap is `REVIEW_CAP` (3) passes, or `YOLO_REVIEW_BUDGET` (10) under YOLO, plus `extra_cap`. Outside YOLO the cap opens a ReviewCap gate. Under YOLO the ResolveReview judge either writes instructions per finding or blocks the phase; resolution repeats while the open count shrinks.
assumptions: Each Fix decision of the ResolveReview judge adds one resolution round and one extra review pass.
Resolution stops converging when a round leaves as many or more findings open than before it; the loop then blocks with the ledger path in its reason.

The phase stays blocked; dependents stay removed.

subsections.title: Rescue and handoff
subsections.purpose: A pass that submits STUCK is never simply retried. The Rescue judge chooses: research the missing fact with a targeted explore, rerun with a fact it states, or ask the user through a Stuck gate. A pass that submits HANDOFF runs prompt-generation, then resumes the work agent with the handoff's resume instructions.

A handoff prompt-generation run belongs to the loop of the execution it serves.

subsections.title: Loop failures and interrupts
subsections.purpose: When a loop's execution ends without OK, STUCK, or HANDOFF, the loop retries once on Error, then fails and opens a failure gate. An interrupted execution re-runs with the same instructions (HANDOVER 11.2).
assumptions: An error starting with `harness-` is never retried automatically and opens a HarnessFailure gate instead of ExecutionFailed.

subsections.title: Staging reviewed files

sections.title: Auto-fixes
sections.purpose: The engine applies review findings whose Fix text has an exact form, without an agent run. Two forms exist: ``Change `old` to `new` on line N.`` and ``Add `text` above line N: `anchor`.`` The runner calls `apply_findings` on a blocking thread and appends `AutofixApplied`.

does_not_own: Choosing which findings are auto-fixable, which the Work loops section owns from the project's review rule set.

A file whose normalized path leaves the project is not touched.

business_flow.action: Adds failed HIGH and MEDIUM auto-fixes to the remaining findings and continues the loop.

subsections.purpose: `context::render` writes `ostra-session-context.md` in the session root: the request, route, research documents, spec, plan, phases with status and reports, and each feedback round. A revision reads this file instead of a conversation, so a session can take any number of rounds without its context growing (Rule F2).

sections.title: Closing stages: format, tests, documentation, and the book
sections.purpose: After the implementation is accepted, each project whose phases are finished runs its closing stages: the format command once, the closing gate that asks for tests and documentation, the test stage, and the documentation stage. When every documented part is written, the engine writes the architecture for books of two or more projects and then the workspace book.

EPA and test loop scheduling, docs writer fan-out, architecture, and the book write step.
does_not_own: The book file format and merge logic, which ostra-core's `ostra_core::book::apply` owns.
Test and documentation content, which the write-test and documentation agents own.

assumptions: Only projects with at least one phase that passed review run closing stages.
A request for both tests and documentation, from the form toggles or the Classify judge's `opts_in`, replaces the closing gate (Rule T3).
An open BLOCKER in any passed phase of a project blocks its documentation (Hard rule 21).

subsections.title: Format command
subsections.purpose: Format runs once per project after its last phase and is not gated (Rule D8). The command comes from the project's `commands.format` in `.ostra/project.toml`.
assumptions: A format command runs only when `Services::command_approved(project, command)` is true (Rule A1); otherwise it is skipped once with `FORMAT_NOT_APPROVED` as output and no exit code.
The command runs as `bash -c <command>` through `ostra_sandbox::host_command` under the workspace sandbox, with a 600-second timeout.
Command output keeps its last 4000 bytes, prefixed with `...` when cut.

subsections.title: Closing gate
subsections.purpose: The ClosingGate asks, per project, whether to write tests and whether to write documentation. Projects reaching it together are asked in one gate (Rule T6).
assumptions: An item asks only what the request did not already ask for; the other choice takes the request's value.
Under YOLO the gate takes its defaults: no tests and no docs unless the request asked for them.

subsections.title: Test stage
subsections.purpose: Tests cover phases without a file (no plan) and phases with test policy Required (Rule T4). The execution-path analyzer (EPA) runs for every covered phase in parallel; then write-test loops run one at a time in phase order, each with its own review loop.
assumptions: The test loop waits for every covered phase's EPA to be Done or Abandoned.
An EPA that errors is retried once; a second failure opens a failure gate; abandoning it skips that phase's tests.

subsections.title: Documentation parts, architecture, and the book
subsections.purpose: Each documented project gets one documentation writer, which submits that project's part of the book. When all parts are known, a book of two or more parts first gets a system-architecture run, then the engine writes the book into the workspace (Rules B4 to B7).
assumptions: At most `MAX_DOCS_WRITERS` (4) documentation writers run or are queued at once.
A docs or architecture run is Done only with a submit that parses; an Ok run without one fails with `The run ended without a readable submit call, so there is nothing to put in the book.`
The book ID is the one picked on the New task form when it is a valid book ID, else `ostra_core::book::book_id` of the documented project keys, so an abandoned part names no book (Rule B6).
Before the architecture run the runner writes every part as JSON to `ostra-docs-parts.json` in the session root.

This section lists every gate payload, its answers, and its effect.

sections.title: YOLO mode
sections.purpose: Under YOLO the engine answers every open gate without waiting for the user (HANDOVER 10.5). Most gates get a fixed answer; open questions, approvals, and stuck agents get an answer from the YOLO judge, which the engine checks before applying.

Turning YOLO on mid-session takes effect from the next gate or tool call; the planner then answers gates already open.

sections.title: Subagent coordination
sections.purpose: Running agents can ask each other questions and wake each other with the answer, so a subagent continues from its own conversation instead of reading a report cold (HANDOVER 10.8). A subagent is one conversation; its ID is the ID of the conversation's first execution. Pair loops, such as generate-spec and its fact-checker or an implementer and its reviewer, continue their conversations across rounds.

owns: The `asks` map, `subagents` roots, and `waiting_keys`.
Routing a question, delivering messages, consult runs, and pair-loop continuation.
does_not_own: The tool definitions and input parsing (`AskInput`, `ReplyInput`), which `ostra_core::coord` owns.
Exposing the tools to models, which the executor and MCP crates own.

assumptions: Every coordination fact is derived from the log: `AgentAsked`, `AgentReplied`, `MessageDelivered`, and execution events.
A native run that asks ends with status Waiting; a harness run that asks stays alive and waits in `wait_for_wake`.

Limits from ostra-core: 3 helpers per run (`MAX_HELPERS_PER_RUN`), 24 asks per session (`MAX_SESSION_ASKS`), 6 runs per conversation before a pair loop starts fresh (`MAX_CONVERSATION_RUNS`), and explore as the only helper agent (`HELPER_AGENTS`).

subsections.title: Asks, routes, and deliveries
subsections.purpose: A question goes to a new helper (an explore run in a project) or to an existing subagent. `route` decides where a question to a subagent goes now: wake it in place, start a consult run that continues its conversation, keep it pending, or fail with a message the asker receives as its answer (Rule H3).
assumptions: A subagent that waits on the asker is woken in place with the question.
A subagent whose last run ended OK, STUCK, or HANDOFF with a submit is consulted; one that ended Error, Denied, or Cancelled cannot answer.
A helper that errors is retried once before its failure becomes the asker's answer; a helper's failure never opens a gate.

sections.title: Project init flow
sections.purpose: Init prepares a project for Ostra by generating its skills, `.ostra/INVENTORY.md`, and `.ostra/project.toml`. It runs the initializer agent in modes: detect, scout per slice (parallel, at most 6), propose, a skill approval gate, generate-skill per approved skill (parallel, Advanced tier), and generate-inventory (HANDOVER 8.4). The same flow runs as its own init session and for each project an agent created in a pipeline session (Rule O4).

owns: `InitTrack` for the init session and for each created project.
The advisor loop for created projects (Rule O5).
does_not_own: What each initializer mode writes, which the initializer prompts in ostra-agents own.
The project's init status row, which ostra-store owns and the runner sets through `set_project_init_status`.

assumptions: Detect's result JSON has `slices` (with `slug`, `descriptor`, `paths`), `existing_skills`, `scout_plan_path`, and `reference_name`; missing fields read as empty.
Propose's result has `skills` with `name`, `kind`, `status`, `recommend`, `description`, `rationale`, `existing_path`, and `component_type`, plus `proposal_path`.
A result sent as a JSON-encoded string is decoded before use.
An init session completes only when the inventory and a valid profile exist on disk.

parts.overview: ostra-exec-harness is the Ostra crate that runs one leaf agent inside an installed harness CLI: Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, or Antigravity. The CLI runs under a pseudo-terminal (PTY) and, when the configuration asks for one, inside Ostra's sandbox. The crate implements the `Executor` trait from ostra-core as `HarnessExecutor`, and ostra-engine calls it through ostra-server's `HarnessRuntime` for every route whose executor is `ExecutorKind::Harness`. For each execution it writes a launch plan that registers `ostra hook` for the CLI's hook events and `ostra mcp-stdio` as the CLI's `ostra` MCP server. Those two subprocesses forward every hook payload and every MCP message to the server's `/internal/policy` and `/internal/mcp` routes, where `HarnessBridge` checks each tool call with the policy engine through the `BridgeServices` trait, which ostra-server implements. The main parts are the executor and its supervision loop, the launch plans, the bridge and MCP shim, the per-harness adapters, the PTY sessions that the web console's Terminal tab streams, the sandbox wrap, the harness setup helpers, and the transcript and usage readers. The run ends when the agent's `submit_<agent>` call is recorded, or when the executor maps a timeout, idle session, sign-in screen, early exit, or cancel to an `ExecutionResult`.

sections.title: Harness execution lifecycle
sections.purpose: `HarnessExecutor::run` runs one leaf agent execution in a harness CLI from start to result. ostra-engine calls it, through ostra-server's `Wrapped` executor, for every `ExecutionSpec` whose route executor is `ExecutorKind::Harness(kind)`. It registers the execution, launches the CLI in a PTY, supervises it until an `End`, tears everything down, and returns one `ExecutionResult`.

owns: Registering the execution in `LiveRegistry` at start and removing it at the end, which also invalidates the execution's bridge token.
Inserting the `PtySession` into `PtyRegistry` while the CLI runs and removing it at the end.
Creating the per-execution config dir `harness_execution_dir(session_root, execution_id)`.
Starting and stopping the live usage follower task (`usage_watch::follow`).
Removing the Codex restricted profile file and calling `sandbox::cleanup` after the run.
The read-only (inspect) result: an inspection that ends by exit or timeout returns `Ok` with final text `The read-only session ended.`.
does_not_own: Choosing the route, the model, the timeout, and building `ExecutionSpec`: ostra-engine.
Registering the per-execution policy and tool environment before the run: ostra-server's `Wrapped` executor in `src/bridge.rs`.
Deciding each tool call: the hook bridge section and ostra-server's `ServerBridge`.
Mapping an `End` to status and error text: the execution outcome section.
Building the command line and config files: the launch plans section.

assumptions: `spec.route.executor` is `ExecutorKind::Harness`; `run` returns `ExecutionResult::error("the harness executor was given a native route")` otherwise.

`HarnessExecutorConfig::ostra_binary` is an executable that serves the `hook` and `mcp-stdio` subcommands; ostra-server passes its own executable, whose `hook` and `mcp-stdio` commands call `run_hook_cli` and `run_mcp_stdio`.
The server registers the execution's policy entry before `run` starts, so the first hook call finds it; ostra-server's `Wrapped::run` inserts it before calling `inner.run`.
The server calls `set_global` before each execution, because `launch` reads `config().global` once per run; ostra-server's `HarnessRuntime::inner` does this.
`dirs::home_dir()` is the home of the user whose harness CLIs are installed and signed in; `HarnessExecutorConfig::new` falls back to `/` when there is none.
`spec.ctx.repo_root` and `spec.ctx.workspace_root` are the only git repositories whose metadata needs repair; `ostra_sandbox::git_repos` is called with those two paths only.

subsections.title: Git metadata repair
subsections.purpose: A harness CLI runs its own shell commands, and a hook sees the command only before it runs, so a command could plant a `commondir` file in a repository's git dir that points the user's own git at another location. The executor checks the execution's repositories every 2 s while the CLI runs, and once more at the end, and undoes each planted `commondir`.

owns: When the repair runs: every `GIT_CHECK_EVERY` inside the supervision loop and once after it.
Reporting each repair to the host as an `ExecutionDelta::Policy` denial by the `git-metadata` guard.
does_not_own: Finding git dirs and undoing the file: `ostra_sandbox::git_repos`, `ostra_sandbox::repair_git_dirs`, and `ostra_sandbox::git_repair_note` in ostra-sandbox.
Counting denials as containment signals: ostra-engine.

assumptions: A planted file that exists for up to 2 s does no harm before it is removed; the check runs on a clock, not on each command.
The emitted denial has an empty `call_id`, and consumers accept a policy delta without a tool call id.

sections.title: Supervision loop
sections.purpose: `HarnessExecutor::supervise` watches one running CLI and decides when the execution ends. It wakes on every change to the `LiveExecution`, every 500 ms, on process exit, and on cancel. It returns an `End`: `Submitted`, `GaveUp`, `Exited`, `Timeout`, `Cancelled`, `Idle`, `Auth`, or `Fatal`.

owns: The time budget: `max(spec.timeout_secs, 30)` seconds, extended by time spent waiting for a subagent answer.
When a recorded submit ends the run.
Answering startup prompts: folder trust and new-model offers.
Recognizing sign-in screens and fatal startup errors on screen.
Typing idle reminders and wake notes into the terminal.
does_not_own: Recording the submit, stop counts, and waiting state: the live execution registry section, driven by the hook bridge and MCP shim.
Producing the wake note: ostra-engine through `ExecutionHost::wait_for_wake`.

assumptions: `LiveExecution::changed` is notified on every state change that matters; the loop also wakes every 500 ms, so a missed notification delays a decision by at most 500 ms.
Screen prompts appear before the first tool call and within 120 s of start; the startup checks run only while `tool_calls == 0` and `started.elapsed() < 120 s`.
An inspect run (`resume.inspect`) is driven by the user; submit, wait, give-up, and idle checks are skipped for it, and it ends on exit, timeout, or cancel.
The harness's selection cursor is drawn as a line starting with `❯`, `›`, `▸`, or `> `; `trust_key`, `restricted_key`, and `keep_model_key` find the selected option that way.

At most 6 trust answers are typed (`trust_steps < 6`), with 400 ms between screen reads after an answer.

sections.title: Launch plans
sections.purpose: `launch::plan` builds a `LaunchPlan` for one execution: the program, its arguments, environment, working dir, the files and symlinks to create, and the session id Ostra chose. Each harness has its own builder, because each CLI takes hooks, MCP servers, prompts, and trust settings in its own way. Every flag was checked against claude 2.1.280, codex 0.153.4, grok 1.0.30, and agy 1.2.6.

The Antigravity plugin and agent file format: the harness setup section.

The CLI runs hook commands through a shell, so `hook_command` quotes the binary path with `shell_quote`.
`spec.capabilities` lists the agent's tools; Claude Code's `--tools` and Antigravity's agent `tools:` are derived from it.
`ostra_core::git::agent_env()` returns the git config variables every agent command must carry (the tests expect `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`); `plan` adds them to every plan.

subsections.title: Shared plan rules
subsections.purpose: Rules every harness plan follows: the four bridge environment variables, the hook command line, the prompt argument, the effort word, the credential filter, the extra `--add-dir` folders, quoting, and how files are written.

owns: `HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS`, `MAX_ARG_PROMPT`, `sign_in_env`, `resume_prompt`, `shell_quote`, `posix_quote`, `materialize`, `artifacts_dir_args`.
does_not_own: The list of credential variable names, which `ostra_core::config::credential_env_names` builds from the global config and the workspace's MCP servers.

assumptions: A hook can wait for a user's permission answer for up to a day, so every hook and MCP tool timeout is `HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS` (86,400 s).

A first message longer than 96 KiB (`MAX_ARG_PROMPT`) does not fit safely on the command line; it is written to `first-message.md` in the config dir and the prompt tells the agent to read that file first.
`materialize` skips a link whose path already exists (`symlink_metadata` succeeds), so an old link is never replaced.

On Windows the hook shell can be Git Bash or cmd, so `shell_quote` turns backslashes into `/`, leaves plain words bare, double-quotes words with spaces, and falls back to POSIX single quotes when a word holds `"`, `%`, `$`, a backtick, `!`, or `'`.

subsections.purpose: `plan_claude` writes three files in the config dir and passes them by flag: `claude-settings.json` with Ostra's hooks, `claude-mcp.json` with the `ostra` stdio server, and `system-prompt.md`. does_not_own: The user's `~/.claude` settings, which still load through `--setting-sources user`.

assumptions: Flag settings (`--settings`) take precedence over the user's settings file, so `disableAllHooks: false` there cannot be switched off by the user.
Interactive Claude Code exposes MCP tools only as deferred tools, so `ToolSearch` is always added to `--tools`; without it the `mcp__ostra__*` tools never reach the model.
The prompt must follow a non-variadic flag, so the argument list ends with `--effort <word>`, the artifacts `--add-dir` pairs, and then the prompt.
When Ostra runs the CLI in its own sandbox, Claude Code must not start its own, because macOS cannot nest Seatbelt sandboxes; the settings then carry `sandbox.enabled: false`.

subsections.purpose: `plan_codex` passes hooks, the MCP server, the developer instructions, and the effort as `-c key=value` overrides, each value a TOML literal. It opens the repository restricted through a per-execution profile, so the repository's `.codex/` config, hooks, and exec policies stay off and the user's saved trust is not changed.

does_not_own: The user's own Codex profiles; a user profile in `[harness.codex].args` replaces Ostra's restricted profile.

assumptions: Codex reads folder trust only from config files, not from `-c`, so trust is set by a profile file in `$CODEX_HOME` or `~/.codex`.

Codex applies project config from every folder between the repository and its git root, so the profile marks the repository and each parent up to the first one with `.git`, at most 32 levels; with no git root only the repository is marked.
When `[harness.codex].args` holds `-p`, `--profile`, or `--profile=...`, Ostra writes no profile; the trust prompt then appears and the supervision loop refuses it.
Codex updates itself at startup and exits, so `check_for_update_on_startup=false` is always set.
Ostra's hooks change on every execution and cannot hold persisted hook trust, so `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` is passed; project hooks stay off because the folder opens restricted.

sections.title: Hook bridge
sections.purpose: `HarnessBridge::handle_policy` answers one hook event that `ostra hook` forwarded to the server's `POST /internal/policy`. It authorizes the execution token, parses the payload with the harness's adapter, asks the policy for PreToolUse calls, passes post-tool outcomes to the policy observer, and decides whether a Stop may end the turn. It never fails open: anything it cannot authorize or read on a PreToolUse is denied.

owns: Token checks through `LiveRegistry::authorize` and then `BridgeServices::authorize`.
Refusing a call to another agent's `submit_*` tool.
Turning `PolicyDecision` values into `Decision` values and denial texts.
Updating live state: session id, transcript path, tool call count, activity time, and stop verdicts.
does_not_own: The guards and permission rules: ostra-policy, through ostra-server's `BridgeServices` implementation.
Showing permission cards: ostra-engine and the web console, through `BridgeServices::resolve_ask`.
The payload and response shapes of each CLI: the harness adapters section.

assumptions: The server has already read the bearer token from the `Authorization: Bearer` header; ostra-server's `policy_route` returns 401 when there is none.
`req.harness` matches the execution's harness; a mismatch is denied with `The hook's harness does not match the execution's harness. Stop now.`.
`BridgeServices::resolve_ask` waits for the user's answer, and the hook subprocess sets no HTTP timeout on PreToolUse, so a pending ask holds the CLI's tool call open.

business_flow.action: Runs Ostra's hook command before a tool call, with the payload on stdin.
business_flow.outcome: `ostra hook` posts a `PolicyRequest` with the execution's token.

business_flow.action: Authorizes the token and checks the harness.
business_flow.outcome: An unknown or ended execution is denied with `This execution is not running under Ostra any more, so no tool call may run. Stop now.`.

business_flow.action: Reads the session metadata and turns the payload into a canonical tool call, or a refusal.
business_flow.outcome: Subagent spawns, user questions, and truncated inputs are refused without the policy.

business_flow.action: Checks the call against guards and permissions, and asks the user when the rule says ask.
business_flow.outcome: The call is allowed or denied with a reason and the rule that fired.

business_flow.action: Formats the decision in the CLI's hook output schema.
business_flow.outcome: The CLI runs the tool, or shows the model the denial reason.

subsections.title: PreToolUse decision
subsections.purpose: For a PreToolUse event, the bridge counts the tool call, then `decide` returns the final allow or deny. `decide` also runs for Ostra MCP tool calls from the MCP shim, so the same rules apply to both paths.

owns: `decide`, `denial_text`, and the texts for another agent's submit and a user's denial.
does_not_own: The rule texts and reasons, which come from the policy.

assumptions: A tool whose canonical name starts with `submit_` and whose rest is not the agent's snake-case name is another agent's submit tool.
An allowed call never carries a note; `decide` returns `Decision::Allow { note: None }` for every allow.

subsections.title: PostToolUse observation
subsections.purpose: For PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure, the bridge marks activity, parses the tool call and its outcome, and passes them to `BridgeServices::policy_observe`. The notes that come back, such as a recalled lesson after a failed build, are returned to the model as additional context where the harness supports it.

owns: Forwarding the outcome and returning the notes in the adapter's post response.
does_not_own: Build streaks and lesson recall: ostra-policy and ostra-tools through ostra-server.

assumptions: A payload the adapter cannot parse is not observed and gets an empty answer.
Antigravity's post response is always `{}`, so its notes are dropped; its hook output rejects unknown fields.

subsections.title: Stop and session events
subsections.purpose: For a Stop event, the bridge tells the server (`stop_event`), records the last assistant message, and asks `LiveExecution::on_stop` whether the turn may end. A Stop without a submit is turned back twice with an instruction to submit, or to reply first when the run owes an answer. SessionStart, PreInvocation, and PostInvocation only mark activity.

owns: Returning the adapter's stop response with or without a block reason.
does_not_own: The stop counting rules: the live execution registry section.

assumptions: The harness honors `{"decision": "block", "reason": ...}` as a request to continue the turn; Claude Code, Codex, and Grok Build do, and Antigravity sends no Stop event.
ostra-server's `stop_event` only emits the status `The harness ended its turn.`; the bridge alone decides blocking.

Submit schemas and validation rules: `ostra_core::submit` and `ostra_core::doc`.

assumptions: A message with no `id` or no `method` is a notification and gets no response.
The harness lists tools once at startup, so ostra-server opens the workspace MCP connections before the CLI starts.
`2026-07-28` is left out of `MCP_VERSIONS` because its results need `resultType`, `ttlMs`, and `cacheScope`, and Claude Code rejects a `tools/list` without them.

sections.purpose: `run_hook_cli` and `run_mcp_stdio` are the bodies of the `ostra hook` and `ostra mcp-stdio` commands that the harness CLI starts. They read the execution id, server URL, and token from the command line and environment and forward to the server. Outside an Ostra execution both are inert, because the Antigravity integration is installed globally.

The hook prints its answer and exits 0 on every fail-closed path, so the CLI reads the deny JSON instead of treating the hook as broken; only an argument error exits 1.
PreToolUse requests have no HTTP timeout, because a permission ask may wait for the user; other events time out after 60 s.

sections.title: Wire protocol
sections.purpose: `protocol.rs` defines the shapes that pass between the `ostra hook` and `ostra mcp-stdio` subprocesses and the server, the environment variable names that carry the execution's identity, the two internal routes, and the hook event names.

owns: `PolicyRequest`, `PolicyResponse`, `McpRequest`, `McpResponse`, `HookEvent`, the `OSTRA_*` names, `POLICY_PATH`, `MCP_PATH`, and `MCP_SERVER_NAME`.
does_not_own: The HTTP handlers and the bearer header parsing: ostra-server's `policy_route` and `mcp_route`.

assumptions: Both sides are built from the same crate version, so the serde shapes match; there is no version field.
`HookEvent::parse` accepts the snake_case and PascalCase spelling of each event, so a harness that passes either works.

sections.title: PTY sessions
sections.purpose: `PtySession` runs the launch plan's program in a pseudo-terminal and mirrors its output in a `vt100` screen model, so the supervision loop can read the screen and a browser that attaches mid-run gets the current screen with its scrollback. Ostra alone answers the terminal queries a TUI sends, so any number of viewers, or none, gives the CLI exactly one answer. `PtyRegistry` holds live sessions by execution id for the server's Terminal tab.

owns: Spawning with the cleaned environment, and the reader, writer, and wait threads.
The screen model, snapshots, and the broadcast stream of output chunks.
Terminal query replies.
Input queueing, `type_line`, resize clamping, and termination of the process tree and sandbox members.
does_not_own: The WebSocket that carries the stream, input, and resizes: ostra-server's `ws.rs`.
The terminal view in the browser: web.
Process tree handling: `ostra_core::proctree::Tree`.

assumptions: Browsers mute their own replies to terminal queries; otherwise the CLI would get one reply per viewer.
On Unix the PTY child leads its own session, so its process group is it and its descendants; `Tree::adopt_running` adopts it.
A viewer that falls behind by more than `STREAM_BUFFER` (256) chunks gets a lagged receiver and must resync from a new snapshot.

tables.title: Constants
rows: vt100 0.16 panics the reader thread on a one-row screen that wraps and a one-column screen with a wide character.
Largest size; ostra-server also rejects resizes above these.

subsections.title: Spawn and environment
subsections.purpose: `PtySession::spawn` opens a PTY of the given size, resolves the program with `command::resolve`, and builds the command: the resolved prefix, the Seatbelt TTY parameter, the plan's args, cwd, and environment. It then starts the writer, reader, and wait threads.

owns: The environment order and `PARENT_SESSION_ENV`.
does_not_own: Which credential variables are removed: the launch plans section.

assumptions: The CLI inherits Ostra's whole environment first; then `PARENT_SESSION_ENV` and `plan.env_remove` are removed, `TERM=xterm-256color` and `COLORTERM=truecolor` are set, and `plan.env` is applied last.

A child that inherits the variables of the harness session Ostra itself was started from runs as that session's nested child, and Claude Code does not persist such a session, so `CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_*` session variables, `CLAUDE_PID`, `CLAUDE_EFFORT`, `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, `CODEX_SANDBOX`, `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED`, `GROK_SESSION_ID`, and `ANTIGRAVITY_AGENT` are removed.
`plan.tty_param` is set only by Seatbelt; the PTY passes `-D <param>=<tty device>`, and on non-Unix platforms a set parameter is an error.

subsections.title: Terminal query replies
subsections.purpose: The reader thread scans each output chunk for terminal queries and writes the replies into the CLI's input. Bytes that may start a sequence the next read completes are carried over, up to 64 bytes. Only fixed replies and digit-only mode numbers are echoed, so program output cannot type into its own input.

owns: `answer_queries`, `parse_query`, `is_mode_query`, and `reply_bytes`.
does_not_own: Rendering, which vt100 does.

assumptions: An unterminated CSI with more than 32 parameter bytes, or an unterminated OSC over 256 bytes, is not a query.
A control or high byte inside a CSI makes it a non-query, so nothing is echoed.

tables.title: Replies
rows: CSI c or CSI 0 c (primary device attributes)

subsections.title: Viewer streaming
subsections.purpose: `PtySession::stream` returns a snapshot and a broadcast receiver taken under the same screen lock, so a viewer neither misses nor repeats output. The snapshot resets the terminal, replays scrollback as plain lines, and then draws the formatted screen and input modes.

owns: `snapshot`, `stream`, and `PtyRegistry::inserted` for viewers waiting for a run to start.
does_not_own: Sending bytes to the browser: ostra-server's `ws.rs`.

assumptions: Scrollback rows are sent as plain text because formatted rows position the cursor absolutely; the visible rows follow as text too, then the formatted redraw replaces them.
On the alternate screen there is no scrollback to replay; the snapshot switches to the alternate screen and draws it.

subsections.title: Input and termination
subsections.purpose: Input goes through a bounded queue to a writer thread, so a CLI that stops reading never blocks a caller. `terminate` asks the CLI to exit, kills its process tree after a grace period, and then drops the sandbox members so nothing the CLI started outlives it.

owns: `write`, `type_line`, `resize`, `wait_exit`, `hold`, and `terminate`.
does_not_own: Killing sandbox members, which ostra-sandbox does when `Members` drops.

assumptions: `write` returns `WouldBlock` (`the program is not reading its terminal input`) when the queue is full and `BrokenPipe` (`the terminal is closed`) when the writer ended.
`type_line` uses bracketed paste so embedded newlines are not treated as submits, and presses Enter 150 ms later.

The exit request is SIGTERM to the process group on Unix and closing the pseudoconsole on Windows; after the grace the tree is killed and the wait is 2 s more. On Windows the tree is killed afterwards in every case, because programs the CLI left running are still in its job.

sections.title: Sandbox wrapping
sections.purpose: `sandbox::wrap` runs the harness CLI under the execution's sandbox profile, so the CLI's own shell tool and everything it starts inherit the sandbox. It keeps the CLI's model API, the hosts of user-chosen base URLs, and Ostra's hook bridge reachable. Under bubblewrap the home is overlaid so the CLI can write its state dirs but cannot leave files the user's later shells or sessions would run; Seatbelt has no overlay, so there the rest of the home stays read-only.

owns: Which harness dirs are writable and which settings inside them stay read-only (`harness_dirs`).
Forwarding the bridge into the sandbox, and rewriting `OSTRA_URL` and plan files to the inside URL.
Collecting base URL hosts from the plan, Ostra's environment, Claude Code settings, and Codex model providers.
The per-execution copy of `~/.claude.json` under bubblewrap, and the Seatbelt variables.
does_not_own: The sandbox decision, profiles, egress proxy, decoys, and launcher commands: ostra-sandbox.
The list of model API hosts per harness: `ostra_sandbox::egress::model_hosts`.

assumptions: `server_url` is `http://<ip>:<port>`; `bridge_addr` returns `The hook bridge URL `<url>` is not http://<ip>:<port>.` for a host name such as `localhost`.
A URL replacement in plan files applies only where the port is not followed by another digit, so `:4100` does not match inside `:41000`.
A base URL without a port that starts with `http://` uses port 80, which a forward needs spelled out.
Settings, instructions, and hooks inside a harness state dir must stay read-only, because a hook written there would run in the user's own later sessions of that CLI.

Under Seatbelt, which denies `/tmp` and the keychain, Claude Code needs `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR` set to the sandbox's `TMPDIR`, and CLIs built on rustls-native-certs need `SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/cert.pem` unless it is already set.

sections.title: Command resolution on Windows
sections.purpose: `command::resolve` turns a harness command name into a program that can be started. On Unix it returns the name unchanged. On Windows it searches `PATH` with `PATHEXT` and, for an npm `.cmd` shim, runs the shim's JavaScript file with `node` directly.

owns: `Resolved`, `resolve`, `find`, `from_file`, and `npm_shim_script`.
does_not_own: The installed-check in `HarnessExecutor::launch`, which uses `which::which` on the raw command.

assumptions: npm installs a CLI as an extensionless `sh` script, a `.cmd`, and a `.ps1`; CreateProcessW cannot start the first, and `cmd.exe` cannot pass the multi-line arguments a harness receives.
`PATHEXT` defaults to `.COM;.EXE;.BAT;.CMD` when unset, and the first match in `PATH` order wins.
A command with more than one path component is taken as a path, not searched.
The npm shim's script is the quoted `%dp0%\...` path before `%*`; `node.exe` next to the shim is preferred over `node` on `PATH`.

subsections.title: Antigravity global integration
subsections.purpose: Antigravity reads hooks and MCP servers only from global config. `ensure_agy_integration` installs an `ostra` plugin whose hooks call `ostra hook --harness agy`, enables it, and registers the `ostra` MCP server with `agy mcp add`, which is the one registration Antigravity honors. It runs before every Antigravity launch and changes nothing when everything is in place.

owns: `~/.gemini/config/plugins/ostra/plugin.json`, `hooks.json`, `agents/ostra-<agent>.md`, and `plugins.ostra.enabled` in `~/.gemini/config/config.json`.
does_not_own: The user's other Antigravity config, which is read and kept.

assumptions: The hooks are inert outside Ostra, because `ostra hook` without an execution id prints nothing and exits 0, and `ostra mcp-stdio` answers with no tools.
`agy mcp list` prints one server per line starting with its name; the server counts as registered when a line starts with `ostra` and contains the binary path.
An agent file with no `tools:` list gets no native tools, and one unknown tool name makes the session fail to start (measured on agy 1.2.8), so `agy_tools` lists only verified names.

sections.title: Terminal transcript
sections.purpose: `TermLog` keeps the raw bytes of a harness terminal on disk at `harness_execution_dir(session_root, id)/terminal.log`, so the Terminal tab can replay an ended run. `read_transcript` returns the stored bytes for the server.

owns: The file's size bound, trimming, owner-only permissions, and the append-or-replace choice.
does_not_own: Serving the replay: ostra-server's `ws.rs`.

assumptions: Harness output can carry secrets, so the dir is owner-only (0700) and the file is 0600, including after a trim.
The file grows to at most twice `TRANSCRIPT_CAP` (2 MiB); past that it is rewritten with its last 2 MiB through a `.log.tmp` file and a rename, so writes stay appends and memory stays flat.
A failed write stops the transcript and the run goes on.
A new run replaces an earlier transcript at the same path; a resumed run with the same execution id appends.

sections.title: Session transcripts and usage
sections.purpose: Each harness writes its own session file. `transcript.rs` reads it for the final assistant message and token usage with cost, and `usage_watch::follow` follows it during the run so harness spend shows while the run is live, as native spend does. Reads are best effort: a missing or unreadable file gives empty facts.

owns: Finding each harness's session file, parsing lines per harness, and emitting `ExecutionDelta::Usage` while the run is live.
does_not_own: Model prices: `ostra_core::pricing::cost`.
Storing usage: ostra-engine.

assumptions: Session files are JSON Lines; a last line without a newline counts once it parses as JSON.
A file shorter than the read offset was replaced or truncated, and reading starts over.
Antigravity records no token counts, so its usage is zero and the follower does not run for it.

tables.title: Session files
rows: One line per content block repeats the message's usage, so usage counts once per message id; each message is priced with its own model, including 1-hour cache writes and web search requests.
Hook `transcript_path`, else a `.jsonl` under `$CODEX_HOME` or `~/.codex` `/sessions/` whose name contains the session id
`token_count` events carry running totals where input includes cached input; each increase is normalized and priced with the current `turn_context` model.
`updates.jsonl` next to the hook's transcript, else `$GROK_HOME` or `~/.grok` `/sessions/*/<session>/updates.jsonl`
Each `turn_completed` update adds that turn's usage; cost is `costUsdTicks / 10^10`, which Grok computes.
No usage; the last `PLANNER_RESPONSE` content is the final message.

subsections.title: Live usage follower
subsections.purpose: `follow` runs as a task beside the supervision loop. It finds the session file, watches its directory, reads appended lines, and emits a usage delta whenever the total changes. It stops when the executor cancels its token, and the executor awaits it so no usage lands after the final result.

owns: `LOCATE_EVERY`, `SETTLE`, `POLL_EVERY`, and the watch-or-poll choice.
does_not_own: The final usage in the result, which `outcome::result` reads again from the file.

assumptions: The file's path depends on a session id the harness may report late, so it is looked for every 2 s until found.
The directory is watched rather than the file, so a replaced file is still seen; when the platform watcher cannot be created, the file is polled every 5 s.
A turn writes many lines in a burst, so each event is followed by a 500 ms settle before the next read.
The emitted usage's `tool_calls` is the live count from `LiveExecution`, not the transcript's.

diagrams.title: Follower loop
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
a{"Harness is Antigravity?"} -- yes --> r[Return]
a -- no --> l["locate every 2 s until found or stopped"]
l --> w["Watch the parent dir, else poll every 5 s"]
w --> p["reader poll"]
p --> c{"New lines and usage changed?"}
c -- yes --> e["emit ExecutionDelta Usage"]
c -- no --> wt["Wait for a file event or the poll interval"]
e --> wt
wt --> s["Settle 500 ms, drain events"]
s --> p

The same binary serves as the `hook` and `mcp-stdio` commands the harness calls back.

does_not_own: Production policy and tools, which the probe replaces with logging stubs.

The scratch dir is writable; the probe creates `repo/` and `ws/.ostra/sessions/s_probe` in it and writes `<harness>-events.jsonl` and `<harness>-terminal.bin`.
The default budget is 240 s and the idle nudge is 90 s.

sections.title: How this crate works with the other Ostra projects
sections.purpose: ostra-exec-harness is the harness side of Ostra's executor layer. ostra-engine decides what runs, ostra-server hosts the executor and the callback routes and implements `BridgeServices`, ostra-sandbox contains the CLI, and the web console shows its terminal. This section lists each connection so a change on either side can be checked against the other.

owns: The executor, bridge, launch, PTY, and transcript code in this crate.
does_not_own: `Executor`, `ExecutionSpec`, `ExecutionHost`, `ExecutionResult`, `HarnessKind`, `ToolCall`, `PolicyDecision`, config types, paths, pricing, submit schemas, and coordination texts: ostra-core.
Routes, resume, retries, and the harness session id for Claude Code and Grok Build: ostra-engine.
The HTTP server, the bridge socket, the per-execution policy and tools, the Terminal WebSocket, and the setup terminal: ostra-server.
Guards and permissions: ostra-policy. Tool implementations: ostra-tools. Sandbox backends, egress, decoys, git repair: ostra-sandbox.
The Terminal tab and permission cards: web.

assumptions: ostra-engine chooses `harness_session_id` for Claude Code and Grok Build (the resumed id, or a new UUID v4) and leaves it `None` for Codex and Antigravity.
ostra-engine does not auto-retry an `Error` whose text starts with `harness-`, so `harness-auth:` and `harness-launch:` failures wait for the user.
ostra-server creates one `HarnessExecutor` lazily and passes `http://<callback>` as the server URL and its bridge socket path, which must be set before the first harness execution.

ostra-server's `Wrapped` executor registers the execution's `ExecutionPolicy` and `ToolEnv` before calling `HarnessExecutor::run` and removes them after, and opens workspace MCP connections first because the harness lists tools once at startup.
For an inspection, ostra-server's policy refuses every tool call with `Answer from what you already did, without tools: ...`.

parts.overview: ostra-exec-native is the Rust crate that runs one execution of one leaf agent against a model provider's API key, inside Ostra's own process. Its public type `NativeExecutor` implements the `Executor` trait from ostra-core. ostra-server builds one shared instance at startup and hands it to ostra-engine whenever a route selects `ExecutorKind::Native`. Each execution has three stages. It first sets up the provider, the policy engine (ostra-policy), the tool environment (ostra-tools), and the OS sandbox (ostra-sandbox). It then loops over model turns (ostra-providers), and every tool call passes the policy engine and, when the policy says so, a user permission ask before it runs. It ends when the agent calls its `submit_<agent>` tool, when a coordination tool makes the run wait or finish, or on an error, a cancellation, or the timeout. The crate never writes to a database itself. It reports everything through the `ExecutionHost` trait, which ostra-engine implements to persist Activity deltas and transcript messages in ostra-store. The only store it opens directly is the memory database, which it reads to recall lessons after repeated build failures. Its main sections cover the executor entry, run setup, the turn loop, tool dispatch, the tool call pipeline, submit validation, subagent coordination, context compaction, transcript and resume, streaming and usage, and integration with the rest of Ostra.

sections.title: Native executor entry, cancellation, and timeout
sections.purpose: `NativeExecutor::run` is the only public way to start a native execution. It builds a private `Run` value from the executor's shared connectors and the `ExecutionSpec`, then races the run's future against the caller's cancellation token and a wall-clock budget of `spec.timeout_secs`. This bounds every execution in time and always returns an `ExecutionResult` with the usage spent so far.

owns: The race between the run future, the caller's `CancellationToken`, and the `timeout_secs` budget.
The child cancellation token (`inner`) that the run, the provider calls, and the tools observe.
The `CLEANUP_GRACE` wait of 3 seconds that lets tools be killed before the result returns.
The final `Status` delta text "Cancelled." or "Timed out after N s." and the `error` string "timed out after N s".
does_not_own: Choosing when an execution starts, which agent it runs, and its timeout value: ostra-engine builds the `ExecutionSpec`.
Choosing the native executor over a harness executor: `ServerServices::executor` in ostra-server.
Everything inside the run: the Run setup, Turn loop, and Tool call pipeline sections of this part.

assumptions: `spec.timeout_secs` is a number of seconds. A value of 0 is raised to 1 by `spec.timeout_secs.max(1)`, so the budget is never zero.
The tools and provider calls stop promptly when `inner` is cancelled. The executor waits only `CLEANUP_GRACE` (3 s) for the future and then drops it, so the result's own return value is discarded.
The `usage` mutex holds the running total at any moment, because the result of a cancelled or timed-out run is built from `*usage.lock()` and not from the run's return value.
`ostra_sandbox::git_repos` is called once with `ctx.repo_root` and `ctx.workspace_root` before the run starts. An empty root is skipped by that function.

business_flow.action: Calls `run` with an execution spec, an execution host, and a cancellation token.
business_flow.outcome: The native executor starts the run and a timer.

business_flow.action: Waits for whichever ends first: the run, a user cancellation, or the timeout.
business_flow.outcome: A finished run returns its own result unchanged.

business_flow.action: On cancellation or timeout, cancels the run's child token and waits up to 3 seconds for tools to stop.
business_flow.outcome: Running shell commands and model streams are stopped.

business_flow.action: Builds a result with status `Cancelled` or `Error`, the usage spent so far, and a status line for the Activity log.
business_flow.outcome: The engine records the execution as cancelled, or as failed with "timed out after N s".

diagrams.title: How one execution ends
diagrams.source:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Engine as ostra-engine runner
    participant NE as NativeExecutor
    participant Run
    participant Host as ExecutionHost
    Engine->>NE: run(spec, host, cancel)
    NE->>Run: execute() with child token inner
    alt run returns first
        Run-->>NE: ExecutionResult
        NE-->>Engine: ExecutionResult unchanged
    else cancel.cancelled()
        NE->>Run: inner.cancel()
        NE->>Run: timeout(CLEANUP_GRACE 3 s, fut)
        NE->>Host: emit Status "Cancelled."
        NE-->>Engine: status Cancelled with usage so far
    else sleep(timeout_secs)
        NE->>Run: inner.cancel()
        NE->>Run: timeout(CLEANUP_GRACE 3 s, fut)
        NE->>Host: emit Status "Timed out after N s."
        NE-->>Engine: status Error, error "timed out after N s"
    end

sections.purpose: `Run::execute` starts by preparing everything the turn loop needs. It resolves the model's provider, opens MCP servers, builds the policy engine and the tool environment, decides on the OS sandbox, assembles the tool list, and builds the first message list. Any failure here ends the execution with status `Error` before the first model call.

assumptions: `spec.route.model` has the form `provider:model`. `Providers::for_model` returns `BadModel` otherwise, which becomes "Cannot run model ...".

The workspace settings live at `paths::workspace_toml(workspace_root)` and the global config at `paths::global_config_path()`. Both are read fresh for every execution, so a settings change applies to the next execution.
`ctx.permissions.allow` holds rule strings, and `ostra_tools::webfetch_hosts` takes the exact `WebFetch(domain:...)` rules from them as private hosts that WebFetch may reach.

subsections.purpose: `sandbox_for` decides whether the execution's Bash commands run inside the OS sandbox. When they do, it creates a scratch directory, builds the sandbox profile, starts one egress proxy, and plants decoy credential files, all shared by every Bash call of the execution. assumptions: `paths::home()` can be absent. The code falls back to `/` as home.
The `_scratch` binding lives until `execute` returns or its future is dropped, so the scratch directory exists for every Bash call of the run.

sections.title: Agent turn loop
sections.purpose: The turn loop sends the conversation to the model, records each response, and decides what happens next from the response's stop reason and tool calls. It runs at most `MAX_TURNS` (400) times. It ends only on a submit, a coordination end, an error, a refusal, a cancellation, or a second response without tool calls.

owns: The request fields sent on every turn.
The handling of each stop reason.
The one-time reminder to call the submit tool, or to reply when the run owes a reply.
The "continue" messages after an output limit, capped at `MAX_TOKEN_CONTINUES` (3).
The `final_text` kept for the result: the last non-blank text of any response.
does_not_own: Streaming and cost reporting: the Streaming and usage section.
Compaction of a long conversation: the Context compaction section.
Running tool calls: the Tool dispatch and Tool call pipeline sections.

assumptions: The model's context window and output limit come from the models.dev catalog in `ostra_core::pricing`. An unlisted model gets `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` (200,000) and `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT` (32,000). A catalog output limit above `u32::MAX` is clamped to `u32::MAX`.
`max_tokens` is always the model's whole output limit, so the effort level chosen by the user is never cut short by the request.
The cancel token is checked at the start of each turn. A cancel during a model call arrives as `ProviderError::Cancelled` and returns status `Cancelled`.
`reminded` and `continues` are never reset. After one reminder, any later response without tool calls ends the run with status `Ok` and no submit payload.

A `PauseTurn` response is pushed as an assistant message and the next request is sent with no new user message. The provider is expected to accept a conversation that ends on an assistant turn in that case.
