sections.title: Tool dispatch within a turn
sections.purpose: `run_tools` processes every tool call of one response in the order the model made them. It runs adjacent read-only calls concurrently, runs every other call alone, and stops the turn early when the submit call succeeds or a coordination call ends the run. Every tool call gets exactly one tool result, because the provider rejects a conversation with an unanswered tool call.

owns: The grouping of adjacent concurrent calls.
The "Not run" results for calls after a successful submit or a coordination end.
Coercion of JSON-in-string arguments of the submit call before validation.
does_not_own: Checking and running one call: the Tool call pipeline section.
Validating the submit call: the Submit validation section.
What a coordination call does: ostra-tools `Coordinate` and ostra-server `Coordination`.

assumptions: The read-only tools that may run concurrently are Read, Grep, Glob, WebFetch, MemoryRecall, DocsSearch, Skill, and the 8 code tools CodeOutline, CodeFind, CodeCallers, CodeCallees, CodeImplementations, CodeNeighbors, CodeImpact, CodeMap. Their concurrent runs do not change shared state.
Only consecutive concurrent calls are grouped. A Bash call between two Reads splits them into separate groups, so the model's order of side effects is kept.
The submit input is coerced with `ostra_core::submit::submit_schema(agent)`, not with `spec.submit_schema`, because weaker models pass object or array arguments as JSON strings.
Calls made before a successful submit in the same turn have already run and their effects stay.

sections.title: Tool call pipeline
sections.purpose: `tool_end` checks and runs one non-submit tool call. The policy engine judges the canonical form of the call, the user answers an ask when the policy asks, and the tool then runs that same canonical call. After the call, the pipeline repairs planted git metadata, counts build time, applies policy observations such as lesson recall, and emits the result to the Activity log.

does_not_own: Rule layers, YOLO, and session allow rules: ostra-policy `ExecutionPolicy`.
Path resolution and the shell working directory: ostra-tools `ToolEnv::canonical_call`.
Running the tool and producing a diff: ostra-tools `execute`.
The permission gate shown to the user: ostra-engine `EngineHost::ask_permission`.
Git metadata repair rules: ostra-sandbox `repair_git_dirs`.

assumptions: The provider marks a tool input whose streamed JSON did not parse with the key `__invalid_json` (`INVALID_INPUT_KEY` in ostra-providers anthropic). The raw text is shown truncated to 500 bytes.
`host.yolo()` can change during an execution, so `policy.set_yolo` is called before every check.
`AlwaysInWorkspace` adds `policy.allow_rule_suggestion(call)` as a session allow rule for the rest of this execution. When no suggestion exists, the answer behaves as AllowOnce.
A model-supplied `cwd` for Bash is replaced by the shell's own working directory in `canonical_call`, so the policy and the tool see the same target.
A failed tool call never ends the run, even if the tool returned a Wait or Finish run end.
When a tool returns a diff, the Activity output is the tool text plus the diff, without the policy notes. The model receives the tool text plus the notes, without the diff.

sections.purpose: `Run::submit` decides whether the agent's `submit_<agent>` call is accepted. sections.purpose: Agents with the `Coordinate` capability can call SubagentList, SubagentAsk, and SubagentReply. A coordination call runs through the normal tool pipeline, and its result carries a `RunEnd` that can stop the run without a submit. sections.title: Context compaction
sections.purpose: When the conversation reaches `COMPACT_AT` (95%) of the model's context window, the loop asks the provider to replace the whole conversation with a summary before the next request. This lets a long execution continue past the window. The summary window is stored as a `compaction` transcript record, so a later resume starts from it.

owns: The size estimate and the 95% threshold.
The rule that compaction runs only when the last message is a user turn.
The retry rule after a failed or empty compaction: wait until the context grows by `COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH` (2%) of the window.
The summary instructions `COMPACT_INSTRUCTIONS` and the follow-up message `AFTER_COMPACTION`.
does_not_own: How a provider compacts, server side or with `compact_on_client`: ostra-providers `Provider::compact`.

assumptions: The context size is the last response's `context_tokens` (input + cache_read + cache_write + output) plus an estimate of the messages added after it at 4 characters per token.
A user turn last means no tool call is open, which `Provider::compact` requires.
The compaction request is a clone of the turn's request with the full message list, so the cached prefix is reused.
A compaction error other than cancellation does not fail the run: the run continues with the full conversation.

diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
    est["next = measured + estimate_tokens(unmeasured)"] --> th{"next >= 0.95 x window?"}
    th -->|no| send[Send the turn request]
    th -->|yes| retry{"Earlier failure and growth below 2% of window?"}
    retry -->|yes| send
    retry -->|no| last{Last message is user?}
    last -->|no| send
    last -->|yes| comp[provider.compact with COMPACT_INSTRUCTIONS]
    comp -->|summary| rep["Replace messages, add AFTER_COMPACTION, record compaction"]
    comp -->|"no summary or error"| mark[failed_compaction_at = next]
    comp -->|Cancelled| can[Return Cancelled]
    rep --> send
    mark --> send

sections.title: Transcript recording and resume
sections.purpose: Every message of a native execution is recorded through `ExecutionHost::record_message`, so the execution can be resumed after an interruption, a wait, or a restart. A resume rebuilds the conversation from the stored transcript, answers each tool call the interruption left open, and adds a note as the next user turn.

owns: The role names written to the transcript: `user`, `assistant`, and `compaction`.
How a stored transcript becomes a message list: `stored_messages`.
The resume user turn: `resume_turn`, and merging it with a trailing user message: `append_turn`.
Which messages are recorded again on a resume (Rule P2).
does_not_own: Storing and loading transcripts: ostra-engine `EngineHost` and ostra-store `append_message`.
Deciding to resume and choosing the note: ostra-engine.

assumptions: `host.transcript(id)` returns messages oldest first as `(role, content)` pairs.
A record whose content does not deserialize into blocks, or whose block list is empty, is skipped. A record with an unknown role is skipped.
A `compaction` record holds a whole message list that replaces every message before it. A record that does not parse is skipped.
Two adjacent stored records of the same role are merged into one message, because a resume that stopped after a user turn stores its note as a message of its own.

When resuming in place (`resume.from == spec.id`) with a non-empty transcript, the stored prefix already belongs to this execution. Only the new turn is recorded, so the replayed prefix hits the prompt cache.
`rebuild_transcript` is public, but no other crate of the workspace calls it. It is exercised by the tests of this crate.

parts.overview: ostra-mcp is the Model Context Protocol (MCP) client of Ostra. It connects to the external MCP servers a workspace configures, lists their tools, and calls those tools for agent executions. It supports two transports. The stdio transport starts a child process and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC over its stdin and stdout. The streamable HTTP transport POSTs each message to a URL and reads the reply as JSON or as a server-sent event stream. The crate also contains the OAuth 2.1 sign-in helpers for remote servers: challenge parsing, protected resource and authorization server discovery, dynamic client registration, PKCE, code exchange, and token refresh. It does not store tokens, read settings, or build server commands. Its only consumer is the `McpGateway` in ostra-server (`ostra-server/src/mcp.rs`), which builds each `Endpoint`, keeps OAuth records in the encrypted registry, and exposes the tools to executors. The crate depends on ostra-core for `proctree`, the process-group handling that ends a stdio server and every process it started.

sections.title: Client connection and initialize handshake
sections.purpose: `Client::connect` starts or reaches one MCP server and runs the MCP `initialize` handshake. It returns a `Client` that holds one live connection. ostra-server calls it whenever a workspace server has no live client, which happens when an execution opens or the settings screen asks for server status.

owns: The choice of transport from the `Endpoint` variant.
The `initialize` request body: `protocolVersion` set to `PROTOCOL_VERSION`, empty `capabilities`, and `clientInfo` with name `ostra` and the crate version.
The check that the server's protocol version is in `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS`.
The `server_info` string (`name version`) and the negotiated `protocol_version` of the `Client`.
Sending `notifications/initialized` after a successful handshake.
does_not_own: The program, arguments, environment, URL, headers and token source inside the `Endpoint`. The `McpGateway` in ostra-server builds these from workspace settings and the sandbox.
The handshake timeout value. ostra-server passes `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` (30 s).
Reconnecting after a server exits. The `McpGateway` in ostra-server does this.

assumptions: The server answers `initialize` with a `protocolVersion` string. When the field is missing, `connect` takes `PROTOCOL_VERSION` as the version and continues.
The client never offers an older version. It always sends `2025-11-25` and accepts any version in `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS` that the server answers with.
`serverInfo.name` is optional. When it is missing the name is `server`, and a missing `version` leaves the name alone.
The caller holds the `Client` for as long as the connection should live. Dropping the `Client` drops the transport, which ends a stdio server's process tree.

business_flow.action: Passes an `Endpoint` and a timeout to `Client::connect`.
business_flow.outcome: A stdio child process is started, or an HTTP client is built for the URL.

business_flow.action: Sends the `initialize` request with id 1.
business_flow.outcome: The server returns its protocol version, capabilities and server info.

business_flow.action: Checks the returned version against the supported list.
business_flow.outcome: An unsupported version ends the connect with a `Transport` error. A supported version is stored.

business_flow.action: Tells the transport the version, then sends `notifications/initialized`.
business_flow.outcome: The HTTP transport sends `mcp-protocol-version` on every later request. The server can take tool requests.

sections.title: Request lifecycle, timeouts, cancellation and errors
sections.purpose: `Client::rpc` sends every JSON-RPC request the client makes. It numbers each request, applies the caller's timeout and cancellation token, tells the server about an abandoned request, and turns a JSON-RPC error into `McpError::Rpc`. `McpError` is the only error type the crate returns to callers.

owns: Request ids: a per-client `AtomicI64` that starts at 1 and increments by one per request.
The race between the transport's answer, the timeout, and the cancellation token.
Sending `notifications/cancelled` for an abandoned request other than `initialize`.
Mapping a response's `error` member to `McpError::Rpc` and its `result` member to the return value.
The `McpError` variants and their display text.
does_not_own: Delivering a message and matching its response. The stdio and HTTP transports do this (see the stdio transport and streamable HTTP transport sections).
Choosing timeouts. ostra-server passes `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` for connect and listing, and the server's `timeout_secs` setting for tool calls.
Turning `McpError` into user-facing text. The `McpGateway` in ostra-server does this with `ConnError`.

assumptions: The server echoes the numeric request id in its response. Both transports match responses by `as_i64`, so a server that answers with a string id is never matched and the request times out.
`McpError::Timeout` carries whole seconds from `Duration::as_secs`, so a timeout under one second reports `0 s`.
The spec forbids cancelling `initialize`, so `rpc` sends no `notifications/cancelled` when `initialize` times out.
The result of sending `notifications/cancelled` is ignored. A dead server does not turn a timeout into a different error.
A response `error` without `code` gets code -32603. An `error` without `message` gets the text `error`.
A response with neither `result` nor `error` returns `Value::Null`.

business_flow.action: Takes the next id and builds a `jsonrpc` 2.0 request.
business_flow.outcome: The request carries a unique id for this connection.

business_flow.action: Waits for the transport's answer, the timeout, or the cancellation token, whichever comes first.
business_flow.outcome: One of the three outcomes is chosen.

business_flow.action: On timeout or cancellation, calls `abandon(id)` and sends `notifications/cancelled` with the id and the reason.
business_flow.outcome: The transport forgets the request and the server is told to stop the work.

business_flow.action: On an answer, checks for an `error` member.
business_flow.outcome: The caller gets `McpError::Rpc` or the `result` value.

diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
    start["rpc(method, params, timeout, cancel)"] --> id[Take next id from next_id]
    id --> race{"Which comes first?"}
    race -->|answer| haserr{"Response has error?"}
    race -->|transport error| terr[Return the transport error]
    race -->|timeout| ab["transport.abandon(id)"]
    race -->|cancel| ab
    ab --> isinit{"method is initialize?"}
    isinit -->|no| note["notify notifications/cancelled"]
    isinit -->|yes| fail[Return Timeout or Cancelled]
    note --> fail
    haserr -->|yes| rpcerr["Return McpError::Rpc"]
    haserr -->|no| ok["Return result, or Null"]

sections.title: Tool discovery and tool calls
sections.purpose: `Client::list_tools` reads every page of the server's `tools/list` result into `ToolInfo` values. `Client::call_tool` runs one tool through `tools/call` and returns its result as text. `Client::take_tools_changed` reports whether the server sent `notifications/tools/list_changed` since the last check, so the caller knows to list again.

The mapping from an MCP tool object to `ToolInfo`, with its defaults.
Replacing non-object tool arguments with an empty object.
Reading and clearing the `tools_changed` flag.

Tool naming, disabled tools, and deduplication across servers. ostra-server does this in `Connector::open`.
When to relist. ostra-server relists after `RELIST_AFTER` (30 s) or when `take_tools_changed` returns true.

assumptions: A tool without a string `name` is skipped without an error.
A missing `description` falls back to `title`, and then to the empty string.
An `inputSchema` that is missing or not an object becomes `{"type": "object", "properties": {}}`, because tool schemas sent to model providers must be objects.
`annotations.readOnlyHint` defaults to false, so a tool is treated as writing unless the server says otherwise.
An empty-string `nextCursor` ends paging, the same as a missing one.
A server that returns cursors for more than 50 pages is cut off. `list_tools` returns the tools it has collected and raises no error, because each page is one round trip.
The same timeout applies to each page separately, not to the whole listing.

sections.title: Server-initiated messages
sections.purpose: An MCP server can send the client requests and notifications, not only responses. `is_response`, `on_server_message` and `answer_server_request` decide what each incoming message is and what to send back. Both transports call them for every message that is not the response they wait for.

The reply to a server request: an empty result for `ping`, and error -32601 for every other method.
Setting `tools_changed` when `notifications/tools/list_changed` arrives.
does_not_own: Writing the reply. The stdio transport writes it to stdin. The HTTP transport POSTs it (see those sections).

assumptions: Ostra declares no client capabilities in `initialize`, so servers should not send `sampling/createMessage`, `roots/list` or `elicitation/create`. If one does, it gets error -32601 with the text `Ostra does not support {method}`.
A message is a response when it has no `method` and has `result` or `error`.
A non-response message with an `id` is a request. One without an `id` is a notification.
Every notification other than `notifications/tools/list_changed` is ignored, including progress and log messages.

sections.title: Stdio transport
sections.purpose: `Stdio` runs a local MCP server as a child process and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC with it over stdin and stdout. It keeps the end of the server's stderr so that a crash can be explained. It ends the whole process tree when dropped, because servers started through `npx` or `uvx` run in grandchildren.

owns: Starting the child with piped stdin, stdout and stderr, `kill_on_drop`, and its own process group.
Removing the variables in `env_remove` from the inherited environment, then setting `env`.
The table of pending requests, keyed by id, each with a one-shot sender.
The stdout reader task: parsing lines, splitting batches, delivering responses, and answering server requests.
The stderr task that keeps the last 4096 bytes.
The `Closed` error text built from the last stderr lines.
Terminating the process tree on drop.
does_not_own: The sandbox wrapper, program path and environment content. ostra-server builds them with `ostra_sandbox::host_command` and passes them in the `Endpoint`.
Process group creation and signalling. `ostra_core::proctree` in ostra-core does this.
Restarting a server that exited. The `McpGateway` in ostra-server does this.

assumptions: The server writes one JSON message, or one JSON array of messages, per line on stdout. A line that is not JSON is skipped and logged at debug level with its first 200 characters, because some servers log to stdout.
Messages the client writes contain no raw newline, because `serde_json` serializes strings with escaped newlines.
A response's id is an integer. A response with any other id, or an id nobody waits for, is dropped.
stderr is decoded with lossy UTF-8 in 2048-byte reads, so a multi-byte character split across two reads shows as replacement characters.
When stdout closes, the server is taken as gone: `alive` becomes false and every pending request fails with `Closed`.

`ostra_core::proctree::Tree::of_tokio` succeeds for a started child. When it fails, `spawn` returns `Transport` with the text `could not start` and drops the child, which kills it through `kill_on_drop`.
The `guard` is dropped after `Drop` has sent the terminate signal, because the struct field `_guard` is dropped after `drop` runs.

business_flow.action: Calls `Stdio::spawn` with the program, arguments, environment and working directory.
business_flow.outcome: The child runs in its own process group, and the stdout and stderr tasks are started.

business_flow.action: Sends a request through `request`.
business_flow.outcome: The id is placed in the pending table and the line is written to stdin.

business_flow.action: Reads the response line and finds the pending id.
business_flow.outcome: The waiting request receives the response.

business_flow.action: Exits or crashes.
business_flow.outcome: Pending requests fail with `Closed` carrying the last five stderr lines, and later writes fail the same way.

business_flow.action: Drops the `Client`.
business_flow.outcome: The process group gets SIGTERM on Unix, or the job is closed on Windows, and the direct child is killed.

    participant Stdio

    participant Child as server process

sections.title: Streamable HTTP transport
sections.purpose: `Http` implements the MCP streamable HTTP transport. Every message is one POST to the endpoint URL. The server answers with a JSON body or with a `text/event-stream` body that carries the response among other messages. The transport adds bearer tokens from a `TokenSource`, keeps the `mcp-session-id` the server assigns, and retries once with a refreshed token when the server refuses one.

owns: Validating configured header names and values when the transport is built.
The reqwest client: user agent `ostra/{version}`, 15 s connect timeout, and the same-origin redirect policy.
The request headers: `Accept`, `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `mcp-session-id`, and `mcp-protocol-version`.
The status handling for 401, 403, 404 and other non-success answers.
Parsing JSON and SSE bodies and picking out the response with the awaited id.
Handing the other messages in a body to `on_server_message` and POSTing any reply.
does_not_own: Where tokens come from and how they refresh. The `TokenSource` implementation does this. In Ostra that is `Stored` in ostra-server (see the token source contract section).
OAuth discovery and sign-in. The OAuth sign-in section covers the `oauth` module, and ostra-server runs it.
The total time a request may take. `Client::rpc` applies the caller's timeout.

assumptions: The server accepts `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream` and answers one of the two.
A body whose `Content-Type` does not start with `text/event-stream` is parsed as JSON, and a parse failure is a `Transport` error.
A 403 is a sign-in request only when `WWW-Authenticate` contains `insufficient_scope`. Any other 403 is a plain refusal.
A token refresh is tried only when the transport has a `TokenSource` and a token was sent. With no token held, a 401 goes straight to `NeedsAuth`.
A 404 is a session end only when the transport holds a session id. A 404 before any session is an ordinary `Transport` error.
The session id from the most recent successful response replaces the previous one.
The version header is sent only after `initialized` is called, so the `initialize` request carries none.
The transport opens no standalone GET event stream and sends no DELETE to end a session. Server messages arrive only inside POST response bodies.
`abandon` is not implemented. When `rpc` stops waiting, the dropped future cancels the HTTP request.
A notification's response body is ignored. A 202 Accepted with no body counts as success.

business_flow.action: Sends a request through `Http::request`.
business_flow.outcome: The transport gets a token, if any, and POSTs the message.

business_flow.action: Answers 2xx with a JSON or SSE body and possibly a session id.
business_flow.outcome: The session id is stored, and the matching response is returned to the client.

business_flow.action: Answers 401 because the token expired.
business_flow.outcome: The transport asks the `TokenSource` for a fresh token and POSTs once more.

business_flow.action: Refuses the fresh token too, or no token source exists.
business_flow.outcome: The client gets `NeedsAuth` with the `WWW-Authenticate` header, and ostra-server shows a sign-in.

flowchart TD
    a["send(message)"] --> b["token = TokenSource.token()"]
    b --> c["post(message, token)"]
    c --> d{Status}
    d -->|"401, or 403 with insufficient_scope"| e{"Not retried yet and token sent?"}
    d -->|"other 403"| f["Transport: the server refused the request (403)"]
    d -->|"404 with a session"| g["alive = false, Closed"]
    d -->|"other non-2xx"| h["Transport: the server answered status"]
    d -->|2xx| i["Store mcp-session-id, return response"]
    e -->|yes| j["TokenSource.refused(token)"]
    j -->|fresh token| c
    j -->|none| k["NeedsAuth with WWW-Authenticate"]
    e -->|no| k

diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
    r[2xx response] --> ct{"Content-Type starts with text/event-stream?"}
    ct -->|no| json[Parse body as JSON]
    json --> items[Split an array into messages]
    items --> pick["First message with the awaited id is the answer, others go to side_message"]

sections.title: Same-origin redirect policy
sections.purpose: `same_origin_redirects` returns the reqwest redirect policy that every Ostra HTTP client talking to MCP and OAuth servers uses. It follows a redirect only when the target has the same scheme, host and port as the first request. This keeps a secret header (API key, bearer token, or client secret in a form) from reaching another host and from dropping from https to http.

owns: The redirect decision: follow, stop, or fail.
does_not_own: Building the clients. `Http::new` in this crate and `McpGateway::new` in ostra-server set this policy on their clients.

assumptions: The comparison is against the first URL of the chain, not the previous hop.
Ports are compared with `port_or_known_default`, so `http://h` and `http://h:80` are the same origin.
A stopped redirect returns the redirect response itself (for example 307) to the caller. The HTTP transport then reports it as a non-success status.
The redirect limit is checked before the origin, so the sixth redirect fails even when it stays on the same origin.

business_flow.action: Receives a redirect and asks the policy.
business_flow.outcome: The policy compares the target with the first request's origin.

business_flow.action: Counts the URLs already visited.
business_flow.outcome: More than five visited URLs fail the request with `too many redirects`. Otherwise a same-origin target is followed and any other target is not.

sections.title: Token source contract
sections.purpose: `TokenSource` is the trait the HTTP transport uses to get bearer tokens without knowing where they are stored. The caller implements it and passes it in `Endpoint::Http.auth`. In Ostra the implementation is `Stored` in ostra-server, which reads OAuth records from the encrypted registry and refreshes them with this crate's `oauth::refresh`.

owns: The two-method contract: `token` for the token to send and `refused` for a replacement after a refusal.
does_not_own: Token storage, locking and refresh timing. The implementation owns them (`Stored` in ostra-server).

assumptions: `token` returns an unexpired access token, refreshing first when needed, or `None` when no token is held.
`refused(token)` receives the exact token the server refused. It returns a different token to retry with, or `None` when a new sign-in is needed.
The transport calls `refused` at most once per message, so an implementation that returns the same refused token causes one extra POST and then `NeedsAuth`.
Implementations must be `Send + Sync`, because the transport shares them across tasks.

business_flow.action: Calls `token` before each POST.
business_flow.outcome: The POST carries `Authorization: Bearer` when a token exists.

business_flow.action: Calls `refused` after a 401, or a 403 with `insufficient_scope`.
business_flow.outcome: A fresh token is retried once, or the client gets `NeedsAuth`.

sections.title: OAuth sign-in for remote servers
sections.purpose: The `oauth` module implements the client side of the MCP authorization spec for remote servers that answer 401. It reads the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge, discovers the protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) and the authorization server metadata (RFC 8414 and OpenID discovery), registers Ostra as a public client (RFC 7591), and builds the PKCE S256 authorization URL with the `resource` parameter (RFC 8707). It then exchanges the code for tokens and refreshes them. The module is a set of stateless functions. ostra-server keeps the state between steps.

owns: The data types `AuthServer`, `Discovery`, `ClientCredentials`, `Tokens`, `Pkce`, and `AuthRequest`.
The endpoint scheme rules in `check_endpoint`.
Discovery order and fallbacks, and the issuer check.
The registration request body.
PKCE and state generation.
The authorization URL query.
Token request forms and client authentication choice.
does_not_own: Storing discovery results, client credentials and tokens. ostra-server keeps them as an `OAuthRecord` in the registry secret store under `mcp_oauth:{workspace root}:{server name}`.
Pending sign-ins, the `state` lookup and the link lifetime. ostra-server keeps them in `McpGateway.logins` for `LOGIN_TTL` (600 s).
The redirect URI and its HTTP route. ostra-server uses `{origin}/mcp/oauth/callback` (`CALLBACK_PATH`).
Configured `oauth.client_id`, `oauth.client_secret_env` and `oauth.scopes` settings. ostra-server reads them from workspace settings.
Opening the browser. The web console does this with the URL that ostra-server returns.

assumptions: The caller passes a `reqwest::Client` built with `same_origin_redirects` and a request timeout. ostra-server uses a 30 s timeout. The module sets none of its own.
The caller passes `now` in Unix seconds to the token functions, so they stay testable.
Every metadata fetch failure (network error, non-2xx status, or non-JSON body) is treated as missing metadata and the next candidate URL is tried, without an error.

business_flow.outcome: Ostra holds `ClientCredentials` for this authorization server.

business_flow.action: Creates a PKCE pair and a `state`, then calls `authorization_url`.
business_flow.outcome: The console opens the sign-in URL in the browser.

business_flow.action: Signs in at the authorization server.
business_flow.outcome: The browser is redirected to `/mcp/oauth/callback` with `code` and `state`.

business_flow.action: Calls `exchange_code` with the code and the verifier.
business_flow.outcome: Tokens are saved, the connection is reset, and the next connect sends the bearer token.

subsections.purpose: `parse_challenge` extracts the `resource_metadata` URL and the `scope` value from a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` header. `discover` uses them as the first metadata candidate and as the preferred scopes.

An unquoted value runs to the next comma or space.

subsections.title: Endpoint scheme checks
subsections.purpose: `check_endpoint` decides whether Ostra may fetch an OAuth URL or send the browser to it. A hostile server's metadata could name a `javascript:` or `data:` URL. The browser would run that URL on Ostra's origin, so only https URLs and a small set of http URLs pass.

does_not_own: The URLs themselves. They come from the challenge and metadata that discovery reads.

assumptions: `https` passes when the URL has a host.
`http` passes when the host is `localhost` (any case), an IPv4 or IPv6 loopback address, or when its origin equals the `server_origin` passed in.
The origin string is `scheme://host` plus `:port` only for a non-default port, because `Url::port` returns `None` for the default port.
Every other scheme fails, including `javascript`, `data` and `file`.
`discover` and `check_server` pass the MCP server's origin as `server_origin`. `register` and `authorization_url` pass the issuer's origin.

subsections.title: Resource and authorization server discovery
subsections.purpose: `discover` finds the authorization server for an MCP server URL. It tries the protected resource metadata locations in order, reads the issuer from it, then fetches that issuer's metadata. When the server publishes no metadata at all, it falls back to the 2025-03-26 default endpoints on the server's own origin and sets `guessed`.

does_not_own: What to do when a guessed server cannot register a client. ostra-server tells the user to put a token in a header instead.

assumptions: Protected resource metadata counts only when it has an `authorization_servers` member.
Only the first entry of `authorization_servers` is used.
The resource defaults to the server URL without its fragment. The metadata's `resource` field replaces it when present.
Scope priority: the challenge `scope`, then the resource metadata's `scopes_supported`, then the authorization server's `scopes_supported`.
Issuer comparison ignores trailing slashes.
Issuer metadata must deserialize into `AuthServer`, so `issuer`, `authorization_endpoint` and `token_endpoint` are required. A document missing them is skipped as not found.

When resource metadata exists but no issuer metadata can be read, discovery fails. It guesses endpoints only when neither document exists, because servers from before RFC 9728 host their own authorization server.

sections.title: How ostra-server uses this crate
sections.purpose: This crate has one consumer in the workspace: `McpGateway` in `ostra-server/src/mcp.rs`. The gateway turns workspace settings into `Endpoint` values, caches one `Client` per workspace and server name, runs the OAuth sign-in with the `oauth` functions, and exposes the listed tools to agent executions through its `Connector` and `ExecMcp` types. This section records the contract between the two crates so a change on either side keeps the other working.

owns: The public API that ostra-server depends on: `Client`, `Endpoint`, `McpError`, `TokenSource`, `ToolInfo`, `same_origin_redirects`, and the `oauth` module.
does_not_own: Connection caching, relisting, retry back-off, workspace trust checks, sandboxing, secret storage, and tool naming. The `McpGateway` in ostra-server owns all of these.
Building the sandboxed command and the `guard`. `ostra_sandbox::host_command` in ostra-sandbox does this.
The list of credential variable names put in `env_remove`. `ostra_core::config::credential_env_names` in ostra-core provides it.

ostra-server treats `is_alive() == false` as a reason to reconnect, both when it prepares tools and before each tool call.
ostra-server maps `McpError::NeedsAuth` to its own `ConnError::NeedsAuth` and keeps the `WWW-Authenticate` value for the next `discover` call. It maps every other error to text with `to_string`.
ostra-server's `Stored` token source passes the refused token back unchanged only when no other call refreshed in between, which gives the HTTP transport a different token or `None`.

parts.overview: ostra-notify is the Ostra crate that sends Web Push notifications to browsers. It needs no OpenSSL: it uses the pure-Rust p256, hkdf, aes-gcm and sha2 crates. It encrypts each message with RFC 8291 in the RFC 8188 `aes128gcm` content coding, and it authenticates to the push service with an RFC 8292 VAPID ES256 JWT. The whole crate is one file, `src/lib.rs`, with five parts: the `Notifier` that POSTs to a subscription endpoint, the `encrypt`/`encrypt_with` functions, the `VapidKeys` key pair and JWT signer, the `Notification`/`SendOutcome`/`NotifyError` types, and two helpers, `b64_decode` and `origin_of`. It reads the browser subscription type `PushSubscription` from ostra-core. ostra-server builds one `Notifier` at startup from a VAPID key that ostra-store keeps, and publishes the public key to the React console through `GET` server info. When ostra-engine raises a `Notice`, ostra-server calls `Notifier::send` for every stored subscription and deletes each subscription whose outcome is `SendOutcome::Gone`.

sections.title: Push delivery
sections.purpose: `Notifier::send` delivers one `Notification` to one browser push subscription. It decodes the subscription keys, encrypts the JSON payload, signs a VAPID `Authorization` header, POSTs the body to the subscription endpoint, and turns the HTTP status into a `SendOutcome`. ostra-server calls it once per stored subscription each time the engine raises a notice.

owns: The HTTP request to the push service: its URL, its five headers, and its encrypted body.
The mapping from the push service's HTTP status to `SendOutcome::Delivered`, `SendOutcome::Gone` or `SendOutcome::Failed`.
The reqwest client and its 20-second timeout.
The contact URI `subject` that goes into each JWT `sub` claim.
does_not_own: The encryption of the body. The message-encryption section owns it (`encrypt`).
The JWT and the `Authorization` header value. The vapid-authentication section owns them (`VapidKeys::authorization`).
Storing subscriptions and deleting dead ones. ostra-store (`RegistryDb`) and ostra-server (`ServerServices::notify`) own that.
Retries. The crate never retries; the caller decides what to do with `SendOutcome::Failed`.
Deciding whether push is enabled and which subscriptions to target. ostra-server owns that (`settings().notifications.push` and the workspace filter).

assumptions: The caller built `Notifier` with a `subject` that is a `mailto:` or `https:` URI. `Notifier::new` does not check it; ostra-server passes `mailto:ostra@localhost`.
`sub.keys.p256dh` and `sub.keys.auth` are URL-safe base64 as the browser produced them. `send` decodes them with `b64_decode` and returns `NotifyError::Key` when decoding fails.
`sub.endpoint` is an absolute `https` or `http` URL. `origin_of` rejects any other scheme. ostra-server's `push_subscribe` already refuses endpoints that do not start with `https://`.
The system clock is at or after the Unix epoch. `send` uses `unwrap_or_default()`, so a clock before 1970 produces an expiry of 12 hours after the epoch, which push services reject.
The call runs inside a Tokio runtime, because reqwest's async client needs one. ostra-server calls `send` from a `tokio::spawn` task.
A new JWT for each message is acceptable. `send` signs a new JWT on every call and caches none.

sections.title: Message encryption
sections.purpose: `encrypt` and `encrypt_with` turn a plaintext payload into an RFC 8188 `aes128gcm` body that only the subscribed browser can decrypt, as RFC 8291 specifies. `encrypt` generates a new sender key pair and a new 16-byte salt for every message. `encrypt_with` takes both as arguments so the tests can reproduce the RFC 8291 Appendix A test vector.

owns: The payload size limit `MAX_PLAINTEXT` (3993 bytes).
The ECDH, the three HKDF-SHA-256 derivations, and the AES-128-GCM encryption.
The byte layout of the body: salt, record size, key id length, key id, ciphertext.
The single-record framing with the `0x02` padding delimiter.
does_not_own: The browser's key pair and auth secret. The browser creates them and ostra-store keeps them as a `PushSubscription`.
Serializing the `Notification` to JSON. `Notifier::send` in the push-delivery section does that before it calls `encrypt`.
Decryption. The browser's push stack decrypts; the crate has a `decrypt` helper only inside its tests.

assumptions: `ua_public` is the browser's 65-byte uncompressed SEC1 point, as `PushSubscription.keys.p256dh` carries it. `PublicKey::from_sec1_bytes` also accepts a 33-byte compressed point, but `encrypt_with` puts `ua_public` into the key info as given, so a compressed key produces a key the browser does not derive.
`auth_secret` is the browser's 16-byte auth secret. The code does not check its length; HKDF accepts any salt length.
The whole message fits in one record. The code writes exactly one record and always ends it with the last-record delimiter `0x02`, with no extra padding.
The sender key id is 65 bytes, so `as_public.len() as u8` does not truncate. `uncompressed` always returns a 65-byte P-256 point.
The operating system random source works. `encrypt` calls `rand::fill` for the salt and `rand::rng()` for the sender key without error handling.

business_flow.outcome: `encrypt` generates a random 16-byte salt and a random P-256 sender key and calls `encrypt_with`.

business_flow.action: Refuses a payload longer than 3993 bytes and parses the browser's public key.
business_flow.outcome: The payload fits in one push body and the browser key is a valid P-256 point, or a `NotifyError` returns.

business_flow.action: Runs ECDH between the sender key and the browser key, then derives the input keying material, the content encryption key and the nonce with HKDF-SHA-256.
business_flow.outcome: A 16-byte key and a 12-byte nonce exist that the browser can derive too.

business_flow.action: Appends the `0x02` delimiter to the payload and encrypts it with AES-128-GCM.
business_flow.outcome: The ciphertext includes the 16-byte GCM tag.

business_flow.action: Writes the header (salt, record size 4096, key id length 65, sender public key) and then the ciphertext.
business_flow.outcome: The `aes128gcm` body is returned.

diagrams.title: RFC 8291 key derivation and encryption in encrypt_with
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
    size{"plaintext.len() > 3993?"} -- yes --> tl["Err TooLarge"]
    size -- no --> parse["PublicKey::from_sec1_bytes(ua_public)"]
    parse -- error --> ke["Err Key p256dh"]
    parse -- ok --> ecdh["as_secret.diffie_hellman(ua_key)"]
    ecdh --> ikm["HKDF salt=auth_secret, info='WebPush: info' + ua_public + as_public, 32 bytes = IKM"]
    ikm --> cek["HKDF salt=salt, info='Content-Encoding: aes128gcm', 16 bytes = CEK"]
    ikm --> nonce["HKDF salt=salt, info='Content-Encoding: nonce', 12 bytes = nonce"]
    cek --> gcm["Aes128Gcm encrypt(plaintext + 0x02)"]
    nonce --> gcm
    gcm --> body["salt + RECORD_SIZE + 65 + as_public + ciphertext"]

rows: Random per message (`rand::fill`), or the caller's salt in `encrypt_with`.
65, the length of the sender public key.
Sender (application server) public key, uncompressed SEC1 point.
AES-128-GCM of plaintext followed by `0x02`, including the 16-byte tag.

sections.title: VAPID authentication
sections.purpose: `VapidKeys` is the application server's P-256 key pair. With it the push service can identify Ostra as the sender (RFC 8292). It signs an ES256 JWT for the push service origin and formats the `Authorization: vapid t=<jwt>, k=<public key>` header. It also exports the public key in the URL-safe base64 form that the browser passes as `applicationServerKey` when it subscribes.

owns: The P-256 secret key and its export and import as raw 32 bytes (`private_bytes`, `from_private_bytes`).
The public key encoding: 65-byte uncompressed point, URL-safe base64 without padding.
The JWT header `{"typ":"JWT","alg":"ES256"}`, the claims `aud`, `exp`, `sub`, and the 64-byte signature.
The `Debug` output, which shows only the public key and never the secret.
does_not_own: Persisting the key. ostra-server's `vapid_keys` stores `private_bytes()` in ostra-store under the secret name `vapid_private`.
Choosing the audience and the expiry. `Notifier::send` in the push-delivery section computes them.
Publishing the public key to browsers. ostra-server's `info` handler returns it as `ServerInfo.vapid_public_key`.

assumptions: The `audience` passed to `jwt` is the push service origin `scheme://host[:port]`. `jwt` puts it into the claims without checking it; `Notifier::send` gets it from `origin_of`.
`expires` is a Unix time in seconds no more than 24 hours ahead, as RFC 8292 requires. `jwt` does not check it; `Notifier::send` uses now plus 12 hours.
`from_private_bytes` receives a 32-byte big-endian P-256 scalar. Any other length or an out-of-range value returns `NotifyError::Key`.

The key pair stays the same for the life of every browser subscription. If the key changes, subscriptions created with the old `applicationServerKey` fail at the push service. ostra-server generates a new key only when the stored key is missing or does not parse.

business_flow.action: Reads the secret `vapid_private` from the registry and passes it to `VapidKeys::from_private_bytes`.
business_flow.outcome: The stored key is loaded; if it is missing or invalid, `VapidKeys::generate` creates a new one and the server stores it.

business_flow.action: Fetches the server info and subscribes with `public_key_b64url()` as `applicationServerKey`.
business_flow.outcome: The push service ties the subscription to Ostra's public key.

business_flow.action: Calls `authorization(audience, subject, expires)` for each message.
business_flow.outcome: A signed JWT and the public key travel in the `Authorization` header, and the push service can verify the sender.

diagrams.title: Building the VAPID Authorization header
diagrams.source:
sequenceDiagram
    participant N as Notifier
    participant V as VapidKeys
    participant K as SigningKey
    N->>V: authorization(audience, subject, expires)
    V->>V: jwt(audience, subject, expires)
    V->>V: header = b64 of typ JWT, alg ES256
    V->>V: claims = b64 of aud, exp, sub
    V->>K: sign(header.claims)
    K-->>V: Signature (64 bytes r and s)
    V->>V: public_key_b64url()
    V-->>N: vapid t=header.claims.sig, k=public key

sections.title: How ostra-notify works with the other projects
sections.purpose: ostra-notify is a library with no entry point of its own. It sits between the Ostra server, which decides when to notify, and the browser push services. This section traces the two cross-project flows: how a browser subscribes, and how an engine notice becomes a notification on the user's screen.

owns: The encryption, the signing and the HTTP delivery of each message, as described in the other sections.
does_not_own: The `PushSubscription` and `PushKeys` types and `ServerInfo.vapid_public_key`. ostra-core `src/api.rs` owns them.
Subscription storage (`add_push_subscription`, `list_push_subscriptions`, `remove_push_subscription`) and the `vapid_private` secret. ostra-store `RegistryDb` owns them.
The `POST /api/push/subscribe` route, the server info route, key loading (`vapid_keys`) and the fan-out in `ServerServices::notify`. ostra-server owns them.
The `Notice` values (title, body, url, tag) and when they are raised. ostra-engine (`Services::notify`) owns them.
Permission prompts, subscription and display. The web console owns them in `web/src/lib/push.ts` and `web/public/sw.js`.

assumptions: ostra-server creates exactly one `Notifier`, shares it as `Shared.notifier` (an `Arc<Notifier>`), and uses the same `VapidKeys` for `ServerInfo` and for signing.
Subscriptions are stored with the endpoint as their identity. ostra-server removes a `Gone` subscription with `remove_push_subscription(&endpoint)`.

A subscription with no workspace receives notices from every workspace. `push_subscribe` stores new subscriptions with workspace `None`, and `ServerServices::notify` keeps a subscription when its workspace is `None` or equals the notifying workspace.
Push is sent only when the workspace setting `notifications.push` is true. `ServerServices::notify` returns early otherwise.
Delivery runs in the background. `ServerServices::notify` sends from a `tokio::spawn` task, one subscription after the other, and never reports results to the engine.

business_flow.outcome: ostra-server builds a `Notification` with the URL prefixed by `/w/{workspace}`.

business_flow.action: Calls `Notifier::send` for each matching subscription.
business_flow.outcome: Dead subscriptions are removed and failures are logged.

business_flow.action: Receives the push, shows the notification, and opens its `url` on click.
business_flow.outcome: The user lands on the screen that needs them.

parts.overview: ostra-policy is the Rust crate that decides what happens to every tool call an Ostra agent makes. For each call it returns Allow, Ask (the user must answer), or Deny, and each decision names the rule that produced it. Each call passes two layers in order. Layer 1 is the guards: containment, ownership, and pipeline rules that no permission rule, user answer, or YOLO setting can override. Layer 2 is the permissions: Claude Code's model of permission modes (default, acceptEdits, plan, bypass) plus allow, ask, and deny rules. The crate also parses shell commands with tree-sitter-bash to find the simple commands and the files each one writes. After a tool runs, it watches build and test results, which drives the build-streak gate and the lesson gate. The native executor (ostra-exec-native) and the harness bridge (ostra-server) each create one `ExecutionPolicy` per agent execution and call `check` before each tool call and `observe` after it. ostra-workspace calls `validate_rule` on the permission rules in the settings, ostra-server's file watcher calls `apply_patch_paths`, and all shared types come from ostra-core.

sections.title: Execution policy and the check pipeline
sections.purpose: `ExecutionPolicy` is the object an executor creates once per agent execution. Its `check` method runs Layer 1 guards, then Layer 2 permissions, then applies the YOLO conversion, and returns a `PolicyDecision`. It also holds the mutable per-execution state: the YOLO switch, the allow rules the user granted during the session, and the build streak.

owns: The order of evaluation: Layer 1, then Layer 2, then the YOLO conversion (`ExecutionPolicy::check`).
Parsing the allow, ask, and deny rule lists of the `ExecContext` once at construction (`parse_rules`).
The per-execution `State`: `yolo`, `session_allow`, and `streak`.
How a call's paths are read from its input: `start_cwd`, `file_path`, `read_path`, `write_paths`.
does_not_own: The guards themselves (section Layer 1 guard dispatch and the sections it names).
Rule syntax and matching (section Permission rules).
Asking the user and showing the answer choices (ostra-exec-native and ostra-server, see section How other projects use the policy engine).
Running the tool (ostra-tools).

assumptions: The `ExecContext` passed to `ExecutionPolicy::new` does not change during the execution. `Roots::new` canonicalizes every root once at construction.
The caller calls `set_yolo` before each `check` so the policy follows the host's current YOLO switch. ostra-exec-native calls `policy.set_yolo(self.host.yolo())` before every check.
Permission rule strings were validated earlier with `validate_rule`. `parse_rules` drops an invalid rule with a `tracing::warn!` and does not report it to the caller.
A Bash call carries its shell text in the input field `command`. A missing field parses as the empty string.
A harness reports the tool's working directory in the input field `cwd`. `start_cwd` uses it only when it is an absolute path and otherwise uses the repo root.
A file tool names its path in `file_path` or, failing that, `path` (`file_path`).
A poisoned mutex is recovered with `into_inner` (`lock`), so a panic in one call does not disable the policy.

business_flow.action: Creates the policy for one agent execution from the execution context and the project's build and test commands.
business_flow.outcome: The policy holds canonical roots, parsed rules, and an empty streak.

business_flow.action: Sends one tool call to `check`.
business_flow.outcome: For a Bash call, the command text is parsed into simple commands.

business_flow.action: Check the call against every guard that applies.
business_flow.outcome: A guard refusal is returned as Deny and the permission layer is skipped.

business_flow.action: Match the call against deny, ask, and allow rules and apply the permission mode.
business_flow.outcome: An Allow, Ask, or Deny decision naming its rule.

business_flow.action: When YOLO is on, turns every Ask into Allow and relabels a bypass allow.
business_flow.outcome: The final decision goes back to the executor. Denials are never changed.

sections.title: Shell parsing
sections.purpose: The `bash` module parses shell text with tree-sitter-bash into simple commands in execution order. For each command it records the words, redirects, heredoc bodies, and the paths it would create, overwrite, move, or delete. It replaces the regex heuristics of Ultracode's shell-paths.js and keeps its rules. A heredoc body handed to a data sink is content, and a body fed to a shell runs. `<ID>` placeholders are not redirects, dot-only tokens are prose, and dynamic tokens are skipped.

owns: Word, Redirect, SimpleCommand, Parsed, TargetSpec, WriteTarget.
The `complete` and `modelled` flags.

does_not_own: Resolving target paths against the filesystem (section Shell guards).

assumptions: tree-sitter-bash is available. If the language fails to load or parsing returns no tree, the result has no commands and `complete` and `modelled` are false.
Subshell scoping of `cd` is not modelled. A `cd` inside `( )` affects later commands in the model.
Nested shell code (`bash -c`, `eval`, a heredoc fed to a shell) is parsed at most MAX_DEPTH = 4 levels deep. Deeper code sets `complete` to false.

diagrams.title: How the walker visits a node
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
    V[visit node] --> E{"error or missing node?"}
    E -->|yes| IC["complete = false"]
    V --> K{"node kind"}
    K -->|command| CM["command: words, assignments, redirects"]
    K -->|redirected_statement| RS["attach redirects and heredocs to the last command"]
    K -->|pipeline| PL["set piped_input on later stages"]
    K -->|test_command over plain words| SK[Skip]
    K -->|comment| SK
    K -->|"other named, not structural"| UM["modelled = false, visit children"]
    K -->|structural| VC[visit children]
    CM --> SUB["visit substitutions, parse bash -c and eval code"]
    RS --> HD["heredoc: parse body if a shell reads it, else store heredoc_body"]

subsections.title: Simple commands and words
subsections.purpose: A simple command is one command name with its arguments, assignments, and redirects. A word keeps its raw source and, when it contains no expansion, its unquoted static value.

owns: Static value rules and the effective command.
does_not_own: Permission matching on these texts (`perms::bash_forms`).

assumptions: A word is static when it is a plain word, a number, a single-quoted string, a double-quoted string with only literal content, or a concatenation of these. Any expansion makes `value` None.
A word has `glob` set when it has an unquoted `*`, `?`, `[`, or a brace expansion with `,` or `..`.

`effective_index` skips `VAR=value` words and wrappers with their options. Wrapper value flags such as `sudo -u` consume the next word, `env` assignments are skipped, and `timeout` consumes one duration word.
`Redirect::writes` is true for `>`, `>>`, `>|`, `&>`, `&>>`, `<>`, and `>&` with a target that is not a number or `-`.
A `[ ]` or `[[ ]]` test over plain words is skipped. A test containing `$`, a backtick, `[`, `]`, or `(` marks the script unmodelled, because evaluating it can run a command.

subsections.title: Bash permission
subsections.purpose: `bash_permission` decides a Bash call across all its simple commands. A deny rule on any command refuses the call. An ask rule on any command asks. Then each command must be allowed by a rule, be read-only, or be allowed by the mode.

owns: The Bash decision order and the unmodelled and unparsed handling.
does_not_own: Read-only classification (subsection Read-only commands).

assumptions: A command whose name is dynamic is never allowed by an allow rule.
A git command runs unasked only when its directory (the cwd plus any -C) is inside the repo, because git reads the repository's own config, which can name programs.
A command with an unresolved target, or with a target that runs code later, has unknown targets and is never auto-allowed as read-only.

In AcceptEdits mode, mkdir, touch, cp, and mv run unasked when all their targets are inside the repo, session, or temp. The command must have no assignments, no wrapper, and no path-named command word.

subsections.title: Read-only commands
subsections.purpose: `is_read_only` names the commands that run unasked in every mode, including plan. Only a command Ostra fully understands qualifies. An assignment or a wrapper can change what runs, a path-named command can be a script the agent wrote, and a dynamic word or glob can expand to an option that starts a program.

owns: READ_ONLY, GIT_READ, GIT_SAFE_GLOBAL, EXEC_CAPABLE, and the per-command flag checks.
does_not_own: The shell guard's PLAIN_READERS list, which is a separate and longer list (section Shell guards).

assumptions: The command has no assignments, the command word is the first word, the name is static, and the name contains no `/`.
For git, rg, sort, find, tree, file, and uniq (EXEC_CAPABLE), every argument must be static and glob-free.

subsections.title: Failure detection and diagnostic signatures
subsections.purpose: `failed_from` reads a `ToolOutcome` and returns Some(true), Some(false), or None for no evidence. `diagnostic_signature` finds the first diagnostic line and normalizes it, so the same error reads the same across attempts.

owns: FAILURE_MARKERS, EXIT_CODE_PATTERNS, INTERRUPTED, DIAGNOSTIC, and the normalization regexes.
does_not_own: The exit code value, which the tool runner reports.

assumptions: The order of evidence is: the reported exit code, then an exit code in the output (`Exit code N`, `exited with code N`, `exit status N`), then an error with timed out, interrupted, or canceled (no evidence), then any error (failed), then unknown results with empty output (no evidence), then failure markers in the output.

A diagnostic line is 12 to 400 characters long and matches DIAGNOSTIC, for example `cannot find symbol`, `error TS2345`, `error[E0308]`, `AssertionError`, `ModuleNotFoundError`, or `expected ... but`.

Normalization strips an ERROR/WARN/E/FAIL prefix, replaces paths with `<path>`, removes `[n,n]` and `:line:col`, replaces versions with `<v>`, collapses whitespace, and keeps 160 characters. A result shorter than 8 characters is discarded.

parts.overview: ostra-providers is the Rust crate that connects Ostra to model providers. It hides each provider's API behind one neutral chat interface, the `Provider` trait. It has two real implementations, both of which stream over server-sent events: `Anthropic` for the Anthropic Messages API (`POST /v1/messages`) and `OpenAi` for the OpenAI Responses API (`POST /v1/responses`). It also has `ScriptedProvider`, which returns queued answers in tests. The `Providers` registry builds one provider per configured name. It resolves each API key and base URL from environment variables, credentials saved in the browser, or the OS keychain. It turns a `provider:model` route string into a provider and a bare model id. Shared code covers retries with exponential backoff that never repeat a request after output has started, a mapping from HTTP status codes and stream errors to `ProviderError`, compaction of long conversations (on the provider's servers where the provider supports it, otherwise on the client), and `structured`, which forces a model to call a `decide` tool so judges get machine-readable decisions. The crate depends on ostra-core for `Effort`, `Usage`, the provider config and status types, and the models.dev pricing catalog. ostra-server builds the registry at startup, rebuilds it when credentials change, and uses it for judge calls. ostra-exec-native uses it for every model call of the native agent loop.

sections.title: Neutral chat interface
sections.purpose: Defines the provider-independent types that every model call goes through: the request, the content blocks, the streamed events, the response, the stop reasons, the errors, and the `Provider` trait. The native agent loop and the judge code build a `ChatRequest` once and send it to whichever provider the route names. Each provider translates these types to and from its own wire format.

owns: The shape of `ChatRequest`, `Message`, `Block`, `StreamEvent`, `ChatResponse`, `StopReason`, and `ProviderError`.
The `Provider` trait contract: `name`, `server_tools`, `chat`, and `compact` with its default implementation.
The defaults of `ChatRequest::new`: `max_tokens` 32000, `effort` `High`, `tool_choice` `Auto`, `refusal_fallback` true.
The rule that `Opaque` and signed `Compaction` blocks are sent back only to the provider that produced them.
does_not_own: Translating the types to wire JSON, which each provider owns (sections `anthropic-provider` and `openai-provider`).
The `Effort` enum and the `Usage` struct, which ostra-core owns (`ostra_core::Effort`, `ostra_core::exec::Usage`).
Deciding what to do with each `StopReason`, which the native agent loop in ostra-exec-native owns (section `workspace-integration`).

assumptions: `ChatRequest.model` holds the bare model id without the `provider:` prefix. `Providers::for_model` strips the prefix before a caller builds the request.
`Message` alternates user and assistant turns as the provider APIs expect. No code in this crate checks the ordering.
Every `Block::ToolResult.tool_use_id` matches the `id` of a `Block::ToolUse` in the previous assistant turn. The providers pass the ids through without checking them.
An `EventSink` callback returns quickly and does not block, because providers call it inline while they read the stream.

`Block::Opaque.provider` and `Block::Compaction.provider` hold the value of `Provider::name()` of the provider that produced the block (`anthropic` or `openai`), or an empty string for a summary made on the client.

business_flow.outcome: The request describes one model turn without any provider-specific field

business_flow.action: Translates the request to its API and streams the answer, calling the event sink for each text, thinking, and tool-input fragment
business_flow.outcome: The caller can show progress while the turn is still running

business_flow.action: Assembles the finished content blocks, the stop reason, the token usage with its cost, and the model that answered
business_flow.outcome: The caller receives one `ChatResponse` or one `ProviderError`

business_flow.action: Appends the assistant content to the conversation unchanged, runs the tool calls, and adds the results as a user turn
business_flow.outcome: The next request carries the provider's opaque blocks back to that provider

sections.title: Provider registry and credentials
sections.purpose: `Providers` holds the model providers configured on this machine, keyed by name. It builds them from the global config and the credentials saved in the browser. It reports each provider's key and base URL source to the console. It turns a `provider:model` route string into a provider and a bare model id. The server builds it once at startup and rebuilds it in place whenever the credentials or the config change.

owns: The map from provider name to `Arc<dyn Provider>` and the list of `ProviderStatus` values.
The lookup order for API keys and base URLs.
The redaction of base URLs shown in the browser (`display_url`).
The rule that providers added with `register` survive a `reload`.
The `ApiKey` wrapper, whose `Debug` and `Display` never print the value.
does_not_own: Storing saved credentials and validating edits to them, which ostra-server owns (`ostra-server/src/credentials.rs`, `PATCH /api/providers/{name}`).
The `ProviderConfig`, `SavedCredentials`, `ProviderStatus`, and `SavedProviderView` types and the default provider table, which ostra-core owns (`ostra_core::config`, `ostra_core::api`).
Building the HTTP clients, which `Anthropic::new` and `OpenAi::new` own (sections `anthropic-provider` and `openai-provider`).

assumptions: Only the config names `anthropic` and `openai` map to real providers. `rebuild` logs `unknown provider in config; ignored` for any other name and builds no provider, but still records a status for it.
`for_model` reports `NoKey` only for the names `anthropic` and `openai`, which are hard-coded in the match. Any other missing name gives `UnknownProvider`.
The model id may contain `:`. `for_model` splits on the first `:` only.
The keychain entry uses `ProviderConfig.keychain_service` as the service and the provider name as the account, as `keyring::Entry::new(service, name)` shows.
Callers hold an `Arc<dyn Provider>` returned by `get` for the length of one call. A `reload` replaces the map, but calls already running keep the old provider and its key.
`rebuild` and `register` both take the `statuses` write lock before the `map` write lock. Keeping this order avoids a deadlock between them.
Environment variables are read at build time. A variable changed after `from_config` or `reload` has no effect until the next `reload`.

sections.title: Anthropic provider
sections.purpose: `Anthropic` implements `Provider` for the Anthropic Messages API. It builds a streaming `POST {base_url}/v1/messages` request that fits the capabilities of each Claude model. It sets prompt-cache breakpoints, thinking, effort, and beta headers. It reads the SSE stream into a `ChatResponse` with usage and cost. The native agent loop and the judges call it for every route that starts with `anthropic:`.

owns: The per-model capability table `caps` and the model matching in `is_model`.

Server-side compaction through the `compaction` request field.
does_not_own: Retries, HTTP status mapping, and SSE framing, which the section `retry-and-errors` owns.
The model output limits and prices, which the ostra-core models.dev catalog owns (`ostra_core::pricing::max_output` and `pricing::cost`).
Running client tool calls and answering `__invalid_json` inputs, which the native agent loop in ostra-exec-native owns.

assumptions: The model id is a Claude id with the hyphenated version form, such as `claude-opus-4-6` or `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`. `caps` matches ids by exact string, by a dated snapshot suffix, or for older models by prefix.
An unknown model id is a newer model. `caps` gives it adaptive thinking, full effort, compaction, no forced tool choice, and no fallbacks.
When models.dev lists no output limit for the model, the requested `max_tokens` is taken as the limit (`request_body`, `ceiling`).
The server sends `content_block_start` before any delta for an index. Deltas and stops for an unknown index are ignored.
The key does not follow redirects. The HTTP client uses `redirect::Policy::none()` so the `x-api-key` header is never sent to another host.
The connection must open within 20 seconds. The client sets no limit on the total length of a streamed response.

parts.overview: ostra-sandbox is the Ostra crate that confines agent commands and the programs Ostra starts for a project, using the operating system kernel. The policy layer (ostra-policy) judges each tool call by the paths it names, and a shell command can hide those paths. This crate enforces the boundary underneath it: the host file system is read-only, only the execution's own roots are writable, Ostra's data dir and the user's credentials are hidden, and network traffic leaves only through a per-execution egress proxy. The crate has three layers. `Profile` describes one execution's boundary without naming a backend. A `Backend` (bubblewrap on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS) turns a profile into a command line. The `sys` module is the only code that calls the kernel, through one `Os` implementation per operating system. Its callers are ostra-exec-native (the native Bash tool), ostra-exec-harness (harness CLIs), ostra-tools, ostra-engine, ostra-code (language servers and code providers), ostra-workspace (settings validation and status), and ostra-server (startup, the `ostra sandbox-init` entry point, MCP servers). It reads its settings types (`SandboxConfig`, `ExecContext`) and path helpers from ostra-core.

subsections.title: Profiles for project programs
subsections.purpose: `Profile::for_program` builds the profile for a format command, a language server, a code provider, or a stdio MCP server. It applies the same hiding and read-only rules as an agent execution, with the given roots writable and the same network choice.
assumptions: The first root identifies the project for its cache dir; with no roots the key is `/` (`profile.rs` line 304).
Programs get no session dirs, no protected paths, and no memory database rules, because they run outside an execution.
No harness is running, so every `HOME_CREDENTIALS` entry is hidden (`own` is None).

subsections.title: Rule ordering and conflict resolution
subsections.purpose: Both backends need the rules in the same order: shallower paths first, so a deeper rule overrides a shallower one. When two rules name the same path, only the more restrictive one stays. `Profile::ordered` produces this list and also expands the home overlay into one rule per home entry.
assumptions: `std::fs::read_dir(home)` at render time lists the home entries to bind back; entries created later are not bound (`ordered`, lines 659-670).
The rank order `HomeTmpfs` 0, `HomeEntry` 1, `Writable` 2, `ReadOnly` 3, `Hidden` 4, `Link` 5 expresses restrictiveness (`Mount::rank`).

sections.purpose: An agent that can write a repository's `.git/config`, hooks, or `commondir` can make git on the host run a program of its choice. This unit finds every repository under the writable roots, keeps the program-choosing paths of each git dir read-only in the profile, and after each Bash call undoes `commondir` files an agent planted.

does_not_own: Git settings passed through the environment (`ostra_core::git::agent_env`, owned by ostra-core)

assumptions: A `.git` file's first line has the form `gitdir: <path>` and fits in 4096 bytes (`GitDir::of`).
A git dir whose parent is named `worktrees` belongs to a linked worktree, whose config is the main repository's config.
Git never writes a `commondir` into a repository's own git dir, so any such file is planted and safe to remove (`repair_git_dirs` doc).
A linked worktree's `commondir` always contains `../..`.
An empty placeholder for a missing `config.worktree` is harmless, because git reads it only with `extensions.worktreeConfig`, which `config` sets.

business_flow.outcome: Up to 128 repositories are found, shallowest first

business_flow.action: Runs `repair_git_dirs` after each Bash call

sections.purpose: Renders a profile as `bwrap` arguments. The sandbox gets its own mount, pid, and IPC namespaces, and its own network namespace unless the network choice is `host`. sections.title: The sandbox-init helper (Linux)
sections.purpose: `ostra sandbox-init` is the first program inside every bubblewrap sandbox. Inside a private network namespace only the sandbox's own loopback exists, so the helper listens on it and forwards each connection to a Unix socket Ostra bound in: the egress proxy and fixed ports such as the hook bridge. It then loads the seccomp filter, starts the command, and exits with the command's status. It uses std threads only and no async runtime.

owns: Parsing `[--proxy <socket>] [--forward <port>=<socket>]... -- <program> [args...]`
The loopback listeners inside the namespace and the proxy environment variables

Dispatching the `sandbox-init` subcommand before clap parses arguments (owned by ostra-server `main.rs`)

assumptions: The helper runs with exactly one thread when it installs the filter, so the filter covers every thread it starts later (`helper.rs` line 32).
The IPv6 loopback may be missing in the namespace; binding `[::1]` is tried and a failure is ignored.
Fixed forward ports are free inside a fresh namespace; they are bound before the proxy's port 0 so the proxy cannot take one of them.
The proxy socket is reachable only from this sandbox, so the proxy URL inside carries no credential.

sections.title: Seccomp filter (Linux)
sections.purpose: A BPF seccomp program that the helper loads before starting the command and that every descendant inherits. It refuses new user namespaces, which would give the command capabilities over fresh namespaces and mounts, and several kernel calls that builds and tests do not need. Refusals return an error code so programs that probe for a feature fall back instead of dying.

owns: The lists `REFUSED`, `MISSING`, and `TTY_REFUSED`

assumptions: The CPU is x86_64 or aarch64; the module is compiled only there (`sys/linux/mod.rs` line 6).
Both supported CPUs are little-endian, so an argument's low 32 bits sit at its start in `seccomp_data` (`arg_low`).
The first argument of `clone` holds the flags on both CPUs.
glibc falls back from `clone3` to `clone` when `clone3` returns `ENOSYS`, so the flags become readable by the filter.

sections.title: Seatbelt backend (macOS)
sections.purpose: Renders a profile as an SBPL policy passed to `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -p`. Seatbelt has no mount namespace, so a hidden path returns EPERM instead of looking empty, `/tmp` is denied and `TMPDIR` points at the scratch dir, a harness gets no disposable home, and every sandbox shares the host's loopback, where the policy names the ports it may reach.

A `(literal P)` rule also matches a missing path in any letter case, so Seatbelt needs no placeholders (`path_filter` doc).
`set_server_port` is called before the first policy is rendered (ostra-server `app.rs` `build`).
The mach service list in `SEATBELT_BASE` was measured with git, cargo, npm, go, pip, clang through xcrun, and the four harness CLIs; a new tool that needs another service fails inside the sandbox.
`localhost` resolves from `/etc/hosts` without the DNS resolver, which is denied under private networks.

sections.title: Egress proxy
sections.purpose: The egress proxy is the only network path out of a sandbox with a private network. On Linux each execution gets its own Unix socket, bound only into its own sandbox, which the helper serves on the sandbox's loopback. On macOS it gets its own port on `127.0.0.1` with a credential, because every sandbox shares the host's loopback. The proxy sees the destination host and port of every connection, lets through only what the policy allows, and connects to the address it checked without a second lookup.

owns: Host rule parsing and matching (`HostRule`)
The policy per network choice (`Policy`) and address classification (`is_private`)
The HTTP CONNECT and plain-HTTP proxy protocol, the TLS server-name check, and the upstream proxy route
Listeners, splices, the egress runtime, and the socket dir `<data dir>/egress`
Decision reports, deduplicated per host, port, and outcome
does_not_own: Sending decisions to the engine (owned by the reporting section)
The harness model hosts' use in a harness profile (owned by ostra-exec-harness `sandbox.rs`)
Saving `allowed_hosts` and `upstream_proxy` (validated in the settings validation section, stored by ostra-core and ostra-workspace)

assumptions: Clients honor `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `ALL_PROXY`, and skip the proxy for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, and `::1` through `NO_PROXY` (`proxy_env`).
Node honors the proxy variables when `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`.
Requests use HTTP/1.x; any other version is refused.
A TLS client speaks first; when the destination speaks first (an SSH banner), the tunnel is not TLS.
The `OnDecision` callback does not block, because it runs on the proxy's runtime.
The data dir is hidden in every sandbox, so the socket dir inside it is reachable only through the binds a profile adds.

subsections.title: Network choices and access
subsections.purpose: `Policy::new` turns `[sandbox] network` into two rule lists. Trusted rules are hosts the user chose and may resolve anywhere. Builtin rules are Ostra's defaults and must resolve to public addresses. `access` classifies a destination as AnyAddress, PublicOnly, or Refused.
assumptions: Hosts the user listed may be internal mirrors, so trusted rules allow private addresses.
Built-in hosts must resolve publicly, so a poisoned DNS answer pointing at a private address is refused.

subsections.title: Resolution, address classes, and upstream routing
subsections.purpose: After `access` allows a destination, `resolve` looks up the name once and filters the answers. `route` decides between a direct connection and the configured upstream HTTP proxy. The proxy connects to exactly the addresses `resolve` returned.
assumptions: A local-only name (`localhost`, a single label, or a name ending in `.localhost`, `.local`, `.internal`, `.lan`, `.home.arpa`) points at this machine or the LAN, so a PublicOnly destination with such a name is refused without a lookup that would go out on the LAN.
An internal mirror is rarely behind the corporate proxy, so a trusted host that resolves to a private address is reached directly even when `upstream_proxy` is set.
The upstream proxy accepts plain HTTP CONNECT and absolute-form requests, and answers 200 to a successful CONNECT.

subsections.title: Request parsing and the TLS server-name check
subsections.purpose: The proxy accepts CONNECT for any protocol and absolute-form `http://` requests for plain HTTP. A plain HTTP request is rewritten to origin form with `Connection: close` and without `Proxy-*`, `Host`, `Connection`, or `Keep-Alive` headers from the client. For a CONNECT to a host name, the first TLS ClientHello's server name must equal that host, because a CDN that routes by server name would otherwise carry the tunnel to any site it serves.
assumptions: The ClientHello may span several TLS records; `client_hello_name` reassembles them.
A tunnel whose first byte is not 0x16 is not TLS and passes without a name check.
A CONNECT to a literal IP address has no name to check.

rows: Not TLS, or a ClientHello without a server name, or the server spoke first
Continues when equal to the CONNECT host, refused otherwise
Unreadable or oversized handshake, or head timeout

subsections.title: Listeners, splices, and sockets
subsections.purpose: A `Listener` is a Unix socket or a `127.0.0.1` port served on the egress runtime. A proxy listener runs the proxy protocol; a splice listener copies every connection to a fixed target, used for the hook bridge and listed loopback services. Dropping a listener stops it, ends its connections, and removes its socket file.
assumptions: `remove_stale_sockets` runs at server start while no other server of the same data dir runs, because it deletes every `.sock` file in the socket dir.
A loopback proxy's credential is a random UUID; any sandbox that opens the loopback can reach the port, so the credential is what keeps other executions out.
A socket another part of Ostra serves (the hook bridge) must not be removed on drop, so `served_elsewhere` has no stop token.

sections.title: Decoy credential files
sections.purpose: Decoys are credential paths an agent has no reason to read, so an open of one from inside the sandbox is a containment signal (Rule P3). A Bash `cat` is seen as well as a tool call, because the kernel reports it. On Linux a fake file is bound read-only into the sandbox and watched with inotify from outside. On macOS an existing file is refused by the policy and the refusal is read from the system log.

sections.title: Process members and cleanup
sections.purpose: `Members` is what one sandboxed invocation holds while it runs: its egress and forward listeners, its decoys, and two marker names that find its processes on macOS. Seatbelt has no pid namespace and nothing like `--die-with-parent`, so a child that calls `setsid` or double-forks outlives its shell. Dropping `Members` kills every process still marked with the invocation's own name.

assumptions: No daemon registers a mach name starting with `dev.ostra.sandbox.`, so allowing lookup of one marks a process without giving it access to anything.
A Seatbelt policy is inherited and cannot be dropped, so the marker finds every descendant however it detached.
Some system sandboxes allow every mach name, so a member must also be refused `dev.ostra.sandbox.canary`.
`proc_listallpids` returns at most 8192 pids into the buffer.

sections.title: Startup environment scrub (macOS)
sections.purpose: On macOS any unsandboxed program of the same user can read another process's startup environment with `sysctl(KERN_PROCARGS2)`, which reads the strings the kernel placed on the stack at exec. `scrub_startup_env` copies the environment to the heap and zeroes the original strings, so secrets passed to Ostra through its environment are not readable that way. Ostra's Seatbelt policies also refuse that sysctl to sandboxed commands.

assumptions: It is called before any thread starts, because it removes and sets every variable and writes into `environ` strings.
On Linux nothing is needed: `/proc/<pid>/environ` is readable only by the same user and every sandbox has its own pid namespace.
