parts.overview: ostra-server is the crate that builds the `ostra` binary: the local process a developer starts to run Ostra's engineering pipeline and to open the browser console. It starts up the machine-wide state: the global config, the registry database with its credentials sealed by a master key, providers, executors, the MCP gateway, and push keys. It opens every registered workspace through ostra-workspace and serves one axum router on 127.0.0.1:7878 by default. The router carries the REST API under `/api/`, one multiplexed WebSocket at `/ws`, the hook bridge and MCP shim that harness CLIs call under `/internal/`, and the React build from `web/dist`, which is embedded in the binary. Every browser request passes a Host, Origin, and cookie guard, and the cookie comes from a one-time sign-in link that the CLI prints. Around the engine (ostra-engine), the crate adds the Files dock, code navigation (ostra-code), git clone, pull, and the Git dock, workspace artifacts, skills, the Sessions tree and search, and setup terminals for harness installs and logins. It also implements the engine's `Services` trait, so each workspace's engine reaches executors, judges, push notifications, and settings through the server.

sections.title: Binary entry point and CLI commands
sections.purpose: `src/main.rs` defines the `ostra` binary. With no subcommand it starts the server, and its other subcommands manage a running or stopped server from a terminal. It also handles two internal entry points that harness executions and sandboxes call: `hook`, `mcp-stdio`, and the hidden `sandbox-init` first argument.

`ostra_sandbox::scrub_startup_env` must run before anything reads the environment, so it is called before `Cli::parse`.
A first argument of exactly `sandbox-init` means the process is a sandbox helper. It exits with `ostra_sandbox::init::main` before any runtime or logging starts. This path is hidden from `--help`.
`std::env::current_exe()` names the binary that harness hooks call back, and falls back to the name `ostra`.

sections.title: Browser sign-in, cookies, and allowed hosts
sections.purpose: `src/auth.rs` authenticates browsers. The server or `ostra url` mints a one-time token and puts it in a URL fragment. The page exchanges the token once for an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict` session cookie that lasts 30 days. The module also builds the list of Host values the server answers to and the private `ostra-<hex>.localhost` name for a loopback server. It keeps a per-address limit on failed exchanges and records the running server in `server.json`.

owns: Tokens under registry keys `auth:token:<sha256>` and sign-in records under `auth:cookie:<sha256>`.
The private host name under registry key `server:private_host`.
The in-memory cookie cache (`cookies`) and the revoke broadcast (`revoked`).
The failed-exchange limiter (`failures`).
Host allowlist (`Access::hosts`) and Origin check (`Auth::allowed_origin`).
`server.json` in the data dir: `port`, `url_host`, `pid`.
Process liveness checks (`server_running`, `process_alive`).
does_not_own: Applying the checks to requests (section http-guard).
Closing open sockets on revoke (section websocket reads `subscribe_revoked`).
The registry's key-value storage (ostra-store).

assumptions: Tokens and cookies are 32 random bytes in hex (256 bits), so the limiter exists only to keep a guessing loop from filling the log and the registry.
Only hashes are stored; the cookie value itself never reaches the registry.
`RegistryDb::kv_replace` is a compare-and-swap, so two concurrent exchanges of one token cannot both claim it.
A loopback peer is never rate limited, because counting its failures would let any local process lock the user out.
Whether the cookie gets `Secure` is decided from the `Origin` header, which the browser sets. `X-Forwarded-Proto` is not read, because any client could send it.
Browsers resolve every `*.localhost` name to this machine, and a cookie set on the private name is not sent to `127.0.0.1` or other local ports.
A record without JSON (only a number) is a legacy sign-in from an older server. `parse_record` reads it and `load_records` rewrites it with a new id.
A revoke made by another process (the CLI) is seen by a running server only after the cache entry is older than `RECHECK` (5 seconds).

business_flow.action: Mints a token that expires in 15 minutes and prints `http://<url_host>/#token=<token>`.
business_flow.outcome: The registry holds the token hash with its expiry.

business_flow.action: POSTs `{"token": ...}` to `/api/auth/exchange`.
business_flow.outcome: The token is marked `used:<time>`, a sign-in record is stored, and the response sets the `ostra_session` cookie.

business_flow.action: Sends the cookie on every API request and on the socket upgrade.
business_flow.outcome: The guard accepts the request while the record exists and is younger than 30 days.

business_flow.action: Revokes a sign-in from settings or the CLI.
business_flow.outcome: The record is deleted. This server drops it from its cache and closes that browser's sockets; a revoke from the CLI takes effect within 5 seconds.

sections.title: HTTP security guard and response headers
sections.purpose: The `guard` middleware in `src/api.rs` runs before every route, the static fallback included. It refuses unknown Host values. It moves a loopback IP host to the private name, keeps local-only endpoints local, refuses page content and other sites, and requires the session cookie on the API. It adds security headers to every response, refusals included.

owns: Which requests reach a handler: Host, private-name redirect, `/internal/` locality, Origin, `Sec-Fetch-Site`, `Sec-Fetch-Dest`, and cookie checks.
The Content-Security-Policy and the other security headers.
Logging of refused sign-ins with `request_facts`, without token or cookie values.
does_not_own: The allowlists and cookie validity (section browser-auth).
Harness bearer tokens on `/internal/` routes (section harness-bridge).

assumptions: A request counts as API when its path starts with `/api/` or equals `/ws`; other paths are pages or assets.
`/api/auth/exchange` is the only API path that needs no cookie.

The MCP OAuth callback `/mcp/oauth/callback` lives outside `/api/`, because the authorization server's redirect is a cross-site navigation that does not carry a `SameSite=Strict` cookie. Its single-use `state` authenticates it (section mcp-gateway).
Ostra's own hook and MCP clients never send `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site`, while a browser page always sends one of them.

The console calls the API with fetch (`Sec-Fetch-Dest: empty`), the socket (`websocket`), and download links (`document`). Any other destination means page content, such as a Markdown image an agent wrote, is reaching the API.
The peer address comes from axum `ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>`, which `app::run` enables with `into_make_service_with_connect_info`.

business_flow.action: Sends a request.
business_flow.outcome: The guard either passes it to the route or answers with 421, 307, 403, or 401.

business_flow.action: Adds security headers to the response.
business_flow.outcome: Other pages cannot frame or sniff it, and the page cannot load remote scripts or images.

sections.title: WebSocket channels and terminal streams
sections.purpose: `/ws` gives each browser tab one socket that carries every live update, multiplexed by named channels the tab subscribes to. It forwards engine notices and server pushes as JSON text frames and streams PTY output as binary frames. It also accepts terminal input, resizes, and editor hint requests. It rechecks the sign-in every 5 seconds and closes with code 4401 when the cookie is revoked or expires.

owns: Channel subscriptions per socket (at most 256).

assumptions: The upgrade request already passed the guard's Origin and cookie checks. The socket reads the cookie once at upgrade and checks it again right after subscribing to revokes, because a revoke between the two steps is broadcast to no one.
A `lagged` error frame tells the page to refetch its REST snapshot; the socket keeps running.
An execution id longer than 255 bytes is cut to 255 in a binary frame header.
A `term:<id>` subscribe for a run whose PTY has not started waits on `PtyRegistry::inserted` until it appears.
A repeated `term:` subscribe restarts the stream, which resends the current screen.

It serves `/internal/policy` and `/internal/mcp`, which the harness's hooks and its MCP stdio shim call with a per-execution bearer token. `Connector`, the `McpConnector` that opens one execution's MCP tools.

Which servers an agent may use (`ostra_core::mcp::serves`) and name canonicalization (ostra-core `mcp`).
Approval of workspace files (ostra-workspace `trust`).
Policy checks on each call (section harness-bridge and ostra-exec-native).

assumptions: No server starts from a workspace file that is waiting for approval, and a server starts only from the approved copy (Rule A1). A config that differs from the approved copy is refused with `trust::PENDING_MESSAGE`.

Env values and header values may name `${VAR}` from the server process environment. Provider keys, bridge tokens, and OAuth client secrets (`credential_env_names`) are refused and are also removed from the stdio process environment.
A value equal to `mcp::SAVED_SECRET` is read from the encrypted registry through `trust::mcp_secret`.
A refresh token may be single-use, so `Stored` holds a lock and refreshes one call at a time; `refused` returns the newer token when another call refreshed first.
The HTTP client follows only same-origin redirects and has a 30-second timeout.
A pending login lives in memory only, so a server restart invalidates open sign-in links.

Coordination semantics (ostra-engine).

sections.title: Project files: trees, reads, saves, diffs, and live changes
sections.purpose: `src/files/` serves the Files dock. It gives folder trees with ignore flags, git marks, and the execution that changed each file. It also serves capped text reads, the file name index, per-file diffs, a change list, and one write: saving a file from the browser's editor against the hash the edit started from. It turns writes by agents and by the user into cache invalidation and `project_fs_changed` pushes. The module also serves the workspace artifacts view under the key `_artifacts`.

owns: Path containment (`tree::contain`) for every project-relative path the browser names.
Per-project caches: file index (30 s), git status (5 s), attribution (3 s).
Live write records per project and user edit times.
Save with hash check and atomic replace (`save_file`).
Read-only rules: `.git`, Ostra runtime state, project memory, files a running execution writes.
The touch pipeline from bridge and engine notices to `ProjectFsChanged` pushes.
The folder picker cache (`BrowseCache`).
does_not_own: Code index updates beyond `Code::touch` (section code-navigation).
Git operations that change the checkout (sections git-clone-pull and git-dock).
Hidden artifact rules (section workspace-artifacts), which this module applies when the key is `_artifacts`.
Session file changes per phase (ostra-engine `view::file_changes`).

assumptions: Every path from the browser is relative. `contain` refuses absolute paths and `..` that leaves the root. It resolves the longest existing prefix with symlinks followed and requires the result inside the root, so a link cannot lead out.
The project root passed to `contain` is canonical (`project_root` canonicalizes it).
Listings use the same ignore sources as the Grep and Glob tools: `.gitignore`, git excludes, global git ignore, parent ignores, without requiring a git repo.
A file is binary when its first 8000 bytes hold a NUL, the same test git uses.
The hash on a read is set only when the text is the complete, valid UTF-8 file, so a truncated or lossy read cannot be saved over.
Git status runs with `--no-optional-locks` and `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0`, so it never contends with the engine's own `git add`.
Harness write touches carry no workspace. `absorb` searches every open workspace and picks the deepest project root that holds the path.

business_flow.outcome: The file is written atomically when the disk still matches `base_hash`, and browsers get `project_fs_changed`.

business_flow.action: Writes a file with a write tool.
business_flow.outcome: Within 150 ms the caches drop, the code index is touched, the write is attributed to the execution, and browsers get one `project_fs_changed` per project.

subsections.purpose: `Files::attribution` tells which session execution last changed each file of a project, so the tree, the file view, the diff, and the change list can show it. It merges finished work from session state with writes of executions that are still running.

Supersession by user edits: a browser save newer than an attribution removes it.
does_not_own: The per-phase changed file lists (ostra-engine `view::file_changes`).

assumptions: Only the 20 most recently updated sessions that include the project are read, so older changes can lose their attribution.

sections.title: Code navigation and editor hints
sections.purpose: `src/code.rs` answers the Files view's code questions and the agents' code tools. The browser questions are a file's display tokens and outline, symbol usages, file dependencies, symbol search, the dependency graph, completions, signature help, and supertype or implementation navigation. The agents' code tools run over the same indexes. For each project it chains providers: the project's own `code_provider` command, then its language servers, then the built-in index from ostra-code. `src/code_watch.rs` watches project folders so edits made outside Ostra reach the index.

owns: The provider chain per request, read fresh from effective settings.
Input validation: file paths, symbol names, limits, cursor lines, trigger characters, outside URIs.
One folder watch per project (`ensure_watch`) and the handling of outside changes.
`CodeTools`, the `CodeNav` the executors call for agent code tools.
does_not_own: The index, providers, language server pool, and tool answers (ostra-code `Indexes`, `LspPool`, `LspProvider`, `NativeProvider`, `CommandProvider`, `tools::run`).
The file list the index reads (section project-files `Files::index`).

assumptions: Outside URIs are read only when a language server of the project pointed at them since the server started (`LspPool::external_server`), so the browser cannot name an arbitrary file.
A language server that is starting gets 3 seconds (`HINT_WAIT`) for a hint; the index answers completions meanwhile.
Signature help comes only from language servers; the index has none.
Navigation asks the index first, which holds every language it parses, and asks language servers only when the index has no answer.
The watcher adds one non-recursive watch per folder that holds a listed file, plus the root, so ignored build output adds no watches. A refused watch is logged, and the 30-second index TTL covers it.
`CodeTools::call` maps an agent's repo root to the innermost project of an open workspace that holds it.

business_flow.outcome: Display tokens and outline come from the first provider that answers, and the project is watched from then on.

sections.title: Git clone, pull, and saved git credentials
sections.purpose: `src/git.rs` clones a remote repository into a workspace and imports it as a project, streaming git's progress to the browser. It fast-forwards a project from its upstream and stores the git credentials the user saves in the browser. Credentials live sealed in the registry. They reach git only through the process environment and one-off `-c` options, and never land in a repository's `.git/config`.

owns: Saved credentials under registry secret keys `git_credential:<id>`, with ids `gc_<uuid v7>`.
Credential validation and host normalization.
Remote URL parsing and the refusal of local and unsafe remotes.
Credential matching by longest host and path prefix.
`GitAuth`: per-process authentication (HTTPS helper, SSH key file, prompt suppression).
`run_git`: running git with a timeout, progress lines, a redacted output tail, and repair of planted git dirs.
The per-workspace git claim (`claim`, `Claim`) and `session_in`.
Clone and pull flows.
does_not_own: Project import (ostra-workspace `import_project`, `key_and_stack`, `new_folder_issues`).
Git safety options `NO_EXEC`, `submodule_filter_overrides` (ostra-core `git`).
Planted `commondir` repair (ostra-sandbox `repair_git_dirs`).
Git dock commands (section git-dock).

assumptions: Git runs with no terminal: `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, SSH `BatchMode=yes`, and on Windows `GCM_INTERACTIVE=never`, so any prompt fails instead of waiting.
SSH accepts a new host key on first contact (`StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new`).
An HTTPS credential's helper answers only for the credential's own host, so a remote rewritten by `url.*.insteadOf` never gets the token. `http.proxy` is emptied and `http.sslVerify=true` is pinned.
A token is never used for a plain `http://` remote, except loopback hosts.
An SSH private key is written 0600 to a temp dir under the data dir's `tmp`, which the sandbox hides, and removed when `GitAuth` drops.
An SSH key with a passphrase (`ENCRYPTED`) is refused, because git cannot ask for one.
Only one git operation runs per project key or overlapping folder at a time, and none starts while the workspace's `work` lock is held exclusively or the workspace is deleted.
A clone runs in its own task, so a closed tab does not stop git halfway and leave a partial checkout.

business_flow.action: Saves an HTTPS token or SSH private key for a host and optional path prefix.
business_flow.outcome: The credential is validated and stored sealed; only a view without the secret is returned.

business_flow.action: Clones a URL into the workspace, optionally with a branch, key, stack, path, and credential.
business_flow.outcome: The plan is validated, git clones with progress pushed as `git_progress`, the checkout is imported, and browsers get `workspace_updated`.

business_flow.action: Pulls a project.
business_flow.outcome: When no session works in the project, `git pull --ff-only` runs with the credential that matches the upstream URL, and the result reports before and after commits.

sections.title: Git dock: status, stage, commit, fetch, push, and branches
sections.purpose: `src/repo.rs` backs the Git dock in the console. It reports a project's branch, upstream, ahead and behind counts, and its staged, unstaged, and conflicted changes. It runs the git commands the browser asks for: stage, unstage, commit, fetch, push, and switching or creating a branch. Every command that changes the checkout is refused while a session works in the project, and runs under the project's git claim. It then announces the change so the Files dock reloads.

owns: Parsing `git status --porcelain=v2 --branch -z` into `GitRepoStatus`.
Branch listing with `for-each-ref`.
The `Op` runner and the command-specific rules.
does_not_own: Git process handling, authentication, and the claim (section git-clone-pull).
Read-only status for the Files dock (section project-files).

assumptions: Paths from the browser are contained in the project before they become pathspecs, and git runs with `--literal-pathspecs`. No paths means the whole project (`.`).
A project may be a subfolder of its repository. Entries outside the project's prefix are dropped, and `staged_elsewhere` counts staged files outside it.
Before the first commit there is no `HEAD`, so unstage uses `git rm --cached -r -q --ignore-unmatch`.
Commit hooks may run formatters and tests, so commits get 5 minutes.
A branch's remote is its configured `branch.<b>.remote`, else `origin`, else the only remote. Several remotes without an upstream is an error.

business_flow.outcome: Branch, upstream, ahead and behind counts, change lists (2,000 each at most), and a `busy` text when a session works in the project.

business_flow.action: Stages files and commits with a message.
business_flow.outcome: `git add -A` and `git commit --no-edit -m` run; the response carries the output and the new status.

business_flow.action: Pushes.
business_flow.outcome: The branch goes to its upstream, or to a same-named remote branch that becomes its upstream.

business_flow.action: Switches to or creates a branch.
business_flow.outcome: `git switch`, `switch -c`, or `switch --track` runs, and browsers get `workspace_updated`.

sections.title: Workspace artifacts, session files, and documentation books
sections.purpose: Workspace artifacts are files the user keeps for every session of a workspace. Visible ones sit in `<workspace>/.ostra/artifacts/`, which every agent reads. The user can hide a folder or a file as one unit, and a hidden unit lives in Ostra's data dir, where no agent, harness, or sandboxed command can read it (Rule W2). `src/artifacts.rs` lists, uploads, downloads, hides, shows, moves, and deletes them. The API also serves session-dir files as artifacts, and lists, reads, and deletes the workspace's documentation books.

owns: The invariant that a path is stored in the hidden folder exactly when it is within a hidden unit.
The hidden units file (`artifacts::hidden_units_file`) and its legacy fallback.
Relocation of files between the visible and hidden folders, with every target checked before anything moves.
Rule W4: deletes and moves are blocked while a session is running, waiting, stalled, or paused, or an execution runs.
The artifacts view in the Files dock under key `_artifacts` (through section project-files).
does_not_own: Artifact path normalization, listing, and folder locations (ostra-core `artifacts`).
Books on disk (ostra-core `book`).
Agent briefs that list artifacts (ostra-engine).

assumptions: The data dir can be on another file system than the workspace, so a failed rename falls back to copy and delete.
A workspace that hid files before units were recorded has each hidden file as its own unit.
Showing something inside a hidden folder is refused, because the folder hides everything in it.
A move keeps hidden things hidden, and anything that lands inside a hidden folder becomes hidden.
Book ids contain only lowercase letters, digits, dashes, and underscores (`ostra_core::book::is_book_id`).

parts.overview: ostra-store is the Rust crate that owns all of Ostra's persistent SQLite state. It opens three kinds of database files. `WorkspaceDb` is `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db`, one per workspace. It holds the append-only session event log and the tables the engine materializes from it for the console. `RegistryDb` is `registry.db` in the machine data directory. It holds the registered workspaces, Web Push subscriptions, and a key-value table whose credential rows are sealed with AES-256-GCM by `secrets::Sealer`. `MemoryStore` is `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3`, one per project. It holds the lessons agents record and recall, ranked with SQLite FTS5 full-text search. The crate depends only on ostra-core for its data types (ids, events, views, usage). ostra-engine, ostra-server, ostra-workspace, ostra-tools, and ostra-exec-native call it. It runs no background task, opens no network connection, and runs no business logic: each method is one SQL operation, or a few in a transaction, plus the conversion to and from ostra-core types.

sections.title: Store errors and column encoding
sections.purpose: Defines the single error type every store method returns and the helpers that turn ostra-core types into SQLite TEXT columns and back. Every other section in this crate uses these helpers, so all three databases store timestamps and enums in one format.

owns: The `StoreError` enum and its six variants.
The timestamp text format: RFC 3339 in UTC with millisecond precision and a `Z` suffix (`now`).
The rule that a unit-variant enum is stored as its serde string name (`enum_str`, `enum_from`).
does_not_own: The enum definitions themselves (`SessionStatus`, `ExecutionStatus`, `InitStatus`, `Lane`, `Category`, `StageKind`, `JudgeKind`, `AnswerSource`), which belong to the ostra-core project.
How callers turn a `StoreError` into an HTTP status, which belongs to the ostra-server project.

assumptions: `enum_str` assumes the value serializes to a JSON string. A struct-like or tagged enum makes it return `StoreError::Invalid("expected a string enum, got ...")`. This is why `SessionKind` and `ExecPurpose` are stored with `serde_json::to_string` instead (see the Sessions and Executions sub-sections).
`parse_time` assumes every stored timestamp was written by `now()` or by another RFC 3339 writer. Any other text fails the whole read with `StoreError::Invalid("bad timestamp ...")`.
Text comparison of timestamps (`ORDER BY created_at`, `started_at >= ?1`) is correct only because every writer uses the same fixed-width UTC format from `now()`.

tables.title: StoreError variants
rows: Any SQLite call fails: a constraint, a busy timeout, bad SQL, a corrupt file.
Creating the parent directory, setting file modes, or writing the `.gitignore` fails.
A JSON column (payload, usage, params, answer) does not parse into its ostra-core type.
An update or read-after-write finds no row with the given id.
A timestamp does not parse, an enum is not a string, an executor or agent name does not parse, or a workspace root is already registered.
A credential method runs on a `RegistryDb` that has no `Sealer`.
the registry has no encryption key, so credentials cannot be read or saved

sections.title: Opening a database and running migrations
sections.purpose: `open_connection` is the one path that opens an on-disk `WorkspaceDb` or `RegistryDb`. It creates the parent directory with owner-only permissions, sets the SQLite pragmas, applies pending schema migrations, and restricts the database and its side files to mode 0600. It runs once per process for each database, when the owning struct is constructed.

owns: The pragmas `busy_timeout` (5000 ms), `journal_mode=WAL`, and `foreign_keys=ON` on workspace and registry connections.
Schema versioning through `PRAGMA user_version`.
Unix file modes: 0700 on the parent directory, 0600 on the database file and its `-wal` and `-shm` files.
does_not_own: The file paths, which the ostra-core project computes in `paths::workspace_db`, `paths::registry_db_path`, and `paths::project_memory_db`.
The lesson memory connection, which opens its own connections without WAL or migrations (see the Project lesson memory section).

assumptions: Migrations are append-only. `migrate` skips the first `user_version` entries of the `MIGRATIONS` array, so editing or reordering an applied entry never runs again on an existing database.
`restrict` treats a missing file as success, because SQLite creates the `-wal` and `-shm` files only after the first write.
On a non-Unix target `restrict` does nothing, so the owner-only guarantee holds only on Unix.
No table declares a foreign key, so `foreign_keys=ON` has no effect on the current schema.
Each migration runs inside `unchecked_transaction`, so a failing statement rolls back that migration and its `user_version` bump together.

business_flow.action: Asks for a database at a path.
business_flow.outcome: The parent directory exists with mode 0700.

business_flow.action: Opens the SQLite file and sets the busy timeout, WAL mode, and foreign keys.
business_flow.outcome: Writers from other connections wait up to 5 seconds for the file lock instead of failing at once.

business_flow.action: Reads `user_version` and runs each later migration in its own transaction.
business_flow.outcome: The schema is at the latest version and `user_version` equals the number of migrations.

business_flow.action: Sets mode 0600 on the database, `-wal`, and `-shm` files.
business_flow.outcome: Other users on the machine cannot read tool output or credentials.

diagrams.title: Migration loop
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  start[Read PRAGMA user_version] --> loop{"Migration index i >= user_version?"}
  loop -- yes --> tx[Begin unchecked transaction]
  tx --> run[execute_batch migration SQL]
  run --> bump["Set user_version = i + 1"]
  bump --> commit[Commit]
  commit --> next{More migrations?}
  loop -- no --> next
  next -- yes --> loop
  next -- no --> done[Schema current]
  run -- error --> fail[Roll back and return StoreError::Sqlite]

sections.title: Workspace database
sections.purpose: `WorkspaceDb` is the storage handle for one workspace's `.ostra/workspace.db`. The ostra-engine project writes the session event log through it as the source of truth, and writes the materialized tables beside it so the console can list sessions, executions, gates, and costs without replaying events. One `WorkspaceDb` is shared by every task in the process through a cloned `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`.

owns: The ten tables of migration 1, the two columns of migration 2, and the search tables of migration 3.
The `.gitignore` written beside the database on first open.

HTTP routes that read these tables, which belong to the ostra-server project.

assumptions: The process holds one `WorkspaceDb` per file. All calls through clones share one connection behind a `Mutex`, so calls in the process run one at a time.
`lock` recovers a poisoned mutex with `into_inner`, which assumes a panic in another caller left the connection usable.
`WorkspaceDb::open` writes `.gitignore` only when none exists, so a user-edited `.gitignore` is never overwritten.
`workspace_id_of` returns an empty `WorkspaceId` when `meta.workspace_id` was never set, and session reads still succeed with that empty id.

sections.title: Machine registry
sections.purpose: `RegistryDb` is the storage handle for `registry.db` in the Ostra data directory (`OSTRA_DATA_DIR`, or the platform local data directory joined with `ostra`). It holds the list of workspaces on this machine, the Web Push subscriptions, and a key-value table used for credentials, auth tokens, cookies, trust records, and the onboarding time. The ostra-server project opens one at startup and unlocks it with the master key.

owns: The `workspaces`, `push_subscriptions`, and `kv` tables.
`PRAGMA secure_delete=ON`, so freed pages are zeroed and a replaced plaintext credential does not stay in the file.
The uniqueness of a workspace root path.
does_not_own: The master key and where it lives (keychain, file, or `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE`), which belongs to the ostra-server project (`master_key.rs`).

The meaning of most kv keys, which belongs to the project that writes them (ostra-server for `auth:cookie:`, `provider_credentials:`, `mcp_oauth:`, `vapid_private`; ostra-workspace for `workspace_access:` and `trust:migrated:`).

assumptions: The registry has one migration. `open_in_memory` runs it directly with `execute_batch` and does not set `user_version`, which is safe only because the in-memory database is never reopened.
`open_in_memory` attaches an ephemeral `Sealer`; `open` attaches none, so on-disk credentials stay unreadable until `with_sealer` runs.
Workspace root paths are compared as text from `to_string_lossy`, so two spellings of one directory are two different roots. Callers in ostra-workspace canonicalize paths before they build kv keys.

sections.title: Credential encryption at rest
sections.purpose: Seals every registry value whose key is listed in `SECRET_KEYS` with AES-256-GCM under the machine's 32-byte master key. The row's key is the associated data, so a sealed value copied to another row does not decrypt. At startup the ostra-server project attaches the `Sealer` and calls `seal_plaintext_secrets` to encrypt rows left as plaintext by older versions.

owns: The sealed value format `enc:v1:` followed by base64 of a 12-byte nonce and the ciphertext with its tag.
The list of secret keys in `SECRET_KEYS`.
The one-time rewrite (VACUUM and WAL truncate) that removes plaintext from disk after sealing.
does_not_own: Loading or generating the master key and checking it against `secrets:check`, which belongs to the ostra-server project (`master_key.rs`, which calls `generate_key`).

assumptions: `Sealer::open` returns a value without the `enc:v1:` prefix unchanged, because a registry written before encryption holds plaintext until it is migrated.
`secret_get`, `secret_set`, and `secret_scan` check with `debug_assert!` that the key is a secret key; release builds do not check.
A value that fails to decrypt is treated as absent and logged with `tracing::warn!`, so the user enters the credential again instead of the server failing to start.
`seal` uses `rand::fill` for a fresh nonce on every call, so sealing one value twice gives two different outputs.

business_flow.action: Opens the registry, loads the master key, and attaches a Sealer.
business_flow.outcome: Credential methods stop returning `StoreError::Locked`.

business_flow.action: Seals each secret row that is still plaintext with a compare-and-set.
business_flow.outcome: Every credential on disk is encrypted; a row changed by another caller meanwhile is left alone.

business_flow.action: Runs VACUUM and a WAL truncate checkpoint when it sealed a row or `secrets_vacuumed` is missing, then sets `secrets_vacuumed`.
business_flow.outcome: Old plaintext pages are gone from the database file and the WAL.

business_flow.action: Reads or saves a credential through secret_get or secret_set.
business_flow.outcome: The value is decrypted or sealed with the row's key as associated data.

diagrams.title: Plaintext migration at startup
diagrams.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Server as "ostra-server master_key::unlock"
  participant RegistryDb
  participant Sealer
  participant SQLite
  Server->>RegistryDb: with_sealer(sealer)
  Server->>RegistryDb: seal_plaintext_secrets()
  RegistryDb->>SQLite: kv_scan("")
  loop each secret key without enc:v1:
    RegistryDb->>Sealer: seal(key, value)
    RegistryDb->>SQLite: "kv_replace(key, old, sealed)"
  end
  alt sealed > 0 or no secrets_vacuumed
    RegistryDb->>SQLite: VACUUM
    RegistryDb->>SQLite: "PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)"
    RegistryDb->>SQLite: kv_set(secrets_vacuumed, 1)
  end
  RegistryDb-->>Server: count sealed

diagrams.title: Opening a sealed value
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  s["open(row, stored)"] --> p{"Starts with enc:v1:?"}
  p -- no --> plain[Return stored bytes as plaintext]
  p -- yes --> b[Base64 decode]
  b -- fails --> u[OpenError::Undecryptable]
  b --> len{"Length >= 12?"}
  len -- no --> u
  len -- yes --> d["AES-256-GCM decrypt, aad = row key"]
  d -- fails --> u
  d -- ok --> v[Plaintext]

sections.title: Project lesson memory
sections.purpose: `MemoryStore` stores durable lessons for one project in `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3`. Agents record a lesson with an area and recall lessons by area and text. The console's memory browser lists, edits, and deletes them. The schema follows Ultracode's `mcp/lib/memory.js`: one row per unique (area, lesson) pair, FTS5 ranking, and area sub-scopes written `area::sub`.

owns: The `lessons` table, the `lessons_fts` FTS5 index, and its three sync triggers.
Deduplication on (area, lesson): a repeat updates `source` and `created_at`.
The recall bucket order and the default recall limit of 8.
does_not_own: The `memory` tools that agents call, which belong to the ostra-tools project (`misc.rs`).
Injecting recalled lessons into prompts, which belongs to the ostra-exec-native project and the ostra-server project (`bridge.rs`).
The memory browser HTTP routes, which belong to the ostra-server project (`api.rs`).

assumptions: Lessons are never capped and never expire; only `forget`, `delete`, and `update` remove or change them.
Each call opens a fresh connection with a 5000 ms busy timeout and runs the `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` schema, so parallel executions wait on SQLite's file lock instead of sharing a handle.
This database does not use WAL mode, migrations, or file mode restriction, unlike the workspace and registry databases.
`recall`, `forget`, `list`, and `delete` return empty or false when the file does not exist, without creating it. `record` and `update` create it.
`fts_query_from_text` splits on every non-alphanumeric character and joins quoted tokens with OR, so any single matching word is a hit.
`update` does not check that the id exists before updating; it returns `StoreError::NotFound("lesson {id}")` when the read afterwards finds no row.

subsections.title: Lesson recall ranking
subsections.purpose: `recall` returns up to `limit` lessons for an agent, most relevant first, by filling buckets in order and skipping (area, lesson) pairs already taken. It runs when an agent calls the memory recall tool and when an executor preloads lessons for a prompt.

owns: The bucket order and the deduplication across buckets.
does_not_own: The limit the caller passes, which the ostra-tools and ostra-exec-native projects choose.

assumptions: An area matches itself and every sub-area that starts with `area::` (`l.area LIKE 'area::%'`).
An area of only whitespace counts as no area.
A query that produces no tokens counts as no query.

diagrams.title: Recall buckets
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  start["recall(area, query, limit)"] --> both{Area and query?}
  both -- yes --> b1["Bucket 1: area lessons matching query, by bm25"]
  both -- no --> onlyA{Area only?}
  onlyA -- yes --> b1b["Bucket 1: area lessons, newest first"]
  onlyA -- no --> q
  b1 --> q{Query given?}
  b1b --> q

parts.overview: ostra-tools is the Rust crate that runs the native tools Ostra's agents call: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, PowerShell, Cmd, Grep, Glob, Skill, WebFetch, Report, Document, Memory, MemoryRecall, DocsSearch, the code navigation tools, the project management tools, the subagent coordination tools, and the tools of external MCP servers. Tool names and input shapes follow Claude Code's tools, because the agent prompts are tuned to them. The crate checks no permission and no guard: the executor asks ostra-policy about each call first, then calls `execute`, which routes the call to one tool module and returns a `ToolOutput`. Per execution, a `ToolEnv` holds the shell's working directory, the set of files read so far, an HTTP client, the list of environment variables to remove from child processes, and an optional sandbox. The crate also builds the JSON tool definitions that the executor offers to the model, from the agent's capabilities. The native executor (ostra-exec-native) and the harness bridge in ostra-server are the two callers. ostra-server provides the code index, the management engine, the coordination engine, and the MCP connections through the `CodeNav`, `Manage`, `Coordinate`, and `McpTools` traits this crate defines.

sections.title: Tool call dispatch
sections.purpose: `execute` is the crate's single entry point for running a tool call. The executor calls it once per model tool call, after the policy has allowed the call. It coerces the arguments against the tool's schema, routes the call by tool name to one module, applies cancellation, and records the call's duration. `ToolEnv::canonical_call` produces the exact call form that the policy checks and `execute` runs, so both see the same target.

owns: The mapping from a tool name to the module function that runs it.
The cancellation wrapper around every non-shell tool, which returns `Cancelled.` when the token fires.
The `duration_ms` field of every `ToolOutput`.
The canonical form of a call: absolute paths, the Bash `cwd` field, and the parsed WebFetch URL.
does_not_own: Permission checks, guards, and user approval: ostra-policy decides and the executor (ostra-exec-native, or the bridge in ostra-server) asks the user.

Each tool's own behavior: the sections `file-tools`, `bash-tool`, `search-tools`, `web-fetch`, `skill-tool`, `report-tool`, `document-tool`, `memory-tools`, `docs-search-tool`, and `delegated-tools` own it.
The tool definitions offered to the model: section `tool-definitions` owns them.

assumptions: The caller has already run the policy on the result of `canonical_call` and got Allow, or the user approved an Ask; the module doc comment in `src/lib.rs` states that nothing in the crate checks permissions.
`call.input` is a JSON object; `canonical_call` returns the call unchanged when it is not, and each tool then reports its missing required parameter.
The shell tools (Bash, PowerShell, Cmd) honor the cancellation token themselves; `execute` does not wrap them in its cancel `select!`, so their output capture and process-tree kill still run.
The name predicates `is_code_tool`, `is_manage_tool`, `is_coord_tool`, and `is_gateway_tool` from ostra-core do not match any of the fixed names matched before them.

business_flow.action: Turns the model's tool call into its canonical form with `canonical_call`.
business_flow.outcome: Relative paths are absolute against the shell's working directory and the WebFetch URL is in parsed form.

business_flow.action: Checks the canonical call against the policy and asks the user when the policy says Ask.
business_flow.outcome: The call is allowed, or the executor returns an error to the model without calling `execute`.

business_flow.action: Coerces string arguments that hold JSON object or array text into JSON values, using the tool's schema for this agent.
business_flow.outcome: A model that sent an object as JSON text gets the same result as one that sent the object.

business_flow.action: Routes the call by name to the module that runs it.
business_flow.outcome: The tool runs, or an unknown name returns an error output.

business_flow.action: Races a non-shell tool against the cancellation token and stamps the elapsed time.
business_flow.outcome: The executor receives a `ToolOutput` with text, error flag, exit code, duration, optional diff, and run-end signal.

subsections.purpose: `ToolEnv::canonical_call` rewrites a tool call into the form the tool will run. The policy checks this form and `execute` runs it, so a relative path, a Bash working directory, or a URL with confusing characters names the same target in the check, in the approval card, and in the run.

subsections.title: Routing and cancellation
subsections.purpose: `execute` matches the tool name to a module function, then runs it. Every tool other than the three shells runs inside a `tokio::select!` against the cancellation token, so a cancelled execution stops waiting for it at once. The shells run without that wrapper because they must still kill their process tree and return the output captured so far.

does_not_own: The shells' own cancellation handling: sections `bash-tool` and `windows-shells` own it.

PowerShell and Cmd exist only in builds for Windows (`#[cfg(windows)]`); on other systems their names fall through to `Unknown tool`.

subsections.title: Argument coercion and parsing helpers
subsections.purpose: Some models send an object or array argument as a string of JSON text. Before routing, `execute` looks up the tool's input schema for the current agent with `defs::input_schema` and calls `ostra_core::args::coerce_json_strings`, which parses each top-level string argument whose schema type is not a string and whose text starts with `{` or `[`. The helpers `str_arg`, `required`, `u64_arg`, and `bool_arg` then read typed values out of the input.

owns: The typed argument readers shared by every tool module.
does_not_own: The coercion rules themselves: ostra-core `args::coerce_json_strings` owns them.

assumptions: `defs::input_schema` finds the tool in the full capability list `EVERY`; for `Document` it uses the agent's own document schema, so the coercion sees the right field types.
A number argument may arrive as a float; `u64_arg` accepts it, clamps negatives to 0, and truncates the fraction.

sections.purpose: `ToolEnv` holds the state one execution's tools share: the configuration from `ToolEnvConfig`, the shell's persistent working directory, the set of files the model has read, a WebFetch HTTP client, the host names allowed to resolve to private addresses, the environment variables to remove from child processes, and an optional sandbox backend with its profile. The executor builds one `ToolEnv` when an execution starts and passes it to every `execute` call of that execution.

The read set used by Write and Edit.

The values in `ToolEnvConfig`: the executor fills them from the execution context in ostra-core.

sections.title: Bash tool
sections.purpose: Bash runs one command in a bash process and returns its combined stdout and stderr. The working directory persists across calls, the command's environment has credential and Ostra variables removed, git is configured so repository config cannot run hooks, the process tree is killed when the call ends, and the output is bounded in memory and in the returned text. When the environment has a sandbox, the command runs inside the ostra-sandbox backend with the execution's profile.

owns: The launch script, the working directory file, and the persisted working directory.
The removal of secret and `OSTRA_*` variables from the child.
Timeout, cancellation, and process-tree termination.
Output capture limits and live output streaming.
does_not_own: Whether a command may run: ostra-policy parses the command and decides.
The sandbox's file, network, and process isolation: ostra-sandbox builds the command.
Process group and job object handling: ostra-core `proctree` owns it.
Locating the bash executable: ostra-core `shells::bash` owns it.
Repairing git directories after a command: ostra-exec-native calls `ostra_sandbox::repair_git_dirs`.

assumptions: A bash executable is available: on Unix the system bash, on Windows Git Bash through `ostra_core::shells::bash`; the call fails with its error message otherwise.
`std::env::temp_dir()` is writable on the host, because the working directory file is created there.
The command reads no input; stdin is `/dev/null`.
The model does not rely on background processes: any process still holding the output pipe 300 ms after the command exits is killed.

business_flow.outcome: The tool clamps the timeout to 1 through 600000 ms, default 120000 ms.

business_flow.action: Starts bash with the launch script, in the tracked working directory, with scrubbed variables.
business_flow.outcome: The command runs through `eval` in that directory.

business_flow.action: Streams output chunks to the console and into a bounded capture until the command exits, times out, or is cancelled.
business_flow.outcome: The user sees live output and the capture keeps the first and last 128 KiB.

business_flow.action: Kills the process tree when needed, drains remaining output, and reads the final directory.
business_flow.outcome: The next call starts in the directory the command ended in.

business_flow.outcome: Exit 0 is a success; any other end is an error output.

subsections.title: Launch script and working directory
subsections.purpose: The tool runs `bash -c SCRIPT` and passes the command, the working directory, and a working directory file path through the variables `OSTRA_CMD`, `OSTRA_CWD`, and `OSTRA_PWD_FILE`. The script redirects stderr to stdout, copies and unsets the three variables, changes to the directory, installs an EXIT trap that writes the final directory to the file, and runs the command with `eval` in the same shell. Because the command runs in the same shell, a `cd` in it is still in effect when the trap runs, including after `exit`.

owns: The SCRIPT text on Unix and on Windows, and the `ostra-pwd-<uuid>` file lifecycle.
does_not_own: The meaning of a directory the sandbox prints: `ToolEnv::sandbox_to_host` maps it.

assumptions: Passing the command through an environment variable keeps its quoting intact; the test `quoting_survives` checks quotes, spaces, and `$'...'` strings.
On Windows, Git Bash's `pwd -P` prints an MSYS path such as `/c/Users/me`, so the Windows script runs `cd -P . && pwd -W` to print the Windows path the other tools resolve against.
The tracked directory is used only when it is still a directory; otherwise the tool resets it to `repo_root` before running.
A directory read back from the file is applied only when it exists on the host.

subsections.title: Environment scrubbing
subsections.purpose: Before spawning, the tool removes from the child's environment every name in the scrub list and every inherited variable whose name starts with `OSTRA_`, and it removes `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF`. The scrub list starts with the credential variable names that `config.toml` configures plus the defaults and bridge variables, and the executor adds the workspace's MCP secret names. A command therefore cannot read a provider API key or Ostra's own settings from its environment.

owns: The `scrubbed_vars` rule and the `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF` removal.
does_not_own: The list of credential variable names: ostra-core `config::credential_env_names` owns it.
The MCP secret names: ostra-exec-native `mcp_secret_vars` supplies them.

assumptions: Every Ostra-internal variable starts with `OSTRA_`; any other name must be in the scrub list to be removed.

The global config file at `ostra_core::paths::global_config_path()` parses as `GlobalConfig`; a parse failure uses the default config, which still lists the default provider key names such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.

subsections.title: Sandboxed launch
subsections.purpose: When `ToolEnv` holds a sandbox, the tool creates the empty working directory file first, adds it to the profile as a writable file, and asks the profile for the command that runs `bash` in the tracked directory under the backend. The returned command's `members` value is held until the call ends, so the processes it tracks are stopped at the end of the call, as bubblewrap's pid namespace does.

owns: Preparing the directory file for the sandbox and holding the members handle for the call's duration.
does_not_own: The profile's rules for home, credentials, `/tmp`, network, and processes: ostra-sandbox owns them.

assumptions: The EXIT trap inside the sandbox can write the file only when it exists and the profile marks it writable, even when `/tmp` is private or denied.
Under bubblewrap, `/tmp` inside the sandbox is the execution's scratch directory; `sandbox_to_host` maps the recorded directory back so the next call and the in-process tools use the host path.
The sandbox tests skip themselves when `ostra_sandbox::backend()` returns `None`.

Prepares the file, holds `members`, and cleans up on setup failure.

subsections.title: Output capture and live streaming
subsections.purpose: Two reader tasks copy stdout and stderr into one unbounded channel in 8192-byte reads. Each chunk goes into a `Capture`, which keeps the first 128 KiB and a rolling last 128 KiB and counts the bytes dropped between them. When a `LiveOutput` callback is present, a `Utf8Stream` turns the chunks into valid UTF-8 text, holding back an incomplete trailing sequence, and the callback receives it with the call ID. The final text is the head, a `[<n> bytes dropped]` note when bytes were dropped, and the tail, cut in the middle to 30000 bytes.

owns: The capture bounds, the UTF-8 chunking, and the final truncation.
does_not_own: What the console does with live chunks: the executor emits them as `ExecutionDelta::ToolOutput`.

assumptions: stdout and stderr are interleaved in arrival order; the script already sends stderr to stdout, so the stderr pipe carries only output written before the redirect.
An invalid UTF-8 sequence in the middle of the pending bytes is replaced with the replacement character instead of being held back.

concerns.responsibility: Bounds memory and produces the final text.
Splits the byte stream into valid UTF-8 text.
Copies one pipe into the channel.

code_refs.note: Test of live output and truncation of 20000 lines.

subsections.title: Timeout, cancellation, and process-tree termination
subsections.purpose: The tool waits for the first of four events: an output chunk, the command's exit, the deadline, or the cancellation token. On a timeout, cancellation, or wait failure it kills the whole process tree and waits up to 5 seconds for the command to be reaped. It then drains the channel, waiting 300 ms for each chunk; if the wait runs out while a pipe is still open, a background process holds it, and the tool kills the tree again. Finally it calls `tree.end()`, which on Windows closes the job object and kills what remains.

owns: The event loop, the kill decisions, and the drain loop.
does_not_own: How a tree is killed: ostra-core `proctree::Tree::kill` sends SIGKILL to the process group on Unix and terminates the job on Windows.

assumptions: `ostra_core::proctree::prepare_tokio` puts the child in its own process group or job before spawn, so `Tree::kill` reaches every process the command started.
On Windows, a process killed partway through its own creation may never exit, so the reap wait is bounded by `KILL_WAIT`.

diagrams.title: Ending a Bash call
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  w[Wait for chunk, exit, deadline, or cancel] --> ex{Exited?}
  ex -->|no| k1["tree.kill, wait up to 5 s"]
  ex -->|yes| d[Drain channel]
  k1 --> d
  d --> g{"Chunk within 300 ms?"}
  g -->|yes| d
  g -->|channel closed| en[tree.end]
  g -->|"no, pipe still open"| k2[tree.kill]
  k2 --> en
  en --> r[Read pwd file and build output]

concerns.responsibility: Names the four ways a wait ends: Exited, TimedOut, Cancelled, WaitFailed.
Kills and releases the command's process tree (ostra-core).

code_refs.note: Test that a background child does not outlive a timeout.

sections.title: PowerShell and Cmd tools (Windows)
sections.purpose: On Windows the Shell capability also offers PowerShell and Cmd. Both run one command with the Bash tool's timeout, output capture, live streaming, variable scrubbing, and process-tree kill, and both persist the working directory through a file. Ostra's command parser reads bash only, so the policy treats these commands as opaque: never auto-allowed, and refused when the raw text names Ostra's own files or a credential path.

owns: The PowerShell script and cmd command line, the pwd file handling, and the result mapping for these two shells.
does_not_own: The approval and refusal of opaque shell commands: ostra-policy owns it.
The PowerShell and cmd executable paths: ostra-core `shells::powershell` and `shells::cmd` own them.
The shared capture, reader, and scrub helpers: section `bash-tool` owns them.

assumptions: The module compiles only on Windows (`#[cfg(windows)]` in `src/lib.rs`).
These shells never run under a sandbox; `winshell::run` does not read `env.sandbox`.
A single quote in the working directory or pwd file path is doubled for the PowerShell single-quoted literal by `ps_single_quote`.
cmd receives its command line unescaped through `raw_arg`, because std would quote an inner `"` as `\"`, which cmd does not understand.
The pwd file may start with a UTF-8 byte order mark; it is removed before the directory is applied.

business_flow.action: Removes scrubbed variables, adds git agent config, and starts the shell in the tracked directory.

business_flow.action: Waits for exit, timeout, or cancellation, kills the tree when needed, and drains output.
business_flow.outcome: The captured output and exit code are returned and the directory is persisted.

sections.title: Search tools: Grep and Glob
sections.purpose: Grep searches file contents with a Rust regular expression using the ripgrep libraries, and Glob lists files whose relative path matches a glob pattern. Both walk the tree with gitignore rules, include hidden files, skip `.git` directories, and never enter credential stores or Ostra's data directory. Both run on a blocking thread through `spawn_blocking`.

owns: The directory walker settings and the secret filter.
Grep's three output modes and Glob's 100-result cap.
File type aliases and glob list splitting.
does_not_own: The list of credential paths: ostra-core `paths::secret_paths` and `HOME_CREDENTIALS` own it.
Regex and glob syntax: the grep-regex and globset crates own them.

assumptions: `path` defaults to the shell's working directory, not the project root.
Output paths are absolute host paths shown with forward slashes on every system through `disp`.

concerns.responsibility: Content search.
Name search.
Shared filtered walk.

subsections.title: Directory walker and secret filter
subsections.purpose: `walker` builds an `ignore::WalkBuilder` that reads `.gitignore`, `.git/info/exclude`, the global gitignore, and parent directory ignore files, and works without a git repository. It includes hidden files so `.ostra/` is searched, and filters out every `.git` entry and every path `SecretFilter` hides. It adds glob overrides and file type selection for Grep.

owns: Walker settings, the secret filter rule, glob splitting, and type aliases.
does_not_own: Which files are credentials: ostra-core owns the list.

assumptions: `SecretFilter` compares both the raw and the canonical form of each secret path, so a symlinked home still matches.

The data directory's `assets` folder stays searchable: a path is not hidden when it is inside `assets` or is an ancestor of `assets`, so the walk can descend through the data directory to reach it while `registry.db` stays hidden.
A glob string with whitespace or commas outside braces is several globs; `*.{ts,tsx}` stays one.

subsections.title: Grep tool
subsections.purpose: Grep builds a regex matcher and a searcher that quits a file at the first NUL byte, then searches one file when `path` is a file or every walked file otherwise. `files_with_matches` (the default) lists matching files newest first. `count` lists `path:n` per file with a total. `content` lists matching lines as `path:n:text` and context lines as `path-n-text`, separated by `--` where lines are not contiguous or between files when context is on.

owns: Matcher and searcher settings, the three output formats, and the limits.
does_not_own: Walker and secret filtering: sub-section `search-walker` owns them.

assumptions: Without `multiline`, the matcher uses `\n` as a line terminator so a match stays on one line; with it, `.` matches newlines and the searcher runs in multi-line mode.
`-A` and `-B` fall back to `-C`, and context applies only in content mode.
`-n` defaults to true.
A `head_limit` of 0 is ignored.
In content mode, files are visited in walk order, not modification time order.
In count mode, the reported totals count every matching file even when `head_limit` cut the rows.

subsections.title: Glob tool
subsections.purpose: Glob compiles the pattern with `literal_separator(true)`, so `*` does not cross a `/` and `**` does. It walks from `path` and keeps files whose path relative to that root matches, trying both the native form and the forward-slash form so `**/*.rs` matches on Windows. Results are sorted newest first and capped at 100 with a note.

Directories are never returned, only files.

sections.title: WebFetch tool
sections.purpose: WebFetch downloads one http or https URL and returns its content as text, with HTML converted to markdown. It refuses private, loopback, link-local, and other non-public addresses unless a `WebFetch(domain:<host>)` allow rule names the host, and it follows redirects only within the same host and port. The model receives a cross-host redirect as a new URL to fetch, so the policy checks that URL too.

owns: The HTTP client configuration, the public-address resolver, and the redirect rule.
Body size and text size limits and the content conversion.
Extraction of hosts from WebFetch allow rules.
does_not_own: Whether a URL may be fetched at all: ostra-policy checks the canonical URL first.
The private address ranges: ostra-sandbox `egress::is_private` owns them.
Provider-side web fetch: when the provider offers it, ostra-exec-native removes this tool from the list.

assumptions: No HTTP proxy is used (`no_proxy`), because a proxy resolves names itself and would skip the resolver's address check.
Every name is resolved by `PublicResolver` at connect time, so a DNS answer that changes between the policy check and the connect is still checked.
An IP literal host is not seen by the resolver, so `private_literal` checks it before the request.
The private host list is lowercase and compares exact host names; an IPv6 literal matches with or without brackets.

business_flow.action: Calls WebFetch with a URL and an optional prompt.
business_flow.outcome: The tool parses the URL and checks the scheme and literal address.

business_flow.action: Sends a GET request through the client with the public-address resolver.
business_flow.outcome: A private resolution is refused with advice to add an allow rule.

business_flow.action: Stops at a redirect to another host and returns the new URL.
business_flow.outcome: The model makes a new WebFetch call, which the policy checks.

business_flow.action: Reads up to 5 MiB, converts to text, and truncates to 100000 bytes.
business_flow.outcome: The model receives the content with the final URL and HTTP status.

flowchart TD
  p[Parse trimmed url] -->|fails| e1["Error: Invalid URL, or not http or https"]

  s -->|no| e1
  s -->|yes| l{private IP literal not allowed?}
  l -->|yes| e3[Error: add WebFetch domain rule]
  l -->|no| r[GET through client]
  r -->|resolver refusal| e3
  r -->|other error| e4[Error: Fetching failed]
  r --> x{"3xx with Location?"}
  x -->|yes| o1[Return: fetch the new URL]
  x -->|no| b[Read body up to 5 MiB]
  b --> t[to_text]
  t -->|not text| e5[Error: not text]
  t --> st{"2xx status?"}
  st -->|yes| ok[Return content]
  st -->|no| e6[Error with content and status]

subsections.title: Private address checks
subsections.purpose: Two checks keep WebFetch off the local machine and network. `private_literal` refuses a URL whose host is a private IPv4 or IPv6 literal. `PublicResolver` resolves every other host with `tokio::net::lookup_host` and keeps only public addresses, unless the host is in the private host list. When no address is left, it fails with `<host> resolves only to private or loopback addresses`, and `is_resolver_refusal` finds that text in the error chain to return the allow-rule advice.

owns: Both checks and the refusal message.
does_not_own: The ranges `is_private` covers: ostra-sandbox owns them (loopback, private, link-local including the cloud metadata address, CGNAT, unique-local, multicast, reserved, IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, and NAT64 forms).

assumptions: The refusal is detected by the substring `resolves only to private` in the error chain; changing the resolver's message breaks the detection.
`webfetch_hosts` accepts only rules of the exact form `WebFetch(domain:<host>)` after trimming; other rule forms grant no private access.

tables.title: Refusal text
rows: Add the allow rule `WebFetch(domain:<host>)` to fetch <url>, because it points at a private or loopback address, which WebFetch refuses by default.

concerns.responsibility: Checks IP literal hosts.
Filters resolved addresses at connect time.
Extracts allowed hosts from allow rules.

code_refs.note: Test of loopback, IPv6, metadata, mapped, and localhost refusals.

subsections.title: Redirect handling
subsections.purpose: The client's custom redirect policy follows a redirect only when the new URL has the same host and port as the previous one and an http or https scheme. It fails after more than 10 redirects. Any other redirect stops, so the tool receives the 3xx response and returns `Fetch <next> with a new WebFetch call to follow it, because <url> redirected (HTTP <code>) to another host and a redirect to another host is not followed.` as a success output.

owns: The same-host rule and the redirect message.
does_not_own: The check of the new URL: ostra-policy checks it when the model calls WebFetch again.

assumptions: The policy checked only the first URL, so following a redirect to another host would fetch a URL no rule approved.
A relative `Location` is joined to the response URL.

concerns.responsibility: Builds the client with the redirect policy, resolver, no proxy, timeout, and user agent.

subsections.title: Content conversion
subsections.purpose: `read_capped` reads the body in chunks and stops at 5 MiB. `to_text` converts HTML to markdown with `htmd` when the content type contains `html`, or when it is empty and the first 512 characters contain `<html` or `<!doctype html`. Other textual types are returned as they are. A type that is not textual, or a body with a NUL byte in its first 8192 bytes, is refused. The output starts with `Prompt: <prompt>` when a prompt was given, then `Redirected to: <url>` when the final URL differs, then `Content of <url> (HTTP <code>):` and the text.

owns: The textual type list and the output layout.
does_not_own: HTML conversion rules: the htmd crate owns them.

assumptions: The body is decoded as UTF-8 with replacement characters, whatever charset the response declares.
A non-2xx response still returns its content, as an error output.

rows: Contains html, or empty with an HTML start
Contains json, xml, javascript, yaml, or markdown
Anything else, or a NUL byte in the first 8192 bytes
Error: The response is `<type>`, which is not text, so it cannot be shown.

concerns.responsibility: Bounds the body size.
Chooses conversion or refusal.

sections.title: Skill tool
sections.purpose: Skill loads a SKILL.md file of task instructions and returns its content with the line `Skill loaded from <path>. Follow its instructions for this task.`. The model passes either `path`, the exact location of a SKILL.md, or `name`, which the tool looks up in the project, then in the workspace's artifacts, then among the skills Ostra ships.

does_not_own: The project skill folders: ostra-core `paths::project_skill_dirs` and `find_project_skill` own them.
Workspace artifact skills: ostra-core `artifacts::skill_path` owns the location and the symlink check.
Embedded skills: the `SkillResolver` that ostra-server `app::skill_resolver` provides serves them from the assets project.

A name containing `/` or `..` is refused, so a name cannot leave the skill folders; a location must be passed as `path`.
Project and artifact skills are marked read, so the model can edit them; embedded skills are not, because they have no file in the project.
Artifact skills are looked up only when `workspace_root` is not empty.

sections.title: Document tool
sections.purpose: Document writes the typed JSON document of the explore, generate-spec, or plan agent: a research document, a spec, or a plan. ostra-core validates it against the kind's schema, stores the JSON, and renders the markdown the next stage reads; a plan also gets one `-phase-{N}.md` file per phase. The tool accepts a whole document, or an update that replaces top-level fields and merges id-keyed list items, with an optional list of ids to remove. It returns a summary of the counts and every issue ostra-core's checks found.

owns: The agent, file name, and folder checks, the choice between whole write and update, and the result summary.

sections.title: How ostra-tools works with the other projects
sections.purpose: ostra-tools sits between the executors, which talk to models, and the services and libraries that hold Ostra's state. Two callers run its tools: the native executor in ostra-exec-native, which runs Ostra's own model loop, and the harness bridge in ostra-server, which serves Ostra's tools over MCP to external agent CLIs. It depends on ostra-core for shared types and rules, on ostra-sandbox for the Bash sandbox and the private address check, and on ostra-store for lessons. ostra-server supplies the code index, management, coordination, MCP connections, and embedded skills through the traits and callbacks this crate defines.

parts.overview: ostra-workspace is the library crate that owns one Ostra workspace. A workspace is a folder that holds `.ostra/workspace.toml` and `.ostra/workspace.db`. It groups one or more project folders that Ostra's agents work on. The crate creates and validates workspaces in one call (`create`). It opens a registered workspace as a `WorkspaceRt`, which holds the settings, the workspace database, the engine and the project list (`runtime`). It validates settings and resolves each agent's routes (`settings`). It imports and checks projects (`projects`). It stores the console layout (`ui_state`). It also decides which programs a folder file may start, through hash-based approvals, registry-held access settings and sealed MCP secrets (`trust`). It has no HTTP code. ostra-server implements the `WorkspaceHost` trait, calls these functions from its `/api/workspaces` routes, and maps the crate's error enums to HTTP statuses. The React console (web) reaches this crate only through those routes. The crate depends on ostra-core for types, paths and base validation, on ostra-store for `RegistryDb` and `WorkspaceDb`, on ostra-engine for `Engine`, on ostra-agents for agent definitions, on ostra-policy for permission-rule checks, and on ostra-sandbox for sandbox validation and status.

sections.title: Workspace host trait
sections.purpose: `WorkspaceHost` is the trait through which a workspace asks its process for the facts it cannot own. These facts are the registry database, the global config, machine facts, provider and harness status, and the engine's services. ostra-server implements it on its `Shared` struct. Every other section of this crate reads outside state only through this trait, so the crate compiles and tests without a server.

owns: The list of methods a process must provide to open a workspace: `registry`, `global`, `environment`, `providers`, `harnesses`, `services`.
does_not_own: The implementation, which ostra-server owns (`impl WorkspaceHost for Shared` in ostra-server's `src/app.rs`).
The registry database schema, which ostra-store owns.
The `Services` trait the engine calls, which ostra-engine owns.

assumptions: `global()` re-reads the global config on every call, so edits apply without a restart. `WorkspaceRt::detail` and `create::draft_for` call it once per request and rely on a fresh value.
`registry()` is the only source of approvals, the permission mode, YOLO and sealed secrets. The trust section never reads them from a folder file.
The implementor is `Send + Sync` and lives in an `Arc`, because `services` takes `self: Arc<Self>` and `WorkspaceRt` stores `Arc<dyn WorkspaceHost>`.
ostra-server builds `environment()` from its detected harnesses and from the providers whose status has `has_key` set.

sections.purpose: Turns one `CreateWorkspace` request from the console's new-workspace dialog into complete `WorkspaceSettings`. It validates them as a whole and writes the folder, `workspace.toml` and the registry entry only when there are no issues. `POST /api/workspaces/validate` runs the same checks without writing. When the chosen folder already holds a `workspace.toml`, the request's choices apply on top of that file. This lets a user register a folder again after its registry entry was lost.

Opening the new workspace, which ostra-server `setup::create` does by calling `App::attach` and then `RegistryDb::mark_onboarded`.

assumptions: `body.root` must be absolute. A relative or empty root produces an issue and no file-system read.
`paths::canonical` fails for a folder that does not exist yet. `draft` then falls back to `paths::normalize`, and `register` canonicalizes again after `create_dir_all`.

subsections.purpose: When the root is reusable and already holds `.ostra/workspace.toml`, `draft` loads that file and marks the draft `adopted`. Rule A2 says the access settings come only from the request and the registry. So before applying the request, `draft` resets these fields: the permission mode to default, YOLO to false, the limits to their defaults, sandbox_mode, tool_enforcement and sandbox_network to None, sandbox_allowed_hosts, sandbox_decoys and sandbox_blocked_ports to empty, and sandbox_loopback to its default.
assumptions: A file that cannot be parsed is not adopted. It produces a `root` issue, and the draft continues from `WorkspaceSettings::seeded(name)` so the other issues are still reported.
The adopted file's projects stay before the request's projects. `request_path` depends on this order.
An adopted file's instructions, MCP servers, routing and projects are kept as written.

subsections.title: Mapping issue paths back to the request
subsections.purpose: `validate_settings` reports issues on settings paths such as `projects[3].key`. `request_path` renumbers them so the console highlights the right request row. Indexes at or above the adopted file's project count shift down by that count. Indexes below it become `root`, because those entries belong to the folder's file.

subsections.title: Registering the workspace
subsections.purpose: `register` repeats the draft and returns `CreateError::Invalid` when it has any issue. Otherwise it creates the root folder, canonicalizes it, and checks the registry again with the canonical path. It then calls `trust::create_workspace` with the `adopted` flag, generates `WorkspaceId::new()`, and calls `RegistryDb::add_workspace`. `validate` returns only the draft's issues, for `POST /api/workspaces/validate`.
assumptions: A `StoreError` from `add_workspace` converts to `CreateError::Failed` through `From<StoreError>`.

sections.title: Open workspace runtime
sections.purpose: `WorkspaceRt` is one open workspace in the server process. It holds the workspace id, the root, the `WorkspaceDb`, the `Engine`, the host, the list of running git operations and the work lock. ostra-server keeps one `Arc<WorkspaceRt>` per registered workspace and passes it to every `/api/workspaces/{ws}` handler. This section covers opening a workspace, reading settings in their two layers, validating and saving settings, applying automatic fixes, and building the `WorkspaceDetail` the console shows.

owns: The `WorkspaceRt` struct and its fields `cloning` and `work`.
Keeping the `projects` table of the workspace db in step with the settings (`sync_projects`).
The browser view of settings, which masks literal MCP values.
Rule W3: every `[[tag]]` in `instructions.all` and `instructions.agents.<agent>` must name a readable artifact.
does_not_own: The file format, approvals and access overlay, which the command-approval and access-settings sections own.
Session execution and recovery, which ostra-engine `Engine` owns. ostra-server calls `engine.recover()` and `engine.subscribe()` after `open`.
Artifact tag parsing, which ostra-core `artifacts::tag_issues` owns.

subsections.title: Opening a workspace
subsections.purpose: `WorkspaceRt::open` runs when ostra-server attaches a registered workspace, at startup or right after creation. It runs the one-time approval migration first. It then seals literal MCP values the file still holds, opens `.ostra/workspace.db`, and stores the workspace id in the db. It asks the host for services, builds the `Engine`, and syncs the projects table.
assumptions: `trust::migrate` and `trust::seal_file_secrets` run before the engine exists, so no program starts from an unmigrated or unsealed file.

subsections.title: Settings layers
subsections.purpose: The runtime reads settings in two forms. `settings()` is what the user edits: the file with the registry's access settings overlaid by `trust::overlay`. `effective_settings()` is what programs start from: `trust::effective`, which also removes command-bearing entries while the file waits for approval. ostra-server's `ServerServices::settings` uses the effective form for the engine.
assumptions: Each call re-reads `workspace.toml` from disk. No settings are cached in `WorkspaceRt`.

subsections.title: Validating and saving settings
subsections.purpose: `validate` runs `validate_settings` and adds Rule W3 tag issues on `instructions.all` and `instructions.agents.<agent>`. `save_settings` refuses any issue and returns the issue list. When there is none, it writes through `trust::save_workspace` and syncs projects. A write error comes back as one issue with an empty path. `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}` calls `save_settings`, and `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/validate` calls `validate`.
assumptions: The body is a complete `WorkspaceSettings`. A field the browser left out is lost on save.
MCP values that the browser only saw as the saved-value marker are preserved by `trust::save_workspace`, not by this function.

subsections.title: Automatic settings fixes
subsections.purpose: `apply_fixes` applies every fix `settings::settings_fixes` finds. Each fix sets `routing.model.byAgent.<key>` to `default` for an agent that has no model route. It does not validate the rest of the settings, because an unrelated problem must not block a fix. It writes only when at least one fix exists, and it returns the count. `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/settings/fix` calls it and returns 500 on a write error.
assumptions: Every fix path starts with `routing.model.byAgent.`. A fix with another prefix is counted but not applied.

subsections.title: Workspace detail
subsections.purpose: `detail` builds the `WorkspaceDetail` that `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}` and most mutating routes return. It combines the project views, the host's harnesses and providers, the validation issues and fixes, the agent infos, and the stack names from ostra-agents. It adds the global permission rules, the pending commands, the sandbox status, the global sandbox network and hosts, the global tool enforcement, and the browser view of the settings. `browser_view` replaces every literal MCP header or env value with `${ostra_secret}`. Such a value can reach the file through a git pull or a hand edit, and only the MCP connection may read it.
assumptions: `ostra_core::mcp::is_literal_value` defines a literal: not blank, not the marker, and containing no `${`.
The sandbox status uses `global.sandbox.for_workspace(&settings.sandbox())`, so the workspace's registry-held mode replaces the global one.

sections.title: Workspace deletion and the work lock
sections.purpose: `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}` removes a workspace from Ostra. Project folders, session artifact folders and per-project `.ostra/` files stay on disk. The `work` lock on `WorkspaceRt` is a `tokio::sync::RwLock<bool>` that is true once the workspace is deleted. Requests that start work hold it shared. Removals take it exclusively, so no work starts between the busy check and the removal.

owns: The busy rules for deleting a workspace (`busy`).
Marking the runtime deleted (`retire`).
Deleting `workspace.toml`, `workspace.db`, `workspace.db-wal` and `workspace.db-shm` (`unregister`).
The `STARTING` message returned when the lock is held.

Taking the lock shared for new work, which ostra-server `start_work` (waits with `read().await`) and `git::claim` (`try_read`) own.

assumptions: ostra-server holds its `workspaces` write lock across `retire` and the map removal, so no request looks up the runtime in between.
A request holding the lock shared checks the bool. `start_work` returns 404 'No workspace' when it is true.
A missing file during `unregister` is not an error. Other delete errors are only logged with `tracing::warn!`.
