sections.title: Command approval for folder files
sections.purpose: `.ostra/workspace.toml` and `<project>/.ostra/project.toml` can arrive with a repository, a `git pull` or an agent's edit. Rule A1 says the programs they name start only after the user approved exactly that content. Approval is a SHA-256 hash of the command-bearing content, stored in the registry. Saves made in Ostra keep an approved file approved, so edits in the UI never ask again. A save cannot approve a file that waits for approval, and an edit outside Ostra changes the hash and waits for approval.

owns: The canonical form and hash of command-bearing workspace content (`workspace_hash`) and of a project's format command (`format_hash`).
Registry keys `trust:workspace:<root>`, `trust:format:<project>`, `trust:migrated:<root>`, `trust:migrated-paths:<root>`.
The effective settings programs run with (`effective`), the pending list (`pending`) and approval (`approve`).
Migration of workspaces registered before approvals existed, and forgetting approvals on delete.
does_not_own: Starting MCP servers, which ostra-server `mcp.rs` owns. It starts them only from `approved_workspace_file` and reports `PENDING_MESSAGE` otherwise.
Running the format command, which ostra-engine does after asking `Services::command_approved`. ostra-server answers that with `format_approved`.
Saving a project's commands, which ostra-server `commands.rs` owns. It calls `saved_format` before and after.

assumptions: Paths reach the trust functions canonical from some callers and as written from others. `canon` canonicalizes and falls back to the path as given.
`serde_json::to_string` of the canonical struct is stable for equal content, because every map in it is a `BTreeMap`.
A file with nothing command-bearing has hash `None`, and `approved` returns true for `None`.
`raw` treats an unreadable workspace file as absent, so `approved_workspace_file` returns None and no program starts.

the project has a code_provider or language servers

Stores approved hashes outside the folder.
Start programs only from approved content.

subsections.title: Effective settings
subsections.purpose: `effective` returns the settings programs run with. It applies `overlay`. While the workspace content is not approved, it disables every MCP server, clears each project's `code_provider` and `language_servers`, clears `permissions.allow`, and drops projects outside the workspace folder. A project outside the folder waits for approval because agents may write in their project, and a folder file that points one at `$HOME` would widen what they can change.
assumptions: `outside` resolves both paths with `paths::resolve(root, _)` and uses `paths::is_inside`.

flowchart TD
  a[File settings] --> o["overlay(registry, root)"]
  o --> h{"workspace_hash is None or equals trust:workspace key?"}
  h -- yes --> r[Return settings unchanged]
  h -- no --> d1[Set every mcp_servers.enabled = false]
  d1 --> d2[Clear code_provider and language_servers]
  d2 --> d3[Clear permissions.allow]

subsections.title: Saving and creating with approvals
subsections.purpose: `save_workspace` writes the file for a save made in Ostra. It first decides `was_approved`: true when no file exists yet or the current file is approved. It then stashes the file's literal MCP values, seals the new settings' values, writes the file without the Rule A2 fields, and stores the access record. Only when `was_approved` is true does it record the new hash. `create_workspace` writes a new workspace. For an adopted file it deletes any stored approval, so nothing in the file runs until approved. Otherwise it records the hash. Both then mark the migrations done.
assumptions: The approval check reads the file before the write, so a file changed outside Ostra since the last save stays waiting after the save.
A registry write error in `record` or `set_access` is logged and not returned.

subsections.title: Pending commands and approval
subsections.purpose: `pending` lists every folder file whose commands wait: the workspace file when its hash is not approved, and each project whose `project.toml` format command is not approved. Each entry carries the file path, the hash the browser must send back, and the items. `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/approve` calls `approve` with the project key (or none for the workspace file) and that hash. `approve` refuses when the content changed since it was shown. The server then drops cached MCP connections for the root with `mcp.forget` and returns the detail.
assumptions: Header and env values never leave the server. Items carry only the keys and the names of `${VAR}` variables, found with `mcp::expand_with`. An OAuth `client_secret_env` name is added to the variables.
Commands are shown shell-quoted. An argument made only of ASCII letters, digits and `-_./=:,@%+` stays bare, and any other argument is wrapped in single quotes.

subsections.title: Format command approval
subsections.purpose: The format command in `project.toml` is the one project command Ostra runs itself. `format_hash` hashes the trimmed command with a `format\0` prefix, and an empty command needs no approval. `format_approved` answers the engine's check through ostra-server `ServerServices::command_approved`. `saved_format` records the new hash after a save made in Ostra, only when the old command was approved.
assumptions: ostra-server passes the format command before and after the save to `saved_format`.

subsections.title: Migration and forgetting
subsections.purpose: `migrate` runs on every open and does its work once per root. `migrate_paths` upgrades an approval recorded before project paths counted. When the stored hash equals the old hash of the current file (computed without the `outside` part), it records the new hash. `migrate` then approves a pre-approval workspace's current file and each project's format command once. It also copies the file's mode, YOLO and other access fields into the registry, and marks both migrations done. `forget` deletes the four trust and access keys, every `mcp_secret` key of the root, and every `mcp_oauth:<root>:` key.
assumptions: `forget` builds the OAuth prefix from `root.display()` and not from the canonical path. It matches only when the registry root is already canonical.
A second `migrate` call does not approve content changed after the first.

sections.title: Registry-held access settings
sections.purpose: Rule A2: the permission mode, YOLO, spend limits, tool enforcement and the sandbox mode, network, allowed hosts, decoys, loopback choice and blocked ports come from the registry, never from a folder file. Otherwise a repository could lift its own budget, turn off its own guards, open its own sandbox, or plant decoys that pause every session. This crate stores these fields as one JSON `Access` record under `workspace_access:<canonical root>` and strips them from every `workspace.toml` it writes.

owns: The `Access` record and its registry key.
Overlaying the record onto file settings (`overlay`).
The list of TOML keys `write_file` removes.
The workspace sandbox view read by ostra-server's MCP code (`sandbox`).
does_not_own: The meaning of each sandbox field, which ostra-sandbox and ostra-core `config` own.
Enforcing permission modes, which ostra-policy and ostra-engine own.

assumptions: A missing or unparseable record reads as `Access::default()`, so a new registry means default mode, YOLO off and no workspace sandbox overrides.
Records saved before limits moved to the registry have no `limits`. They read as `None` and overlay the default limits.

Every Ostra write goes through `save_workspace` or `create_workspace`, so the file never holds these fields after an Ostra save. A hand-edited value in the file is ignored because `overlay` replaces it.

concerns.responsibility: Writes the record from saved settings.
Replaces the file's access fields with the record's.
Keeps access fields out of the folder file.

sections.title: MCP secret sealing
sections.purpose: MCP server header and env values typed as plain text are secrets. On every save made in Ostra, and on open when the file still holds them, this crate moves those values into the registry's encrypted store and writes `${ostra_secret}` in their place. The browser only ever sees the marker. The MCP connection code in ostra-server reads the value back with `mcp_secret` when it finds the marker.

owns: The secret key format and its prefix.
Sealing on save (`seal_mcp_values`), keeping file literals across a browser save (`stash_file_literals`), and sealing on open (`seal_file_secrets`).
Dropping saved values that no setting names.
does_not_own: Encryption, which ostra-store `RegistryDb::secret_set` and `secret_get` own.
Expanding `${VAR}` values from the environment, which ostra-server `mcp.rs` and ostra-core `mcp` own.

assumptions: A literal value is non-blank, is not `${ostra_secret}`, and contains no `${` (`mcp::is_literal_value`).
Sealed secrets live in the same `kv` table that `kv_scan` and `kv_delete` read, so stale secret keys can be found and deleted by prefix.
`mcp_secret:` keys are listed in ostra-store `SECRET_KEYS`. `secret_set` and `secret_get` assert this in debug builds.
A saved value is bound to the server's name and to its target. Pointing the server at another URL or command never sends it the old value.
`seal_file_secrets` saves through `save_workspace`, so sealing does not approve a waiting file.

business_flow.action: Types a token into an MCP server's env or header in settings and saves
business_flow.outcome: The token is stored encrypted in the registry and the file holds `${ostra_secret}`.

business_flow.action: Loads the workspace detail and later saves again with the marker
business_flow.outcome: The marker keeps the stored value, and no plain value reaches the browser.

parts.overview: `web` is the Ostra console: a React 19 single-page app built with Vite. It is the only user interface of Ostra, the engineering pipeline that runs on the user's machine. Users sign in with a one-time link, pick a workspace, start tasks, and follow sessions on a board. They answer gates, watch each agent execution live (activity stream or harness terminal), and read artifacts such as specs, plans and review ledgers. They also browse and edit project files with a Monaco editor backed by the server's code index and language servers, manage git, settings, MCP servers, memory lessons, skills and documentation books, and read cost reports. The console runs no agent itself. Every action is an HTTP call under `/api` to the Ostra server (the `ostra-server` crate), and every live update arrives on one WebSocket at `/ws`. The request and message types under `src/api/gen` are generated from the Rust crates by ts-rs. Below 720 px wide, a separate mobile shell replaces the desktop shell. A mock mode (`VITE_MOCK=1`) swaps the server for local fixtures, for tests and for the homepage screenshot build (`VITE_SHOT=1`). UI components come from the `@ostra/design` package, which lives outside this project.

sections.title: Boot, sign-in, and top-level routing
sections.purpose: This unit starts the app, signs the browser in, and maps URLs to the shell. `boot()` in `src/main.tsx` runs once per page load. First it trades a one-time sign-in token from the URL for a session cookie. Then it registers the service worker and renders `App`, which holds the router and switches to the sign-in screen whenever any request returns 401.

owns: The token exchange at boot and from the sign-in form (`src/auth.ts`).
The switch to the `SignIn` screen after any 401 (`App` subscribes with `onUnauthorized`).
The top-level route table `routes` in `src/App.tsx`, and the redirects `/s/:id`, `/x/:id` and `/w/:ws/projects`.
The workspace list at `/` and the decision to show first-run onboarding (`src/shell/Home.tsx`).
does_not_own: Issuing, expiring and revoking tokens and cookies. The Ostra server does this (see the section How the console works with the other Ostra projects).
The screens inside a workspace. The Desktop workspace shell and Mobile shell sections own them.
Service worker behavior. The Push notifications and app install section owns it.

assumptions: The server sets the session cookie in its answer to `POST /api/auth/exchange`. The client sends only `credentials: same-origin` and never reads the cookie (`src/api/client.ts` `request`).
A sign-in token is a hexadecimal string of 16 or more characters. `tokenFromInput` accepts a bare token only when it matches `/^[0-9a-f]{16,}$/i`.
The `ostra` command prints a URL of the form `http://host/#token=<token>`. `tokenFromHash` reads only the `token` key of the hash.
A token works once. `exchangeTokenFromUrl` records each token in the module-level `exchanged` set, so a remount does not spend it twice.
The server answers `GET /api/onboarding` with `onboarded_at` and a `workspaces` count. `Home` shows the first-run setup only when `onboarded_at` is null and `workspaces` is 0.
`App` creates the router once, in the module variable `router`. The route table cannot change after the first render.

business_flow.outcome: The page loads with the token in the hash.

business_flow.action: Waits until the page is no longer prerendering, removes the hash from the address bar, and posts the token to the server.
business_flow.outcome: The browser holds a session cookie, or `App` receives the exchange error text.

business_flow.action: Renders the router and loads the requested route.
business_flow.outcome: The workspace list, onboarding, or a workspace shell shows.

business_flow.action: Answers any later request with 401 when the cookie is missing or revoked.
business_flow.outcome: `App` replaces the router with the `SignIn` screen.

business_flow.action: Pastes a new sign-in link or a bare token into the sign-in form.
business_flow.outcome: After a successful exchange the page reloads at `/`.

sections.title: HTTP API client
sections.purpose: `httpApi` in `src/api/client.ts` is the one typed client for every REST endpoint of the Ostra server. Every screen calls it through `api` from `src/api/index.ts`. In mock mode, `api` is the fixture implementation `mockApi`, which has the same `Api` type. The client turns a failed response into an `HttpError` that carries the server's validation issues, so forms can place each issue on its field.

owns: The mapping from each client function to its HTTP method and path.
The `HttpError` class and the 401 listener set (`onUnauthorized`).
Upload helpers: `uploadFile` streams a `File` as `application/octet-stream`, and `rawPost` posts a `Blob`.
does_not_own: Request validation and route handling. The `ostra-server` crate owns them.
The shape of each request and response type. These are generated from Rust by ts-rs into `src/api/gen` and must not be edited by hand.
Retry logic. No client function retries. Callers show the error, and `useAsync` reloads after a socket reconnect.

assumptions: The server sends error bodies as JSON `{ error: string, issues?: ValidationIssue[] }`. `request` falls back to `<status> <statusText>` when the body is not JSON.
A 204 answer, or an empty body, means no value. `request` returns `undefined` in both cases.
All paths are same-origin. In development, the Vite proxy forwards `/api` to the server (see the Mock mode, shot mode, build, and tests section).
Path parameters are passed through `encodeURIComponent`. `q()` drops query parameters that are `undefined`, `null` or the empty string.

sections.title: WebSocket manager
sections.purpose: `SocketManager` in `src/api/socket.ts` keeps one reconnecting WebSocket to `/ws` that every screen shares. It routes JSON server messages to reference-counted channels. It delivers binary terminal frames to terminal views, and it runs request and reply hint calls for the code editor. `socket()` creates the shared instance on first use and starts it.

owns: The connection lifecycle, the reconnect backoff, and the `SocketState` values `connecting`, `open` and `closed`.
Channel routing (`channelsFor`) and the reference counts on subscriptions.
The PTY frame decoding and the per-execution terminal handlers.
The hint sequence numbers, timeouts and replacement.
does_not_own: What screens do with messages. The Shared live data section and each screen own that.
Server-side channel authorization. The server owns it.

assumptions: The server accepts `{type: "subscribe", channel}` and `{type: "unsubscribe", channel}` for the channels `session:<id>`, `execution:<id>`, `term:<execution>`, `workspace:<id>` and `home` (from the doc comment on the generated `ClientMsg`).
Binary frames follow this layout: byte 0 is the execution id length n, then n bytes of UTF-8 id, then terminal bytes. `decodePtyFrame` returns null for a shorter frame.
The server answers each hint with the same numeric `id` in `code_completion`, `code_signature_help` or `code_navigation`.
The server stops an older hint when a newer one of the same type arrives, so the client resolves the older promise to null right away.
`send` drops a message while the socket is not open. Subscriptions are safe because `onopen` resubscribes every channel. `term_input` and `term_resize` typed while offline are lost.

business_flow.action: Subscribes to a channel with a handler.
business_flow.outcome: The first handler of a channel sends `subscribe`, and later handlers only join the local set.

business_flow.action: Sends a JSON message.
business_flow.outcome: `dispatch` calls the `onAny` listeners, then the handlers of each channel that `channelsFor` names.

business_flow.action: Closes the socket.
business_flow.outcome: State becomes `closed`, open hints resolve to null, and a reconnect is scheduled after min(10000, 500 x 2^attempts) ms.

business_flow.action: Reopens.
business_flow.outcome: Every channel is resubscribed and reconnect listeners fire, so stores refetch their REST snapshots.

sections.purpose: This unit gives any number of components the same live copy of a server resource, fetched once, with one socket subscription per key. `SharedStore` in `src/lib/store.ts` holds the mechanism. `src/lib/live.ts` defines the stores and hooks that the shell and the screens read: the sessions tree, session summaries, workspace activity, project file indexes, project changes, the workspace list, the socket state and search. The desktop `Shell` draws the title bar, the left dock, the editor tab strip, the center pane, the quick-question dock and the status bar. Each `turn` delta lists the `call_ids` of that model response, and its cost is shared evenly among those calls.
The server answers terminal queries itself. A browser reply would reach the harness as typed input, so the terminal mutes all query replies.

sections.purpose: `ProjectScreen` (resource `project:<key>`) shows one project. The header shows the init status, the git branch, a Pull button and Browse files. sections.title: File view and code editor
sections.purpose: `FileScreen` (resource `file:<key>:<path>`) shows a project file in one Monaco editor. It is read-only until the pencil starts an edit. The screen also offers a Rendered view for Markdown and a Changes view when a session changed the file. Beside the editor, a code pane shows the file's outline, the usages of a clicked name and the file's dependencies. The editor gets completions, signature help and supertype and implementation jumps over the socket. Definitions and usages come over REST. `DependencyFileScreen` shows a dependency file read-only.

owns: The edit state machine: draft, saved text, base hash, conflict, discard confirmation.
The mapping of server completion, signature and navigation replies into Monaco structures.
The landing rule of a jump: go to one place, pick from a list, or show a note.
does_not_own: Language servers and the code index. The server owns them.
File writes. The server writes the file and checks the hash.

assumptions: `ProjectFile.hash` is null when the file is not UTF-8 or larger than the server's read limit (`truncated`). Such files cannot be edited.
`PUT .../file` refuses a save with 409 and an issue at path `base_hash` when the file changed since the hash the edit started from.
The server sends `project_fs_changed` with paths after any change on disk, so the view reloads the file, diff and code data.
Ostra columns are 0-based and Monaco columns are 1-based. The providers convert with `toRange` and `column - 1`.
`isSymbolClass` mirrors `TokenClass::is_symbol` on the server.
Monaco is bundled locally with one editor worker, because the app runs on localhost and must not fetch code from a CDN.

sections.title: Workspace settings
sections.purpose: `SettingsScreen` (resource `ws:settings`) edits `.ostra/workspace.toml` through a form with ten tabs. The form checks itself as the user edits, and the server validates too. Save writes the whole settings object. The screen also approves folder-file commands that changed outside Ostra, and manages MCP server connections, git credentials, sign-in sessions and shortcuts. It can delete the workspace.

owns: The form model `SettingsForm` and its conversions `toForm` and `fromForm`.
Client-side checks for model routes, limits and MCP rows, and the mapping of issues to fields and tabs.
The `#setting:<dotted key>` deep link, which opens the field's tab and rings it.
does_not_own: The settings schema and its server validation. The server and the config crate own them.
MCP connections and OAuth. The server owns them.

assumptions: `PATCH /api/workspaces/:ws` accepts the full `WorkspaceSettings` and returns the new `WorkspaceDetail`. A 422 carries issues whose `path` is a dotted settings key such as `routing.model.byAgent.implementer`.
The form has no fields for `code_provider` and `language_servers`. `fromForm` copies them from the saved project with the same key, or the same path after a rename.
`native` routing is written as an absent `routing.executor.byAgent` entry.
`GET .../mcp` connects to every saved server, so it can take as long as the slowest server takes to start.
A browser blocks a tab opened after an `await`, so the MCP sign-in opens the tab before requesting the authorization URL.

business_flow.action: Changes `workspace.toml` on disk.

business_flow.outcome: `approveCommands` posts the project and hash, and the commands may run.

business_flow.action: Signs in to an MCP server.
business_flow.outcome: A tab opens the authorization URL, and the status is polled every 2 s for up to 120 s.

sections.title: Setup wizard, workspace creation, and adding projects
sections.purpose: The setup guide creates a workspace in six steps: welcome, a machine check (provider keys and harness CLIs), name and folder, projects, defaults, and review. It runs full screen on first run (`Onboarding`), as the New workspace dialog, and as `MWizard` on phones. `AddProjectDialog` imports an existing folder or clones a repository into an existing workspace.

owns: Wizard step order, the per-step Continue rule, the request body and the `workspace.toml` preview.

does_not_own: Writing `workspace.toml`, the database and the registry. The server owns them.
Installing or logging in harnesses. The server's harness setup terminal owns it.

assumptions: Project keys use lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter or digit, the same rule as the server (`isProjectKey`).
The clone endpoint needs an existing workspace, so clones run one at a time after `createWorkspace` succeeds. A failed clone leaves the workspace in place.
A folder path is chosen when it is absolute (or starts with `~/`) and does not end in a separator. The workspace folder may not exist yet, because the server creates it.
The server expands nothing. The wizard replaces a leading `~` with the home folder from `fsBrowse({path: "~"})` before sending paths.
A harness preset is offered only for harnesses that are installed and logged in (`presetsFor`).

sections.title: Mock mode, shot mode, build, and tests
sections.purpose: The console builds with Vite and tests with Vitest in jsdom. With `VITE_MOCK=1` (`vite --mode mock`, and always in tests), fixtures stand in for the server and the socket. With `VITE_SHOT=1` (`--mode shot`), the build is the console screenshot embedded on the Ostra homepage. It uses a memory router and a page bridge, and it carries its Content Security Policy in the page, because a static host serves it.

owns: The Vite config: proxy, chunk groups and the shot CSP plugin.
The mock API and mock socket behavior.
The shot bridge messages.
does_not_own: The production CSP header. `crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs` sends it (per the comment in `vite.config.ts`).
Serving the built files. The server does it.

assumptions: The development server listens on port 5173. It proxies `/api` and `/mcp/oauth` to `OSTRA_DEV_SERVER`, default `http://127.0.0.1:7878`, and `/ws` to the same host over `ws:`.
Vite compares paths as strings. The config resolves the real path of the project folder, so a miscased Windows path does not load two copies of React.
The shot build always runs with mock mode, and it runs in a same-origin iframe.
Mock fixtures load with a dynamic import, so they stay out of the production bundle.

sections.title: Safe rendering of agent-written content
sections.purpose: Agents write most of what the console shows: Markdown artifacts, answers, terminal output and books. The console treats all of it as untrusted. This section gathers the rules that keep such content from injecting markup, loading remote resources, or typing into a harness.

owns: The Markdown URL transform and the dropping of images.
The terminal query muting and the link confirmation.

sections.title: How the console works with the other Ostra projects
sections.purpose: The console is the browser side of Ostra. It holds no pipeline logic and runs no agents. It calls the Ostra server (the `ostra-server` crate) over HTTP and one WebSocket, and renders what the engine records. This section lists each point where `web` depends on another project, so a change there can be checked against the console.

owns: The browser UI and the user-side validation that mirrors engine rules.
Browser-only state: tabs and prefs (also mirrored to the server), panel widths, shortcuts, theme, and the EARS note flag.
does_not_own: Workspaces, sessions, gates, executions, artifacts, git, the code index, memory, skills and books. The server and the Rust crates own all of them.
Agent prompts and assets. The `assets` project owns them.

assumptions: The types under `src/api/gen` are generated from the Rust crates by ts-rs (each file says "Do not edit this file manually"). A Rust type change requires regenerating these files, and TypeScript then flags every screen that breaks.

Several client tables mirror engine rules by hand and are not generated: `ANSWER_KIND` mirrors `runner::validate_answer`, `HARNESS_AGENTS` mirrors `RoutingPreset::HARNESS_AGENTS`, and `isSymbolClass` mirrors `TokenClass::is_symbol`. A change on the Rust side needs the same change here.
The server serves the built `dist` folder and sends the Content Security Policy header in production (`crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`, per `vite.config.ts`).
UI components, icons, the palette, the file tree, the docs renderer and CSS come from the `@ostra/design` package, which is outside this project.

business_flow.action: Acts in the console.
business_flow.outcome: The console calls a REST endpoint on the server.

business_flow.action: Hands the request to the engine or a service crate.
business_flow.outcome: State changes and events are recorded.

business_flow.action: Pushes messages on `/ws` to subscribed channels.
business_flow.outcome: Stores and screens update without polling, except for the git status poll.

The agent that looks at a failed init step of a created project and suggests a retry or escalates.
The RFC 8188 content coding: a header with salt, record size and key id, followed by AES-128-GCM encrypted records.
One of the 14 leaf roles Ostra runs, such as explore or implementer, each ending its run with a submit tool call.
The `agent.toml` file that sets one agent's description, default tier, timeout, capabilities, and effort.

Context the user added to a running session: text, tagged files, or uploads.

A wrapper for a provider credential that never prints its value. It is flagged as a bearer token or as an API key.

A registry entry that holds the hash of folder-file content the user approved. The content's programs start only while the entry matches.

A file a session produces or receives, such as research, a spec, a plan, a report, a review ledger or an upload.

A 16-byte random value the browser creates with a subscription, used as the HKDF salt for the input keying material.
The RFC 8414 or OpenID discovery document that lists an issuer's authorization, token and registration endpoints.
A review finding whose rule ID the project marks auto-fixable and whose Fix text the engine applies itself.

The imperative sentence of an evidence row that the implementer must obey, copied verbatim onto plan steps.

A `SEC-BLOCK-*` finding from the mandatory security scan; never auto-fixable and never waived.
A plan step whose file has no execution path of its own, such as a DTO, enum, or registration file.
The documentation book of a workspace, stored under a book id with a `book.json`.
One project's overview and sections inside a book.
A Unix socket on which the server answers only `/internal/*`, used by sandboxes with their own network.

The bounded output buffer that keeps the first and last 128 KiB of a shell command's output.

Format, the tests-and-docs gate, tests, and documentation after the implementation is accepted.

The ostra-engine value (title, body, url, tag) that asks the server to notify the user.

The object that holds the VAPID keys, the contact subject and an HTTP client, and sends push messages.

Replacing a file's access fields with the values from the access record.
The browser's P-256 public key, as a 65-byte uncompressed point in URL-safe base64, used for ECDH in message encryption.
Two agents that alternate on one artifact, such as generate-spec and fact-check or implementer and code-reviewer.

The `Providers` struct that holds one provider per configured name and resolves `provider:model` routes.
The ostra-core record of one provider's key presence, key source, and base URL that the console shows.
A pseudo-terminal; the harness CLI runs in one so its terminal UI works and the browser can show it.
A binary WebSocket message that holds a length byte, an execution id and raw terminal bytes.
The WebFetch DNS resolver that drops private addresses unless the host is a private host.
The `ExecPurpose` value saying what an execution does, such as Implement or Review.
A string naming one work loop, review loop, or stage, used to resume or wake the right run.
The broadcast channel for messages the server itself originates, each tagged with the socket channels it goes to.
The vendor server (for example `fcm.googleapis.com`) that accepts POST requests at a subscription endpoint and forwards them to the browser.
The endpoint URL and the `p256dh` and `auth` keys that a browser creates when it subscribes to push.
The temporary `ostra-pwd-<uuid>` file a shell writes its final directory to, so the next call starts there.
An open question with a tag of 12 characters or fewer, 2 to 4 options, and one recommended option.
A read-only answer from the `quick-answer` agent in the side dock, outside the pipeline.
The folded paths of every file the model has read in the execution; Write and Edit require an existing file to be in it.
A fully understood command that runs without asking in every mode, per `is_read_only`.
The value before `.`, `->` or `::` in a member mention, whose type decides which member is meant.
A pass after at least 3 consecutive failures with a known signature. It waits in `Streak.pending` for a lesson.
The category Anthropic gives in `stop_details.category` when a model refuses.
An Anthropic feature, requested with `fallbacks: "default"`, that re-runs a declined request on a fallback model.
The process-wide `RegistryDb` from ostra-store that stores registered workspaces, approvals, access records and encrypted secrets.
An existing test group that covers the changed code and is re-run unchanged.
The Markdown that `augment` appends below the spawn block with project facts, instruction files, artifacts, books, and instructions.
The handling of a STUCK work pass: targeted research, a rerun with a fact, or a gate to the user.
The typed document the explore agent writes at `ostra-research-{run-stamp}-{topic-slug}.md`.
A string such as `session:<id>` or `file:<key>:<path>` that names anything the console can open in a tab and maps one to one to a URL.
The `resource` parameter (RFC 8707) sent in authorization and token requests, which names the MCP server the token is for.
A resume whose `from` execution id equals the running execution's id, so only the new turn is recorded (Rule P2).
Marking a WorkspaceRt deleted after checking that no session, execution or git operation runs.
The backoff settings for retrying failed provider calls before output starts.
A Markdown file named `ostra-review-ledger*.md` whose tables list the review findings per iteration.
The repeated fix-and-review cycle for one phase's code or one phase's tests, capped by iteration count.
The standard for encrypting Web Push messages with ECDH, HKDF and aes128gcm.
The canonical directories and files of one execution, used to classify paths.
An agent name or judge, the keys that workspace model routing must cover.
A model written as `provider:model`, such as `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5`, that `for_model` splits.
A folder file's programs start only while its command-bearing content is approved.
The permission mode, YOLO, spend limits, tool enforcement and sandbox settings come from the registry, never from a folder file.
A run that asks another subagent waits with its process alive, and Ostra types the answer into its terminal.
A run woken with a question must reply with the reply tool before it submits.
A label such as O5, B5, or D3 that code comments use to cite a rule of Ostra's design.
A ProjectCreate call puts its project in a folder under the workspace root, checked the way the Add project dialog checks it.
A tag in an instruction must name an artifact every agent can read. `WorkspaceRt::validate` checks it.
Artifacts and books are moved or deleted only while no session is active and no execution runs.
The layer (`guard` or `permission`) and rule name that produced a decision. The Activity view shows it. Defined in ostra-core.
A `YYYYMMDD-HHmmss` string computed once per run and used in research, spec, and plan file names.
An ostra-core value saying whether a run continues, waits for a message, or finishes after a coordination call.
The `Engine` and `Inner` types that append events and perform steps.
A file such as `.mcp.json` or a CI workflow that makes a tool run a program later. A write to one always gets the mode's default answer.
A wrapped program with its arguments, environment, removals, working dir, and `Members`.
The string `${ostra_secret}` that stands in the file and in the browser for an MCP value sealed in the registry.
The ostra-core record of a base URL, API key, and bearer token entered in the browser and stored by the server.
The Sandbox Profile Language that Seatbelt policies are written in, where the last matching rule applies.
A fresh owner-only host dir mounted at the sandbox's `/tmp` under bubblewrap or named by `TMPDIR` under Seatbelt.
The per-execution directory used as /tmp under bubblewrap or TMPDIR under Seatbelt, removed when the run ends.
The test provider that returns queued responses or a responder's answers.
The environment variable names removed from every child process, plus every inherited `OSTRA_*` variable.
A stored credential in the form `enc:v1:` plus base64 of nonce and ciphertext.
The AES-256-GCM helper that encrypts and decrypts one registry credential under the master key.
The macOS sandbox, driven through `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` with an SBPL policy.
A registry kv key listed in `SECRET_KEYS`, whose value is a credential.
Ostra's data dir except its assets, the master key file, home credential dirs, workspace databases, /proc process entries, and harness state dirs.
The walker filter that hides credential stores and Ostra's data directory, except its assets, from Grep and Glob.
The file `ostra-security-block.json` the code reviewer overwrites every pass with the current BLOCKER state.
The result of one delivery: `Delivered`, `Gone` or `Failed`.
Tools the provider runs on its own servers: web search on both providers and web fetch on Anthropic only.
One run of the pipeline for one user request, or one project initialization, with its stages, gates, executions and artifacts.
A rule added by an "always in this workspace" answer and kept in `State.session_allow` for the rest of the execution.
`ostra-session-context.md`, the session summary a revision reads instead of a conversation.
The per-session, per-project scratch directory where agents read and write artifacts.
The append-only list of SessionEvent values whose fold is a session's state.
The `mcp-session-id` header value a streamable HTTP server assigns. The client sends it back on every later request.
An agent that writes only in its session dir, session root, and OS temp, per `AgentName::is_session_only` in ostra-core.
A change Ostra can apply on its own. Today the only one sets `routing.model.byAgent.<key>` to `default` for an agent with no model route.
A PTY that runs a harness installer or login for the browser, with id `setup_<harness>_<action>`.
State both transports share with the client: the `alive` flag and the `tools_changed` flag.
A per-key cache that gives all readers one fetch and one socket subscription, reloads after each reconnect, and keeps its data after the last reader leaves.
A mock build (`VITE_SHOT=1`) that runs the console in an iframe on the Ostra homepage, driven by postMessage.
An execution with no session id, grouped under `side-panel` in cost reports.
A stored record of one browser's session cookie, listed and revoked by id `si_<hex>`.
A one-time 256-bit value in a sign-in URL fragment, valid 15 minutes, exchanged once for a session cookie.
A token that is neither a comment nor a later line of a multi-line string or comment; the outline analysis walks only these.
One command name with its arguments, assignments, redirects, and heredoc body, as parsed by the shell parser.
A Markdown instruction file for agents, either Ostra's own (`ostra`) or from a harness folder (`harness`).
A callback that resolves an embedded skill name to its path and content.
One unit of parallel scouting in the initializer, at most 12 per project.
One place under the workspace's parallel execution limit.
The `Label: value` parameter block rendered for an agent's first message.
The single requirements document generate-spec writes at `ostra-spec-{run-stamp}-{topic-slug}.md`.
A listener that copies every connection to one fixed target, such as the hook bridge.
Server-sent events, the streaming HTTP format both providers answer in, decoded by `sse::json_events`.
A `text/event-stream` response body made of events, each with a `data` line. MCP servers use it to send several messages in one answer.
A Markdown file under `assets/refs/` headed `# Stack Reference:` that tells the initializer's scout what to look for in one stack.
One step of the pipeline, such as classify, explore, spec or implement, shown as a card in a lane.
One node type of the pipeline or init flow, placed on one lane.
The Stakes judge's rating (low, medium, high); low skips the plan stage.
A pool entry whose server failed to start or died at least 30 seconds after it began, so the next request starts it again.
A file's size and modification time, compared to decide whether the file must be analyzed again.
A random value placed in the authorization URL and returned in the redirect, used to find the pending sign-in.
The transport that runs the server as a child process and exchanges one JSON message per line over stdin and stdout.
One action the planner asks the runner to perform, such as a spawn, a judge call, or a gate.
Why a model turn ended: end of turn, tool use, token limit, paused server tool loop, refusal, or another reason.
The single error enum returned by every public method of the crate.
A harness-specific instruction text in `[strategies.*]` of `tool-mapping.toml`, added to the tool vocabulary.
The transport that POSTs each message to a URL and reads the reply as JSON or as a server-sent event stream.
A progress event a provider sends to the caller's event sink while a response streams.
A judge answer obtained by forcing a call to the `decide` tool and returning its input.
A result status carrying a verbatim diagnostic and a specific need after an agent hits its retry ceiling.
One agent conversation, identified by its first execution's ID.
The execution ID of a conversation's first run, used to ask that subagent a question.
The agent's `submit_<agent>` tool call, whose input is the structured result the engine reads.
The MCP tool `submit_<agent>` whose first valid call is the execution's result.
A recorded fact that one type names another as its supertype, from `extends`, `implements`, `:`, `impl Trait for Type` and similar forms.
A mention meaning that the tokens settled through a declared type or qualifier, as opposed to a guess from graph resolution.
A route from an entry point or a changed contract through several parts of the system to the changed code, numbered S1, S2.
A minijinja placeholder such as `{{tool_read}}` or `{{assets_dir}}` that rendering replaces with a tool name or path.
The owner-only on-disk copy of a harness terminal's bytes, bounded to about 2 MiB, used to replay ended runs.
A per-phase tag, Required or Skip, deciding which phases a requested test run covers.
A model class, fast, balanced, advanced, or frontier, that each executor's tier table maps to a concrete model.
The trait the HTTP transport calls to get a bearer token and to get a replacement after a refusal.
The `enforce_tool_calls` setting, stored as `Roots.strict`. When it is off, write scope, the report path, and self-protection do not apply.
A template placeholder such as `{{tool_read}}` in an asset that rendering replaces with the executor's tool name.
The `## Tool vocabulary` section generated at the top of a harness prompt that maps each capability to the harness's tool.
A tool name with its JSON input, defined in ostra-core's policy module.
The per-execution tool state: configuration, shell working directory, read set, HTTP client, private hosts, scrub list, and optional sandbox.
The fixed inputs of one execution's tools, including paths, the agent, and the service handles.
A tool as listed by a server: name, description, input schema, and read-only flag.
The result of one tool call: text, error flag, exit code, duration, optional diff, and run-end signal.
A record of files one successful write tool call changed, used for cache invalidation and live updates.
The session route. Light builds from the research. Full writes a spec and a plan, each approved by the user, before building.
An incremental reader of a harness session file that totals usage and finds the last assistant message.
The internal trait that delivers messages to a server and returns the response with a given id.
Host rules the user chose, which may resolve to any address, including private ones.
The Rust library that generates the TypeScript types in `src/api/gen` from the server's Rust types.
A research, spec, plan, or phase document stored as JSON and rendered to Markdown by Ostra.
The console layout per workspace, stored as JSON under the workspace db meta key `ui_state`.
The plugin Ostra replaces; this crate ports its `definition.json`, `subagent-parameters.json`, and `context-brief.js`.
A project folder that holds both `.ultracode/INVENTORY.md` and `.ultracode/repo-profile.json`.
A package folder: the nearest folder holding a manifest such as Cargo.toml or package.json, or the project top when none does.
A shell statement outside the command model, such as a standalone assignment, export, a `[[ ]]` test with expansions, a for loop, or a function. It sets `Parsed.modelled` to false.
A write whose path is only known when the shell runs, such as one that uses a variable, a substitution, a glob, `~user`, or a relative path after a dynamic cd.
The `[sandbox] upstream_proxy` HTTP proxy through which the egress proxy reaches public destinations.
An answer part kept for later stages (implement, tests, docs), with an ID N1, N2, and so on.
The SQLite pragma the store uses as the count of applied migrations.
Voluntary Application Server Identification (RFC 8292): the application server signs a JWT with its P-256 key so the push service can identify the sender.
The trait or interface named by the impl block that encloses a method, such as `Display` for `fmt` in `impl Display for Point`.
The browser standard that lets a server send a message to a browser through the browser vendor's push service, even when no page is open.
The `work: tokio::sync::RwLock<bool>` on WorkspaceRt, held shared while starting work and exclusively while removing a project or the workspace. It is true once deleted.
The cycle of work passes and reviews for one phase's implementation or tests.
A folder with `.ostra/workspace.toml` that groups projects and their settings, such as routing, permissions, memory and instructions.
A file the user keeps for every session of a workspace, visible in `.ostra/artifacts/` or hidden in the data dir.
Files the user placed in the workspace artifacts dir. Agents read them and never write them (Rule W1).
The documentation books dir. Only the engine writes it, from the docs stage's submit calls (Rule B5).
The SQLite file `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db` that holds one workspace's event log and materialized tables.
The hex SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the command-bearing content, or None when there is none.
The trait a process implements to give a workspace its registry, global config, environment, provider and harness status, and engine services.
The in-process runtime of one open workspace: id, root, workspace db, engine, host, running git operations and the work lock.
A path a shell command would create, overwrite, move, or delete.
The header of a 401 or 403 answer that can name `resource_metadata` and `scope` for the sign-in.
A session mode in which Ostra answers gates and permission asks itself and records each decision, while guards, deny rules and budgets still apply.
